author: Huyam Salih and Obai Khalifa
title: Africa cannot build a stronger agrifood economy while the livestock sector loses $4 billion a year
content:
Across Africa, the livestock sector supports more than 350 million people. Livestock is much more than an agricultural commodity. For millions of families, cattle, sheep, goats, poultry, and other animals are sources of food and income. They are also productive assets that support trade, processing, services, employment and rural wealth creation. Despite its centrality to Africa’s wider agrifood economy, the systems that govern and influence the continent’s livestock sector remain among the most undercapitalised parts of African agriculture. Africa loses an estimated USD 4 billion every year due to unrealised livestock potential.


Too often, livestock farmers, particularly pastoralists and small-scale producers, are seen through the lens of subsistence and poverty. Investors see fragmented markets, climate exposure and informal production systems and conclude that the risks are too high. The challenge is therefore not only a shortage of capital, but an investability gap: fragmented supply, weak market information, uncertain offtake, and policy and regulatory uncertainty can make otherwise viable opportunities difficult to assess and finance.


Many countries also continue to face widespread circulation of substandard and falsified veterinary products, varying levels of regulatory capacity, high dependence on imported medicines and the escalating threat of antimicrobial resistance.


Public investment is central to addressing these challenges, but spending has often lagged behind government pledges. Under the 2003

Maputo Declaration on Agriculture and Food Security

, African governments pledged to allocate at least 10% of national budgets to agriculture and rural development. More than two decades later, most countries have fallen short. The persistent gap highlights the challenge governments face in financing the services and infrastructure needed to attract and sustain private investment.


Africa’s annual food import bill was estimated at around US

$70 billion

 in 2025, despite its wealth in arable land and livestock. Although this figure covers far more than livestock products, it underscores the scale of food demand that African producers could be better equipped to serve. Meeting more of that demand requires investment not only in production, but also in getting food reliably and competitively to market. The opportunity is not simply to import substitution; it is to build competitive African value chains capable of serving regional demand and other higher-value markets.


The

African Union–Inter-African Bureau for Animal Resources

 (AU-IBAR) is working to address these gaps by bringing together governments, regulators and investors to connect fragmented livestock markets. Its approach seeks to strengthen regional trade while improving farmers’ livelihoods and supporting rural economies.


Through the Integrated Regional Livestock Value Chain Transformation Programme (IRLVC), AU-IBAR links priority livestock value chains with regional trade corridors, market access and investment. The programme focuses on making cross-border trade more workable through coordinated standards and policies, while creating opportunities for private-sector participation and financing. Alongside this, the Africa Pastoral Markets Development (APMD) Platform strengthens pastoralists’ market participation and enterprise resilience and supports commercially viable investment pathways that could help unlock up to US$500 million in pastoral investment opportunities, while improving consumers’ access to livestock products.


Stronger regional markets could attract investment in processing, transport, feed and animal health services, supporting businesses and jobs across rural economies. Harmonised standards, more efficient trade corridors and coordinated disease control would lower barriers to trade and make markets more predictable for producers and investors. In economic terms, these are forms of market infrastructure: they lower transaction costs, reduce uncertainty and improve the risk-return proposition for investment. Ultimately, success should be measured not only in investment flows or trade volumes, but in better returns for farmers and more secure livelihoods for pastoral communities.


Across East Africa, countries are demonstrating what is possible with the right investment. Ethiopia, home to one of the world’s largest livestock populations, is

addressing gaps

 in feed, productivity, processing and markets through …

author: Mada Masr
title: Lina Attalah in custody after court issues LE3 mn fine, orders Mada Masr’s closure
content:
Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah was fined LE3 million by the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, which convicted her on charges of managing an unlicensed website, issuing an order for the website’s closure. Attalah was taken into custody after the issue of the ruling.


Tuesday’s session at the ninth circuit of the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, presided over by judge Mohamed Mubarak, was temporarily suspended for deliberations after Attalah’s defense counsel requested time to review the case file.


After the court returned from deliberations, the judge ordered the courtroom cleared of everyone except Attalah and her defense counsel, the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights’ executive director Hossam Bahgat, who was also present, told Mada Masr. The room then filled with plainclothes officers and guards, with a National Security Agency officer in attendance, he added.


The presiding judge and a Supreme State Security Prosecution representative returned to the session and the judge announced that the court has decided to stand by its rejection of all the procedural arguments presented by the defense, including requests to bring in any documentation or hear any witnesses.


The judge then asked the defense team to present its plea. The counsel insisted that it would not submit a plea as long as its requests were unanswered by the court.


The judge then abruptly asked for a lawyer unknown to any member of the defense counsel to be brought in, “in a move that astonished all those present,” said Bahgat, and announced that the court decided to appoint a lawyer for Attalah.


At that point, all members of the defense counsel cried out to reject the court’s appointment of a lawyer when the eight chosen lawyers were present. Attalah herself spoke to say she did not accept the court-appointed lawyer acting on her behalf, an objection the judge refused to have recorded in the session’s minutes.


“In an even more shocking move,” said Bahgat, the judge himself began to log down the requests of the court-appointed lawyer, without the lawyer having said a word. The judge then read out the conviction amid shouts and protests from the defense counsel.


The judge sentenced Attalah to the maximum possible penalty: a LE3 million fine, the closure of Mada Masr’s website and the confiscation of its property.


Security personnel then surrounded Attalah, lifted her off the ground and took her out of the courtroom, where she remains in custody in the courthouse.

The post

Lina Attalah in custody after court issues LE3 mn fine, orders Mada Masr’s closure

 first appeared on

Mada Masr

author: Abahlali_3
title: Worsening Violence as the Election Comes Closer
content:
25 October 2026 Abahlali baseMjondolo Press Statement

Worsening Violence as the Election Comes Closer

Our country is one of the most violent in the world, worse than some war zones. The rate of violence against women and the rate of murders committed by young men against other young men are among the highest in the world. There is violence in the home and in communities, violence from ordinary people, politicians, criminals and the armed forces in service of the state and the rich.

Our country and its people have been deeply damaged by generations of oppression, which has continued into the present for many people, especially the poor. The ANC has never pursued a project of healing, a project of restoring the humanity of our people and our society. They have just made themselves rich, leaving most of us poor and living in a broken society, a broken society in which the poor continue to be ruled with violence.

Things are getting worse. In KwaZulu-Natal armed mobs now parade through the streets accompanied by the police. People have been driven from their homes and livelihoods, assaulted and killed. The rise of the right, including violent fascist organisations, is a matter of grave concern for our movement and all people of good conscience.

As the election approaches, violence is worsening. So far 43 people have been killed, including people from the ANC, IFP and MKP. The political killings that are taking place are another grave concern for our movement. In a free, democratic country everyone should be free to campaign for election without fear. We know very well that the killing will not be confined to politicians. As killing becomes more common, more and more activists will be targeted in the years ahead.

Right now, the atmosphere in Durban is particularly threatening. Political intolerance has reached a fever pitch. The danger can be felt everywhere. Many politicians and parties have been complicit, and none have built a project in support of healing and a just peace. People are being assaulted and sometimes beaten to death in the streets. The political assassinations continue and will continue after the election as the politicians fight for power and money.

While the situation is at its worst in Durban and KwaZulu-Natal, it is moving into other parts of the country. ANC people have been killed in Katlehong.

People are being encouraged to hate, attack and kill as the election comes closer. But elections come and go. Every time there is an election, politicians come into our communities with promises, food and t-shirts and then they leave. We don’t see them until the next election comes. To them we are voting fodder, people who can be lied to and bribed, and not citizens of a democracy, or even just full human beings.

We have had elections for more than thirty years and the poor remain poor and without land, water, sanitation, electricity and housing. Our dignity continues to be vandalised by the state and the organised power of the rich. We continue to live with our suffering. This election will not resolve any of the problems that we face, and yet we are being encouraged to hate, attack and kill, and to support politicians and parties that are encouraging hate and are involved in political violence.

We cannot now glorify elections as the only thing that can resolve our problems and ensure that our dignity as human beings is recognised. Elections can be important, but all our advances as a movement and as a class have come from building our own power, popular democratic power. We must never allow politicians to divide us. We must never be divided by people who only come to our communities to lie to us when they seek power and then leave us poor and oppressed.

After careful discussions, we have agreed to encourage our members, and others who look to our movement for political direction, to vote according to their conscience if they wish to vote, but not to support those who have disappointed and betrayed them in the past, and who have made the poor suffer for more than thirty years. They must not vote for people who are trying to divide the poor with ethnic politics and political intolerance, for the corrupt who steal from the poor or for people who are xenophobic. They must not vote for any politicians or parties that encourage hate and violence.

When this election has passed, the oppressed will remain oppressed, there will be greater political intolerance and our society will be even more violent …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Morocco’s First Woman Prime Minister and the Terms of Freedom
content:
Something changes when a woman occupies an office men have treated as their natural inheritance. Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri’s

appointment

 on 29 September 2026 makes that change visible in Morocco. For women whose competence is routinely scrutinised, the pleasure is neither naïve nor trivial.


But the woman forming a government and the woman labouring in the fields, raising children without pay and denied an equal share of her inheritance encounter power differently. Representation changes who governs; emancipation changes what all women have the power to do. That distinction shifts our attention from PM Mansouri’s gender to the politics of the centre-right

 Party of Authenticity and Modernity (PAM

)

, which she leads. Will its programme redistribute the resources and rights on which women’s freedom depends?


The history beneath the headline


Calling women’s leadership foreign to Morocco requires forgetting its history. Historian Osire Glacier

documents

 women’s authority long before the contemporary premiership. Kenza al Awrabiya, the Amazigh mother of Idris II, helped secure the Idrisid dynasty, founded in the late eighth century in what is now Morocco. Zaynab al Nafzawiyya influenced eleventh-century Almoravid politics around Aghmat, near Marrakech. Sayyida al Hurra governed Tétouan, a city in northern Morocco, during the sixteenth century. Khnata bint Bakkar intervened in eighteenth-century dynastic politics.


Across the region,

Dihya

 is remembered as an Amazigh queen who led resistance to the Arab conquest in the Aurès, in present-day Algeria, during the late seventh century. Tuareg oral tradition remembers

Tin Hinan

 as a queen and founding ancestress of noble lineages in the Ahaggar, in present-day southern Algeria.


These histories expose how male authority is made to appear natural. Fatima Mernissi’s

The Forgotten Queens of Islam


challenges that selective memory. Colonialism also reorganised authority: French Protectorate administrators

reshaped

 customary courts around imperial priorities. What survives as tradition can carry the history of political intervention. 


Religious interpretation can give exclusion another claim to permanence. Islamist and other conservative opponents invoke this

hadith

 against women’s political authority:


«لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ وَلَّوْا أَمْرَهُمُ امْرَأَةً»


Usually translated as saying that a people governed by a woman will not prosper, it becomes a prohibition irrespective of her competence. Asma Lamrabet, a

Moroccan Islamic feminist thinker

, questions turning a

narration linked

 to Persia’s dynastic succession into a universal ban. She reads it against the Qur’anic Queen of Sheba, whose judgement demonstrates capable leadership. Her argument contests male authority’s claim to divine necessity.


PAM’s promises and its record


Women have long contested how authority is distributed within the family. Fatima Sadiqi

documents

the Union de l’Action Féminine’s 1992 million-signature campaign to reform the Moudawana, Morocco’s family code. The 2004 reform abolished wives’ duty of obedience but retained unequal inheritance and exceptions to the marriage age of eighteen. Proposals announced in December 2024 left fundamental equality demands unresolved. In October 2025, more than sixty civil society organisations and public figures

joined to call for comprehensive reform

. Rights in Morocco have advanced through organised demands, not the gender of an officeholder.


PAM, a centre-right party founded in 2008,

advocates

 social modernisation and positions itself against the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD). It entered government in 2021 alongside the National Rally of Independents and conservative nationalist Istiqlal. Opposition to Islamist conservatism, however, does not itself entail reforming the laws and economic conditions that subordinate women.


PAM’s

2026 programme

 promises improved widow pensions, childcare, safe transport, a women’s enterprise fund and labour inspection. The commitments leave inheritance equality, abortion reform and decriminalisation of consensual same sex relations unaddressed. Mansouri called for

banning child marriage

 without exceptions in 2024, yet PAM’s electoral programme

omits that commitment

. Employment can support independence, but a wage does not cancel criminalisation or unequal property rights. The programme leaves those constraints intact.


Even PAM’s narrow promise to increase …

author: Caleb Okereke
title: Matthew Blaise wants to be your friend and neighbor
content:
Matthew Blaise and I must have been in our mid teens when we first met. I don’t remember the exact year, but I remember that it was on Facebook. It did not take long for that online connection to become a real friendship, and it is one that has persisted despite life carrying us in different directions.   


When we sit down for this conversation in September, I am in Philadelphia and Matthew is in Brazil. He is preparing for

Friends and Neighbors

, a new art and literary festival in Lagos built around a deceptively simple question: What responsibility do we have to the people we call our friends and our neighbors?


It is a question that makes our own friendship an interesting place from which to begin. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 


Caleb:

 Something I find provocative about the title “Friends and Neighbors” is that you also seem to be making a statement about the ways queerness shows up in the ordinary. I’m thinking about this song, “Your driver could be LGBT, your friend could be LGBT, your neighbour could be LGBT.” Was that part of the conceptual framing?


Matthew:

 Actually, that’s another way to see it. When I thought of this concept, I thought of proximity within our community. A trip from Lagos to Europe is cheaper than a trip from Lagos to Abidjan, which is a neighboring country. For me, that’s a metaphor for what a lot of friendship within the African continent, especially around queerness, has been due to bad policy, homophobia and criminalization.


Queer people within Africa are not so familiar with themselves. And in that sense, we really haven’t constructed what queer Africanness is because we are still not so close to ourselves. But I find it interesting that you also see it from the point of everyday life, where people you come in contact with could be of this community or could possess these identities without you knowing.


Caleb:

 That’s what immediately came to my attention. Even when you say, “Hello, friends. Hello, neighbors,” you’re talking to all of us, right? It’s not “queer friends and neighbors.” The implicit read is that even if you’re straight, queer people are all around you. They’re your friends. They’re your neighbors. They might not tell you that they’re queer, but they’re there.


Matthew:

 From the perspective of bell hooks, societies should be built on love and friendship. This very important foundation of love has been taken away from queer people, or we’ve not been given that due to our queerness. Governmental policies and criminalization also make us live our lives in isolation. What it means to be friends right now is also very transactional, especially for queer people.


Caleb:

 One thing that has defined our friendship, at least for me, is honesty. There are things I can tell you that I can’t tell anybody else, obviously, so a sort of radical honesty. And as you were talking about transactional relationships, it made me think, what is the place of honesty in friendship, especially in a context where being honest about yourself can carry consequences?


Matthew:

 I think you don’t owe everyone that truth about yourself. For those who I truly trust, I owe them that responsibility of truth. And I do believe, for every friendship, there has to be that investment in honesty.


Caleb:

 But friendship in and of itself is a risk. I don’t think we realize that, but every friendship is a risk.


Matthew:

 Yeah, friendship sometimes, I mean, it’s not a constant state of feeling a certain way. It’s a roller coaster of emotions. It’s a journey. It’s an adventure. So you encounter a lot of things on the way.


You stretch your hand to someone and they actually bite your hand, then you know they are not really having that good intention towards you. So you can decide to stretch your hand again or push them away. But for me, I think it’s important that we’re able to stretch our hands and bring people together and do the work of educating them until we just know they’re irredeemable.


Caleb:

 Yeah…


Matthew:

 What responsibility do you think you owe me as your friend?


Caleb:

 You are now the one asking me questions. But no, I mean, I think you owe your friend loyalty. That’s one of the things that I’m non-negotiable on. I mean, there are many other things you owe your friend.


Matthew:

 You owe them honesty also?


Caleb:

 You owe them honesty. You also owe your friends grace. I give grace a lot. Maybe it’s not even grace. I’m also like, oh …

author: Kelly Hayes
title: AI Is Class Warfare. Workers Are Fighting Back.
content:
“AI is leveraged as a cudgel against the working class,” says writer and sociologist Alex Hanna.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Big Tech is selling us a future in which workers are increasingly disposable, human expertise is devalued, and corporate power is more concentrated than ever. But is that future inevitable? In this episode of Movement Memos, host Kelly Hayes talks with Alex Hanna, co-author of The AI Con, about AI as a tool of class warfare, the hype that obscures its real-world harms, and how workers are organizing to resist Big Tech’s agenda and win meaningful protections in the workplace.

Music: Son Monarcas and Guustavv

Note: This a rush transcript and has been lightly edited for clarity. Copy may not be in its final form.

Kelly Hayes: Welcome to “Movement Memos,” a Truthout podcast about organizing, solidarity, and the work of making change. I’m your host, writer and organizer Kelly Hayes. Today we are talking about how workers can resist automation and AI in the workplace. We’ll be hearing from Alex Hanna, co-author of the book, The AI Con: How to Fight Big Tech’s Hype and Create the Future We Want. Alex is a writer and a sociologist of technology, labor, and politics. Alex is also the director of research at the Distributed AI Research Institute, and leads the organization’s Luddite Lab project. The greatest promise of AI in the business world is the promise that it will eliminate workers. Some people have already felt those impacts. But far more often, we are seeing AI leveraged to surveil, control, and devalue workers. So, how is AI impacting our work lives, what’s on the horizon in the struggle, and how are some workers fighting back and winning?

We’ll get into that and more as we discuss what we’re up against, and what kind of political education workers need to wage a strong fight.

If you appreciate this podcast, and you would like to support “Movement Memos,” you can subscribe to Truthout’s newsletter or make a donation at truthout.org. You can also support the show by subscribing to “Movement Memos” on Apple or Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts, or by leaving a positive review on those platforms. Sharing episodes on social media is also a huge help.

Truthout is an independent news organization, publishing stories that the craven corporate press won’t touch. We are a union shop with the best family and sick leave policies in the industry, and we could not do this work without the support of readers and listeners like you. So thank you for believing in us and for all that you do. And with that, I hope you enjoy the show.

Kelly Hayes: Alex Hanna, welcome to Movement Memos.

Alex Hanna: Thanks for having me, Kelly.

Kelly Hayes: How are you doing today?

Alex Hanna: I am recovering from whatever is in the air, but I am soldiering through.

Kelly Hayes: Well, thank you for joining us while you’re still recovering. I really appreciate it, and I’m so glad you’re on the mend. I know a lot of our listeners will be familiar with your work, but for the unacquainted, what would you like people to know about who you are and what you do?

Alex Hanna: Yeah, so I am a sociologist and writer on labor, tech, and politics. I’m director of research at the Distributed AI Research Institute, and we’re a research institute that researches the present-day harms of AI. I feel like I have to say that now, because there’s a lot of imaginary harms that are in the conversation now. And we also develop community-based technology. And so then what I focus quite a lot on is understanding the connection of AI and labor and work, as well as working and understanding the kind of ecosystem of who’s in the AI space and what political incentives that they have. And so I have a book called The AI Con, which I co-authored with Dr. Emily M. Bender. And I also have a podcast with her called “Mystery AI Hype Theater 3000.”

Kelly Hayes: Which is such a great name for a podcast. I am really excited to talk about your work, and in particular your work around AI and labor, including the work you’re doing with the Luddite Lab. But before we go deep on labor, I feel like we have to wade through some of the AI headline muck that folks are dealing with right now.

Recently, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark declared that “the singularity” has begun. He made this announcement at a gathering of economists …

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Coral Harbour songwriter’s entry wins Inuktut songwriting contest
content:
A Coral Harbour songwriter has won the Government of Nunavut’s 2026 Qilaut Inuktut songwriting contest.


Jocelyn Malla took first place with

Tukisivunga

, earning an $8,000 prize, the Nunavut Department of Culture and Heritage announced Wednesday.

Malla also placed fifth with her song

Kamatsiaqta

.


The annual contest celebrates Inuktut music and promotes the use of Inuit languages. This year’s theme,

Avatiliriniq

, focused on respect and care for the land, animals and environment, a department news release said.


A panel of three judges assessed 21 submissions on originality, creativity, melody and lyrics.


Grace Metuq of Pangnirtung placed second with

Unikkaaqtuat Ilinniinngaaqtut,

 winning $3,500. Looee Arreak and Lorraine Akulukjuk of Iqaluit took third place with

Piruqsatillunga,

 earning $2,500. The seven other entries each receive $1,000.


The other winner are:


Fourth place:

Uumaniq

 by Kristy Kanayuk, Iqaluit;


Fifth place:

Kamatsiaqta

 by Jocelyn Malla, Coral Harbour;


Sixth place:

Nunami Quvianaqtuq

 by  Jacob and Eva Okatsiak and Eden Napayok, Arviat;


Seventh place:

Alianait

 by Monica Qattalik, Igloolik;


Eighth place:

Tariuq Tautuglavut

by Princess Kusugak, Rankin Inlet;


Ninth place:

Ikpigilavut

 by Letia and Rebecca Kalluk, Arctic Bay;


Tenth place:

Sivulitta

 by Terry Uyarak, Igloolik;


All 10 winning songs will be professionally recorded for a compilation album scheduled for release in winter 2027. Three

concerts will be held throughout Nunavut to celebrate the winners. 


Qilaut has supported the creation and release of more than 100 songs and 11 albums over the years, the department’s website said.

author: Sara Connors
title: Yukon photographer captures caribou’s extraordinary fight for survival
content:
It’s an incredible act of nature.


Two caribou. Their antlers locked in battle. One dead. The survivor, nearly immobilized by the weight of his opponent, preyed upon by a bear as foxes and birds scavenge the dead bull’s remains.


Yukon

 photographer

Peter Mather

 captured the remarkable images earlier this month while filming the Southern Lakes caribou’s rut, when up to a few hundred animals gather and males spar for females.


“I have never seen anything like that before,” Mather said. “Their horns are locked together, and one of them is dead. And the bear is like sitting 10 feet away, just watching, trying to figure out what to do. It was the strangest situation.”


Mather came across the rare sighting about 20 kilometres south of Whitehorse while filming content for the Kwanlin Dün First Nation as part of a project for the Southern Lakes Caribou Steering Committee. Kwanlin Dün is one of six First Nations governments represented on the committee.


With fewer than 1,000 animals in the early 1990s, the Southern Lakes caribou, which is composed of four woodland herds, has increased to about 4,000 today, thanks in part to voluntary harvest moratoriums by First Nations.


Yukon photographer Peter Mather. Photo: Jordan Haslbeck/APTN.


A rare encounter


Mather said he first became aware of the caribou after he and a friend helping him gather footage encountered an aggressive grizzly, something he said is not common around Whitehorse.


He said days later they saw another bear in the same spot, along with several ravens and eagles. Assuming a dead animal was nearby, he flew a drone to investigate.


He said he was shocked to see the two bulls locked together.


“Then you’d see the bear go in to try to get this big caribou, and the caribou would stand up, and the bear would go away scared, which is surprising because you would think a bear isn’t afraid of a bull caribou. But those bull caribou are so big they can take on a bear,” he said.


Mather figures the surviving caribou spent about a week weighed down in one spot while fending off bears and other predators.


After leaving the caribou some lichen, Mather said he appeared to gain back some strength.


He said scavengers and what he believes was a pack of wolves further helped free the animal by removing most of the dead caribou’s carcass, leaving just the head attached.


Mather said he and his friend resolved to remove what was left of the dead caribou with a hacksaw, but by that point the caribou was able to get up and leave.


“Last we saw, he was heading off in the mountains with two heads,” he said.


‘These herds are really special’


Lars Jessop, the steering committee’s project manager, said males are exhausted during the rut, leaving them vulnerable to predation.


He said while it can be a dangerous time for bulls, it’s rare for them to be unable to separate.


He said he’s only seen bulls locked together once before while both were alive, and that a colleague had previously found the skeletons of two locked bulls.


He said that makes the situation all the more remarkable as one bull died and the other survived.


“He would have been extremely vulnerable because he couldn’t move and somehow avoided predation until he managed to get away,” he said.


Lars Jessop, the project manager for the Southern Lakes Caribou Steering Committee. Photo: Jordan Haslbeck/APTN.


Despite the burden of an extra head, Jessop said the caribou has a good shot at survival. That’s because adult males typically shed their antlers after the rut.


“If he can make it another month or so, those antlers will drop. He’ll drop his antlers, and then he will have a good chance,” he said.


He noted that Mather’s images of the entangled caribou, as well as the herds themselves, have helped share the beauty of the

southern lakes caribou

 while also educating the public.


“These herds are really special,” he said.


For Mather, the surviving caribou is a reminder of what can happen when nature is allowed to thrive.


“I think he’s kind of the symbol of that recovery because that resilience that he’s got is indicative of what the herd has and how they’re growing again. They still need more work, but they’re coming back.”


The post

Yukon photographer captures caribou’s extraordinary fight for survival

 appeared first on

APTN News

.

author: Surina Venkat
title: Tens of thousands get ready to defend the vote
content:
This article

Tens of thousands get ready to defend the vote

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


Garnet DeGrave and other organizers with Citizen Action Wisconsin watched in shock as news broke this June that FBI agents had

raided

 the office of the Ohio Organizing Collaborative, a

nonprofit that hosts voter registration drives

 and does political organizing. The incident was largely understood to be an attempt to intimidate progressive organizers in the state and foster uncertainty in the state’s elections. DeGrave realized if a similar situation happened in Wisconsin — if a government agency interfered with community organizers or, in the worst case scenario, the election — they were woefully unprepared. 


“There weren’t enough people that were organized in the western half of the state to be able to handle that,” DeGrave, Citizen Action Wisconsin’s northeast organizer, said. 


This spurred the organization to try to fill the gap. At the end of September, Citizen Action Wisconsin — which does grassroots organizing around electoral and issue-based campaigns for social and racial justice — partnered with local organizations to pivot to election protection  ahead of a crucial midterm. 


It’s one of many community organizations and advocacy groups across the United States that have built out their election protection and defense work this year in an effort to combat misinformation and protect election integrity — a basic tenet of democracy that has come under attack from a president who is

an election denier

. Alongside national groups like the ACLU, which has had

68,000

 sign-ups for its Democracy Defenders Task Force program, these state and local organizations have undertaken an unprecedented coordinated effort to bolster voting rights amid efforts by the federal government to undermine election results. 


According to DeGrave, the work falls into two categories. “Election protection” is pre-election work to help people overcome any barriers to voting — a process that differs in every state. This can include challenging laws that might restrict voter access, running voter assistance hotlines or holding voter education campaigns.


“Election defense,” on the other hand, is work during voting and after polls close to ensure every vote is counted and to defend election results. This can include nonpartisan poll watcher programs and community-led trainings that prepare people to mobilize in the event of a contested count due to political interference. 


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


For Citizen Action, the pivot was a natural one, as the group had done small-scale election protection work and occasional direct action, DeGrave said. Citizen Action partnered with GROWW, a grassroots group that organizes behind progressive candidates in western Wisconsin, to host training sessions on how to mobilize in the event of election interference. In Michigan, Voters Not Politicians is running a similar election defense program, taking inspiration from protests against Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE. In Maine, organizations like the League of Women Voters have worked to grow a statewide poll watching program — a tactic also being used by groups in Florida and California.


Though election protection and defense efforts have been an integral part of American politics for decades, part of the reason this year’s efforts have grown in size is because the stakes feel so high.


“This election is such an important moment for us to be prepared for, in order to vote out authoritarians,” DeGrave said.


A surge of volunteers


In the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections, the Trump administration has

intensified tactics

 that advocates say are meant to intimidate or disenfranchise voters. 


On the pretext of combating voter fraud — which experts say is

virtually nonexistent

 in the U.S. — the administration has demanded sensitive voter information to identify alleged noncitizen voters from every state. Its attempts have been

consistently denied by judges

, though that hasn’t stopped the administration from trying to

remove 20,000 people from voter rolls

 in California or from creating

a federal voter database

 that’s incorrectly flagged some voters as noncitizens. The administration also tried to make voting more difficult for Americans with new Postal Service restrictions on

mail-in voting

, which a district court put on hold …

author: Madelyn Amos
title: ¡Sí Se Puede!: Dolores Huerta’s Feminist Legacy Lives On
content:
Dolores Huerta, the pioneering labor leader, civil rights activist, and feminist who devoted her life to advancing equality and justice, has died at the age of 96. Her groundbreaking work reshaped the labor and feminist movements, leaving an enduring legacy of grassroots organizing, women’s leadership, and collective action that continues to inspire generations.

Huerta was a dear friend and ally of the Feminist Majority Foundation since its founding. She served on the organization’s board for more than 30 years, offering her passion, energy, and visionary leadership to the fight for gender equality.

In the 1980s, Feminist Majority co-founders Eleanor Smeal and Kathy Spillar recruited Huerta to join the Feminization of Power campaign to increase women’s representation in elected office. For four years, Huerta traveled across the country with the Feminist Majority. She mentored women running for office, particularly Latinas and other women of color, and helped them secure endorsements while campaigning alongside them.

Reflecting on their work together, Smeal recalled, “We traveled to 8 states and she was determined to change the composition of California’s state legislature — and she did. When we started the campaign in 1987, the state legislature was only 14.2% women, but because of Dolores, it quickly jumped to 24.2%. And today, the California legislature is 49.2% women.” Now, in Congress, women are 42% of congressional Democrats, getting closer and closer to parity every year.

Spillar added in her memories of the tour with Huerta, “We would gather women active in their communities in their living rooms and talk about the need for more women to run for office. Dolores would always say to them ‘if you can’t recruit someone, then one of you has to step forward and run.’”

Huerta’s tireless organizing helped build momentum for a historic increase in women’s political representation, culminating in the 1992 election widely known as the “Year of the Woman.”

Smeal continued, “She would just keep going, it didn’t matter if it was midnight or 2am. She was my kind of person and we would just stay up all night strategizing. She worked day in and day out for women’s rights, labor rights, civil rights, LGBTQ rights, environmentalism — she was a leader in all the key issues. Her passion was infectious and inspiring.”

Smeal remembers a conversation with Huerta about the lasting impact of their activism. Huerta told her, “Our daughters can have a very different life than us because of the work we did.” Her work will live on in the movements she helped build and the generations who will carry her legacy forward.

author: Crystal Greene, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: In Manitoba, community protests legislation that would fast-track resource projects: ‘Have we not lost enough?’
content:
About 100 people attended a demonstration outside the Manitoba legislature on Saturday, ahead of Monday’s First Nations – First Ministers’ meeting where Bill C-39 was on the agenda in Ottawa. Photo by Crystal Greene


Indigenous people in Manitoba are protesting against proposed federal legislation that aims to fast-track resource development — saying it undermines their rights and sovereignty over their lands.


Activists point to several pieces of legislation that they worry would cause more harm to their territories, which are already impacted by climate change and the biodiversity crisis. They also have safety concerns over “man camps” created by industry and potential harms to vulnerable Indigenous women and girls.


Both

Bill C-5

 and

Bill C-39

 are set to fast-track major infrastructure projects in “Canada,” by designating them to be of “national interest.” C-5 was passed in 2025, and C-39 is in its third reading. Meanwhile, the proposed

Bill C-37

 — under review after a second reading — has heightened concerns over First Nations water rights. 


One such

project of “national interest”

 is

Churchill Plus

. It would see a pipeline and terminal built to internationally export LNG through the Port of Churchill on Hudson Bay. The arctic deepwater seaport would also handle increased mining exports out of Manitoba, eventually including the

Ring of Fire

.


About 20 people gathered outside of the Manitoba Legislature on Monday rallying against the legislation and in response to the First Nations-first ministers meeting in Ottawa, which was part of similar solidarity events that happened across “Canada.”


It was one of a few protests in Manitoba in late October against the bills and the extractive projects being pushed through by colonial governments despite opposition. 


People who once stood together in the same spot – the Manitoba legislature – during Idle No More, are standing together again to oppose the fast tracking of major infrastructure projects. Photo by Crystal Greene


Alex Wilson

 of Opaskwayak Cree Nation, a professor in the Faculty of Education at the University of Winnipeg, and an organizer with Idle No More, was at Monday’s rally outside the legislature


Wilson read

a collective statement from Idle No More

 founders that said “the conditions that gave rise to Idle No More in 2012 are confronting us again.”


Wilson said that includes “sweeping legislative changes, threats to environmental protections, and government decisions affecting Indigenous territories without respecting the authority of the people who belong to those lands.”


Wilson told IndigiNews that there’s been “a constant erosion of treaty rights of Indigenous sovereignty and legislation that protects land, water and the sky.”


“The bills that are proposed are kind of galvanising our understanding that this is an agenda that is continually harming First Nations, Indigenous peoples and our environment.”


At another earlier rally at the Manitoba legislature, on Saturday, Indigenous activists and allies spoke against Bills C-39 and C-37.  It was a finale of the

Arctic Crossroads Tour

 in Manitoba that visited Churchill, Nisichawayasihk, Thompson, Brandon, and Winnipeg.


Anishinaabe water protector Taylor Galvin who works closely with Manitoba First Nations that are impacted by hydro projects on their lands, attended the event.


Taylor Galvin spoke during Saturday’s event to oppose Bills C-37 and C-39 outside the Manitoba legislature. Photo by Crystal Greene


“Have we not lost enough? We are living in a ticket time bomb, and our lands and our waters don’t have time, and in Manitoba, our sturgeon relatives don’t have time,” said Galvin, who is from Baaskaandibewi-ziibiing (Brokenhead Ojibway Nation).


“Our fish and our waters are already sick, traces of life-threatening metals like mercury, lead, arsenic, and cadmium are being found in those fish and in those waters.”


Galvin spoke of political greed and “a broken system” that has harmed the environment and continues to extract from it.


“We have a broken system and yet they want more, Bill C-39, removing Indigenous rights, and trying to move forward at a very quick pace for projects of ‘national interest,’” Galvin said.


“Why aren’t the people considered national interests? What aren’t the animals considered national interests? Why are they talking about these things without protecting anything?”

author: Elizabeth Weill-Greenberg
title: Private Prison Companies Are Pouring Money Into GOP Coffers Ahead of Midterms
content:
This story was co-published with


Truthout

.


PACs and executives from three of the leading private prison companies have donated close to $1.2 million to candidates, fundraising committees, and political party committees during this year’s midterm election cycle, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) records.


A GEO Group subsidiary, GEO Reentry Services LLC,

donated

 an

additional $4.4 million

 to MAGA Inc.,

a super PAC

 supporting President Donald Trump.


Trump’s second term, along with the backing of a Republican-controlled House and Senate, has been a financial boon to the private prison industry. Since Trump took office again, private prison companies CoreCivic and GEO Group

have received

 more than $1 billion in contracts with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE.) As of July, there were

close to 59,000 people

 detained by ICE, the

majority of whom

 are held in privately run immigration jails.


Truthout

 reviewed campaign contributions made by three private prison company PACs — CoreCivic, GEO Group, and Management & Training Corporation (MTC) — as well as donations made by their executives for the 2025-2026 election cycle. We examined donations made for the primary and general elections, to PACs directly controlled by the candidates, campaign fundraising committees, and donations to entities like the Republican National Committee. For executives, we only included donations over $1,000.


Truthout

’s review of FEC records reveals that:


The three private prison PACs

donated

 about $774,000 during the midterm election cycle, including a total of $320,000 to the Republican National Committee, the National Republican Congressional Committee, and the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC.)


GEO Group’s PAC outspent CoreCivic and MTC’s PACs, with donations totaling about $456,000.


Executives from CoreCivic and GEO Group

donated

 a total of about $375,000 during the midterm election cycle.

Truthout

 did not identify donations from MTC executives that fit our criteria for inclusion.


While the overwhelming majority of private prison donations went to Republicans, there were a handful of donations to Democrats. MTC’s PAC

donated $2,000

 to Mississippi Democratic Congressman Bennie Thompson’s campaign, and CoreCivic’s PAC

donated $5,000

 to Texas Democratic Congressman Henry Cuellar’s Texas First

leadership PAC

. CoreCivic’s PAC

donated $1,000

 to the Montana Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, in addition to the $3,000 donated to the Montana Republican Legislative Campaign Committee.


Among the top recipients of private prison cash were

Congressman Andrew Garbarino

 (R-New York) and

Sen. Ashley Moody

 (R-Florida). Garbarino is the chair of the House Committee on Homeland Security and Moody is on the Senate Committee on Homeland Security, as noted in a recent report by

Scripps News

.


CoreCivic, GEO Group, and MTC’s PACs donated a total of $30,000 to Garbarino’s campaign, but the FEC records reviewed did not show any donations from CoreCivic or GEO Group executives.

          Sign Up


GEO Group’s PACs

 and

executives

 donated a total of about $48,000 to Moody’s campaign and a

joint fundraising committee

 for her campaign and the NRSC. CoreCivic’s PAC donated $1,000 to her campaign. The super PAC

Stronger Safer Nation

, which supports Moody, also received a donation of $20,000 from GEO Reentry Services.


Moody is a Trump loyalist who, as Florida’s attorney general,

joined

 Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s

efforts to overturn

 the 2020 presidential election results.


Moody is running against Democrat Angie Nixon, a current state representative, in a race that has drawn national attention. Nixon, who is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America,

secured an upset primary victory

 in August. Sen. Bernie Sanders

has joined Nixon

 on the campaign trail, and

former President Barack Obama

 and

Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez

 have also endorsed her candidacy.


In a statement to

Truthout

, Nixon slammed Moody for accepting donations from the private prison industry, saying that the contributions “from private prison executives and PACs are just more evidence of her corruption.”

author: Valerie Anne
title: ‘The Hunting Wives’ Season 2 Trailer Has Sapphic Sex and Sad Exes
content:
Season one of The Hunting Wives was a wild ride, and I have a feeling season two is going to be even wilder. The full trailer dropped and it has me clapping and kicking my feet at the sapphic chaos about to descend upon us.

The trailer opens with Sophie’s husband asking if Sophie is “still dreaming about her” (“her” being Margo) and a few flashing scenes implies that yes, yes she is.

Other things we see flash by: a glam cowgirl photo shoot, Margo being manipulative to all kinds of people, and Callie being a sad ex and using a photo of Margo as target practice.

This show also knows exactly what it is and is leaning into it. For example, the song playing is Nancy Sinatra’s “Bang Bang”, which is the perfect backdrop for this trailer full of guns and sex and chaos. And the tagline for the season is “someone is going down,” which the narrator says while the visuals cut between a dead body and also a more…explicit interpretation of the phrase.

Based on how season one ended, I can’t wait to find out how Sophie ends up back in Margo’s bed (and her bubble bath!), and luckily we only have one month left to wait.

Check out the whole trailer here:

+ Bravo’s latest reality series looks like it’s channeling…The Hunting Wives in real life? Small Town Trouble: Texas, according to the trailer, features some women who are not-so-secretly hooking up with other women

+ Cara Delevingne once went on a bad date to a lesbian sex party that involved kitten heels

+ Actress Mary Beth Barone talks about Marissa and Alex from The O.C. being her bisexual awakening, her new comedy special, and the return of Overcompensating

+ Broadway Cares is putting on a livestream 30th Anniversary Concert of RENT to raise money for Equity Fights AIDS, and the cast includes most of the original cast, plus some other Broadway legends, including but not limited to queer actress Rachel Zegler

+ Inde Navarrette is working on her Southern accent as she gets ready to play Rogue in the upcoming Marvel X-Men film

author: C4SS
title: C4SS Panelists on the Enduring Legacy of Don Lavoie
content:
The

Markets and Society conference

 this weekend (October 23-26) will feature many interesting panels on topics from public policy to self-governance to digital privacy to immigration and beyond. There will also be longtime C4SSers presenting.


On

Saturday from 9:00-10:30am

, Nathan Goodman is chairing the panel “The Enduring Legacy of Don Lavoie” featuring:


Cory Massimino – National Economic Planning: What is Right?


Don Lavoie argued in “National Economic Planning: What is Left?” that economic planning was inherently reactionary and thwarted genuinely left-wing aims like peace and liberation. Despite the prevailing conservative-libertarian fusionism of Lavoie’s day, his study of economics and history helped him see the transience of such an alliance: libertarianism was left-wing until the left became obsessed with economic planning and the right was always about militarism and hierarchy no matter how much libertarian rhetoric it adopted. Lavoie’s new (yet old) framing went under appreciated during his time and deserves careful reconsidering for anticipating the contemporary right’s increasing authoritarianism. This essay will build on Lavoie’s framing of economic planning as essentially right-wing, apply that framing to the contemporary American political situation, and argue such a framing is essential for any coherent conception of the political landscape going forward.


Jason Lee Byas – A Role For Lavoian Democracy


Don Lavoie argues for detaching our concept of democracy from the particular institution of voting, and instead seeing it as “openness,” or accessible means to shaping the world around you and its rules. An advantage of this approach is its complementarity with markets and property rights, which might otherwise be seen as in tension with democracy — thus partially reuniting liberalism’s “libertarian” and “democratic” commitments. Yet there is still a tension here. Philosophically, many libertarians may think that any social rules involving force should simply be set by natural rights, and so leaving these open to adjustment by anyone at all (let alone with open access to everyone) will be a problem. Practically, open access to reshaping the rules may spell uncertainty in problematic ways. I resolve these remaining tensions by suggesting a specific role for Lavoian Democracy. In short, many things are left radically indeterminate by any socially-practiced system of rights, and so too are many things left radically indeterminate by a commitment to natural rights. Questions of interpretation and resolution loom large, and the process of interpretation and resolution can either be hierarchical and authoritarian, or a product of ground-up contestation. There are principled liberal grounds — both moral and epistemic — for favoring the latter, and this is the role for Lavoian Democracy. I then offer a handful of institutions and practices that Lavoian Democracy might favor, including unions (of a certain form), adverse possession, and the common law.


Akiva Malamet – Beyond Recognition: Identity, Cultural Discovery, and the Limits of Social Planning


Scholars in liberal theory and political economy have long emphasized what Don Lavoie called the “knowledge problem”: social information is dispersed, local, emergent, and personal, and thus inaccessible to centralized or “high modernist” institutions. Lavoie and others showed that state economic planning fails because planners cannot access or generate this kind of knowledge and often undermine its creation. Liberal institutions, by contrast, enable people to align diverse plans and generate forms of knowledge no top-down authority could anticipate. I extend these insights to issues of identity, cultural development, and interpersonal life. Identity and cultural formation are bottom-up, organic processes reflecting the nuances of how people self-conceive, relate, and find meaning. State planning and institutional treatments of identity often obstruct pluralistic self-concepts and cultural discovery, flattening human diversity and complex individual lives into simple, legible categories. Ironically, formal recognition can perpetuate the injustices it was intended to remedy and reinforce intergroup conflict. State recognition of identity undermines the processes through which identity becomes meaningful, and conflicts with core liberal values of pluralism, self-authorship, and cooperation. Immigration restrictions present an analogous case: they …

author: Admin101
title: Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense
content:
Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN) is excited to announce the publication of

Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense

.


Drawing on organizing experiences of Black Rose/Rosa Negra members across the United States, this pamphlet explores how workers, neighbors, and communities are building collective resistance to ICE and defending their immigrant coworkers, classmates, and loved ones. By connecting struggles across workplaces, schools, and neighborhoods, the

transversal organizing

 approach we prioritize builds solidarity across different sectors of society to confront the interconnected structures of domination that shape our lives.


You can find a downloadable PDF version of the pamphlet at the end of this text.


Two Years of Trump II: Immigrants in the Crosshairs, Resistance Under Attack


Upon returning to office, Donald Trump wasted little time fulfilling his white supremacist campaign pledge of “Mass Deportations Now.” Via a flurry of executive orders and congressional acts his administration reinstated the reviled “family separation” policy; directed virtually unlimited resources to stop a fictitious “invasion” of the country’s borders; and sought to end birthright citizenship. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents blitzed Los Angeles in June 2025 with spectacular raids, followed shortly by similar operations in dozens of cities across the country including New York City; Chicago, IL; New Orleans, LA; and Durham, NC. This “shock and awe” strategy culminated in Operation Metro Surge, a months-long invasion of the Minnesota Twin Cities that deported over 2,000 residents. 


Meanwhile, support for the deportation machine plummeted as collective action against it swelled. Everyday people covered their cars, lawns, and lips with the slogan “Abolish ICE;” as of July 2026, nearly 50% of US adults support such a measure. Both May Days since Trump’s second inauguration centered immigrant defense in their celebrations. Rapid-response networks that keep watch for ICE, document kidnappings, and sometimes disrupt them spread wildly. Know-your-rights training flourished at worksites and community centers. Millions of Red Cards–wallet-sized cards outlining the holder’s constitutional protections around interactions with ICE and other police–were distributed at schools, churches, restaurants, and municipal buildings. Children and their parents caged in concentration camps went on hunger strike as constituents bombarded politicians’ hotlines and town halls demanding humanitarian treatment and release outside their walls.


Popular responses in St. Paul and Minneapolis demonstrate the possibilities of mass resistance. Like the Los Angeles Tenant Union’s community defense centers that countered ICE’s Southern California invasion, organizers reactivated dormant neighborhood networks from the 2020 uprising and began building new ones when word spread that Commander-at-Large Greg Bovino was bringing his paramilitary forces to town. Once Operation Metro Surge launched, everyday Minnesotans refined sophisticated systems to track, delay, and disrupt arrests. ICE agents retaliated by killing rapid-responder Renée Good and shooting Julio C. Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan immigrant targeted for deportation. Instead of cowering from the naked clampdown, neighborhood networks coordinated with unions, churches, and other civil societal organizations to shut down their cities on January 23rd. In its wake, Trump ousted Bovino and immigration enforcement plummeted.


But July 2026 saw record high immigrant detentions since Trump’s return to office with little public opposition. What explains it? ICE’s tactical shifts undoubtedly played a role. Bovino replacement and “Border Czar” Tom Homan traded provocative street operations with quiet detainers at jails and prisons and “targeted operations” at sites protected from activist impediment like airports. Escalating repression has also raised the costs of resistance. ICE’s bevy of brutality has included intimidation, beatings, and shootings, culminating in murdering Good and rapid-responder Alex Pretti. Federal grand juries fish from the shadows for information about our movements, stoking fears of informants that slow our organizing. From the Prairieland defendants to the Minnesota 15 and more, indictments and convictions on flimsy charges could make prosecuting dissidents even easier. Evidentiary discovery in the …

author: Chris Walker
title: Tom Tiffany, GOP Candidate for WI Governor, Refuses to Sign Pro-Democracy Pledge
content:
Among other items, the pledge asked candidates to “refrain from knowingly propagating falsehoods” about elections.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Republican candidate for Wisconsin governor Tom Tiffany has refused to sign a pro-democracy pledge that was sent by a nonpartisan group to both him and Democratic candidate David Crowley.

The inaction by Tiffany, who is currently a member of the House of Representatives, comes as he has tried to stave off criticism relating to his past efforts to block the results of the 2020 presidential election.

The pledge was sent to both candidates by an organization known as Wisconsin Business Leaders for Democracy, a bipartisan group of business owners and managers that promotes “free, fair, and regular elections.” It was sent to the two candidates in late August.

Among other items, the pledge asked the candidates whether they would “cooperate with election officials, adhere to rules and regulations, and refrain from knowingly propagating falsehoods about the electoral process.” It also asked them to promise to “encourage a peaceful election atmosphere” during several parts of the election, and to “denounce any attempt to intimidate, harass, threaten, or incite violence against opponents, their supporters, and election workers.”

While the pledge largely concerns actions the two candidates could take as governor during future elections (including the 2028 presidential race), it also includes a vow to accept the outcome of the contest they are currently in.

Tiffany’s refusal to sign and return the pledge to Wisconsin Business Leaders for Democracy resulted in the organization formally endorsing Crowley for governor.

“We asked both candidates for governor to make a simple commitment: respect the voters, respect the results and uphold the rule of law. David Crowley signed that pledge. Tom Tiffany did not,” said John Florsheim, president at Weyco Group, Inc. and a member of the business group. “At a time when our democratic institutions face serious threats, Wisconsin voters deserve to know where their candidates stand.”

Even if Tiffany had signed the pledge, however, he would already be in violation of its standards. During his debate with Crowley last week, the Republican was asked why he supported efforts to disrupt the outcome of the 2020 presidential race, in which Joe Biden defeated Donald Trump.

“One of the reasons that I did that is ‘Zuckerbucks,'” Tiffany said in his response.

That term refers to donations made by Center for Tech and Civic Life, a nonprofit funded by Meta head Mark Zuckerberg that provided $10 million in grants to help cities across the country run their elections during the COVID pandemic. Pro-Trump conspiracy theorists wrongly allege that money was instead used to steal the election.

Tiffany’s answer would have violated the part of the pledge that deals with “knowingly propagating falsehoods” in elections.

Tiffany played a role in attempting to block the certification of Biden’s presidential win. As part of a last-ditch effort to stall the counting of Electoral College votes, Republican-dominated states submitted a lawsuit to the Supreme Court, and GOP lawmakers in Congress submitted an amicus brief in support of that effort. Tiffany was the only member of the Wisconsin congressional delegation (which included five other Republicans at the time) to place his name in support of the amicus brief.

author: Andrés
title: Una tormenta de orgullo recorrerá la Villa 31
content:
La Octava Marcha del Orgullo se realizará este sábado 31 de octubre, desde las 14, en el Barrio 31 de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires. Organizada por la Asamblea Trans Feminista de la Villa 31, la movilización vuelve a reunir a las diversidades y organizaciones territoriales que sostienen esta convocatoria desde hace ocho ediciones. Este año, bajo la consigna «Operativo Tormenta de Orgullo», responderán al operativo «Tormenta Negra» del Gobierno porteño, mientras denuncian hostigamiento policial y reclaman vivienda digna, trabajo y una urbanización con perspectiva de género y diversidad.

Por Mario Canaviri para ANRed.


Las calles de la Villa 31 volverán a ser escenario de una movilización que reivindica la identidad, la organización comunitaria y los derechos de las diversidades desde el propio territorio. La concentración será el sábado 31 de octubre, a las 14, en Carlos Perette e Islas Galápagos, junto al mural de Néstor Kirchner, un punto de encuentro histórico para las organizaciones barriales.


La marcha es impulsada por la Asamblea Trans Feminista de la Villa 31, un espacio que reúne a mujeres y disidencias de distintas organizaciones sociales y políticas. Durante la jornada se realizará un recorrido por las calles más transitadas del barrio, seguido de

presentaciones musicales y espectáculos de drag queens.


Pauli, integrante de la Asociación Civil de la Territorial y secretaria del Bachillerato Popular Casa Abierta, destacó el significado de sostener esta convocatoria: “Las disidencias queremos expresarnos, organizarnos sobre todo para

visibilizar nuestras problemáticas y también nuestra identidad

”.


Una tormenta de orgullo frente a la violencia institucional


La consigna de este año, «

Operativo Tormenta de Orgullo

», hace referencia al operativo «Tormenta Negra», desplegado por el Gobierno de Jorge Macri en distintos barrios populares de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires.


Ramiro Pérez, integrante de la convocatoria, referente del espacio LGBTIQ+ Las Norteñas y militante político de El Hormiguero, explicó que se trata de

una respuesta desde el activismo a las políticas del Gobierno porteño.


“Las vecinas, les vecinos que habitamos la Villa 31, las maricas, las travas, las tortas, lo vamos a responder con Tormenta de Orgullo”, expresó Pérez, quien vinculó la consigna con las

 denuncias de violencia institucional y hostigamiento policial

.


Pauli también cuestionó los operativos de seguridad, que describió como despliegues de numerosos efectivos policiales y helicópteros, especialmente durante el atardecer y la noche.


«Es un poco lo que venimos a denunciar y no solo eso, sino también […]

la prohibición de la venta ambulante, la confiscación de esa mercadería

», señaló.


La referente advirtió que estas prácticas

afectan a trabajadores de la economía popular, jubilados y familias que dependen de sus ingresos cotidianos

. También denunció

restricciones para ingresar materiales

 de construcción y realizar refacciones en las viviendas.


Urbanización, trabajo y derechos para las diversidades


Entre las principales reivindicaciones de la movilización se encuentra el reclamo por una urbanización con perspectiva de género y diversidad.


“Por una vivienda digna, por

una urbanización con perspectiva de género y diversidad

», sintetizó Pérez al explicar las demandas que las organizaciones buscan visibilizar.


El referente cuestionó los criterios de

acceso a las viviendas entregadas

 durante el proceso de urbanización y denunció

desigualdades que afectan a las personas LGBTIQ+

.


También señaló dificultades para acceder a

dispositivos de acompañamiento ante situaciones de violencia de género

 y diversidad, que, según sostuvo, fueron

desmantelados

 o dejaron de funcionar en el barrio.


Por su parte, Pauli denunció obstáculos para el cumplimiento del cupo laboral travesti-trans,

dificultades para acceder a tratamientos de salud contemplados en la Ley de Identidad de Género

 y situaciones de discriminación en el acceso a la vivienda.


“Estamos precarizadas las diversidades”, afirmó al describir las condiciones que atraviesan quienes viven en el barrio.


Las declaraciones de ambos referentes expresan cuestionamientos a las políticas del Gobierno porteño y

reclamos por el cumplimiento efectivo de derechos sociales

 y de las diversidades.

author: Nahuel Lag
title: Aparicio exonerada en el INTA: “Vamos a ir a la justicia para que revise lo absurdo e irregular de todo el procedimiento”
content:
Por Nahuel Lag 


El Consejo Directivo del INTA, presidido por Nicolás Bronzovich —miembro de la Asociación Argentina de Productores en Siembra Directa (Aapresid) y de la Sociedad Rural de Balcarce—, exoneró a la investigadora Virginia Aparicio, la mayor especialista de la institución en estudios sobre el impacto de los agrotóxicos. Lo hizo a través de la Resolución 366, en la que le adjudica cuatro faltas administrativas graves a Ley de Empleo Público durante la coordinación del

proyecto Sprint

 —con el que se documentó la presencia de plaguicidas en muestras ambientales, vegetales, animales y humanas—. La resolución deja a Aparicio fuera de su cargo en el INTA-Balcarce, a pesar de reconocer que la investigadora realizó sus tareas, no obtuvo beneficios económicos ni contaba con antecedentes disciplinarios. 


“Virginia está fuerte”, asegura su abogado Mario Bolla en diálogo con Tierra Viva, y explica que se agotará la vía administrativa y luego se irá por vía judicial para revertir los cargos contra la investigadora que “se caen por su propio peso”. “Si se reconocían los resultados del proyecto Sprint no había que prohibir necesariamente el uso del glifosato, lo que se pretendía estudiar era ver cómo incide en contacto con otras sustancias como la Atrazina, que en Argentina se continúa utilizando pero está prohibida en Europa, Uruguay y Brasil”, señala Bolla sobre los intereses detrás de la persecución y ejemplifica: “Bayer compró a Monsanto por 66 mil millones de dólares, como para dimensionar la plata que hay detrás de todo esto”.  "Los pequeños agricultores podrían ir hacia un cambio de modelo agropecuario, pero detrás de esto están los intereses de los pooles de siembra que quieran más rendimiento y más uso de agroquímicos", concluye.  


En las próximas semanas, mientras se canaliza un recurso administrativo de reconsideración,  Aparicio continuará yendo a ocupar su oficina en el INTA-Balcarce, donde, como

contó Tierra Viva, es sometida a un proceso de aislamiento por parte de las autoridades

 desde inicios de 2025, cuando comenzó el proceso administrativo de exoneración. La resolución 366 será recurrida ante el propio Consejo Directivo del INTA, que deberá ratificar su decisión y elevarla para la firma del secretario de Agricultura, Sergio Iraeta. 


Iraeta se define como “empresario” del agro y tiene una silla en el consejo que ya votó la exoneración, representada por María Inés Amuchástegui. También tienen su lugar allí las organizaciones de la Mesa de Enlace y las facultades de Agronomía y Veterinaria. 


Si Iraeta ratifica la exoneración a pesar de los repudios sindicales, académicos y populares, el paso siguiente para la investigadora y su defensor será ir vía judicial con un pedido. “Vamos a ir a la justicia federal para que un juez revise lo absurdo e irregular de todo el procedimiento, lo arbitrario de los argumentos, y solicitaremos la nulidad de lo actuado por vía administrativa y una cautelar para que la restituyan en su cargo”, señala Bolla. 


La exoneración —la más grave de todas las sanciones administrativas—, dejaría a Aparicio no solo fuera de su cargo en el INTA sino también de su carrera como investigadora del Conicet y de cargos en universidades públicas nacionales. Solo podría ejercer cargos privados o provinciales. 


La resolución del INTA contra Aparicio 


La

resolución 366 del Consejo Directivo del INTA

 tiene 29 páginas en las que realiza un largo recorrido desde el inicio del proceso administrativo iniciado contra Aparicio en 2023, durante el gobierno de Alberto Fernández. En aquel momento, el entonces presidente del INTA Mario Garmendia y la vicepresidenta Nacira Múñoz decidieron la salida de la Argentina del proyecto Sprint. El financiamiento del Programa de Investigación e Innovación Horizonte 2020 de la Unión Europea, la coordinación de la Universidad de Wageningen y el convenio para desarrollar una evaluación integrada de los riesgos de los productos fitosanitarios para los ecosistemas, las plantas, los animales y las personas habían sido aprobados por el INTA en 2020. 


Sin embargo, tres años después, el argumento oficial para abandonar el proyecto fue que el INTA no tenía dentro de sus competencias realizar estudios sobre humanos. El argumento fue rechazado por la coordinación del proyecto Sprint, debido a la firma del convenio que contempló todos aquellos parámetros. La directora de la investigación, Violette Geissen, validó los estudios realizados y el rol de …

author: Rizomatica
title: Documental sobre el estallido social dirigido por María Teresa Larraín llega a la UCT el 5 de noviembre
content:
Cuerpos en Crisis sigue a cinco activistas durante el estallido social de 2019 y el proceso constituyente de 2021-2022 en Chile. La función es de entrada liberada y contará con un conversatorio abierto a la comunidad.


El jueves 5 de noviembre, a las 17:00 hrs, se presentará en Temuco Cuerpos en Crisis, el nuevo documental de la cineasta chileno-canadiense María Teresa Larraín. La actividad, de entrada liberada, se realizará en el Auditorio H2 del Campus San Francisco de la Universidad Católica de Temuco y es organizada por el Observatorio Ciudadano, con el patrocinio del Departamento de Sociología, Ciencia Política y Administración Pública de la UCT.


Tras la exhibición habrá un conversatorio con la directora y con la abogada y ex convencional constituyente mapuche Rosa Catrileo, moderado por Mabel Cobos, codirectora del Observatorio Ciudadano.


La película registra el estallido social de 2019 y el proceso constituyente a través de cinco activistas de los movimientos de la discapacidad, migrantes, diversidades sexo-genéricas y personas privadas de libertad. También participan integrantes de la Convención Constitucional, entre ellos tres mujeres indígenas, y personas que filmaron las calles con imágenes que nunca llegaron a la prensa oficial.


Larraín, ciega y residente en Toronto, dejó Chile tras el golpe de Estado de 1973. Comenzó a perder la vista durante el montaje de un documental anterior. Su primer largometraje independiente fue El Juicio de Pascual Pichun (2007), que retrata la historia de dos familias, la del lonko Pascual Pichun y la del terrateniente Agustín Figueroa, en lo que se conoció como uno de los juicios más emblemáticos de la historia de Chile. Su obra posterior incluye Niña Sombra (2016), sobre los vendedores ambulantes ciegos de la Alameda.


“Esta película es mi respuesta. Un homenaje a quienes perdieron la vida defendiendo un proceso transformador que me marcó para siempre”, afirma la directora.


Estrenada en 2025, Cuerpos en Crisis obtuvo el Premio a Mejor Film de la Diáspora en el Toronto International Nollywood Film Festival 2025, donde además fue nominada a Mejor Documental de Canadá, y fue nominada a Mejor Documental de Derechos Humanos en el Montreal Independent Film Festival 2026.


Tras su paso por Toronto y México, la película recorre Chile antes de su lanzamiento oficial en Sala K de Santiago el 27 de noviembre. En la región, además de Temuco, se exhibirá el 6 de noviembre en Saavedra (Ruka y Huerto Llelliuken, con integrantes de la comunidad mapuche KOLWE) y el 7 en Curarrehue (Aldea Intercultural Trawupeyüm).

Esta información se publicó en

Radio Kurruf
