author: Administrador
title: Zapatistische Vorbereitungen für das umarmende Treffen mit den Familien Sucherinnen.  Teil III. Umsorgen. Schützen. Bewahren.
content:
Musik: Meme del Real: »El mundo en que nací – Die Welt, in die ich geboren wurde«. Aufnahmen, Bearbeitung, Produktion: Terci@s Compas Zapatistas.

Compañeras Familien Sucherinnen.

Es grüßt Euch der Subcomandante Insurgente Moisés, Hauptkoordinator der Reise für das Leben – Kapitel Mexiko.

Nun, ich erzähle Euch, dass wir weiter fortfahren, uns vorzubereiten für die Reise, die wir machen, um Euch kennenzulernen – sowie Euren Schmerzen und Eurem Widerstand zuzuhören und davon zu lernen. Und um Euer Wort in unserem Herzen und in unserer Erinnerung zu bewahren. Wir erwarten wirklich, von Euch viel zu lernen.

Hier, wo wir uns versammelt haben, regnet es plötzlich viel und es ist kalt. Das ist ok für die, die aus den kälteren Regionen kommen; diejenigen aus wärmen Regionen leiden jedoch ein wenig, weil sie es nicht gewohnt sind. Regen sind wir alle gewohnt, denn natürlich regnet es hier in den Bergen des Südosten Mexikos viel. Im Gebirge, auf den Bergen und im Urwald regnet es so lange bis es aufhört.

Aus der Kälte wie aus der Wärme haben die zapatistischen Gemeinden delegierte Frauen, delegierte Männer sowie drei delegierte Otroas-AndEre geschickt, um sich vorzubereiten. Bis jetzt sind es zusammengerechnet 1.530. Vielleicht sinkt die Anzahl noch wegen Erkrankungen oder aus familiären Gründen. Beispielsweise hatte sich eine Compañera schlecht gefühlt; sie wurde untersucht und beim Ultraschall stellte sich heraus, sie ist schwanger. Sie musste [in ihre Gemeinde] zurückkehren, damit es ihr und ihrem heranwachsenden Kind gutgeht. Schnell meinte aber ein Compañero – der Ahnung von Tacos hat (sie zu machen, nicht, sie zu essen; denn Tacos essen, darin sind wir alle* gut trainiert) – er springt ein. Und ja, die Comandantas und Comandantes haben ihn bestätigt, denn er hat natürlich den Gesprächsrunden zugehört, die gegeben werden, um uns gut vorzubereiten.

Hier im Video zeigen wir Euch einige unserer Vorbereitungen.

Sei es die vollständige Delegation, seien es die Teile, in die wir uns organisieren: Wir bereiten uns auf Demonstrationen vor, falls es sie gibt; wie auch auf die Treffen, die Ihr uns sagt. Auf diesen Demonstrationen [marchas] – falls sie gemacht werden – ist unsere Hauptsorge nicht, was wir dort sagen, sondern die Familien Sucherinnen zu umsorgen, zu schützen und zu bewahren. Das heißt, wir sind nicht auf Tumult oder Entspannen aus, sondern Euer Wort zu hören. Und nun, wir müssen danach sehen, die Familien Sucherinnen zu umsorgen: Denn in ihrem Herzen haben sie heftige, harte Worte, welche aufzeigen und im Kampf für das Leben Richtung geben.

Wir wissen, dass wir lernen werden; dazu bringen wir Notizheft und Bleistift mit, sogar Computer, Tabletts, Smartphones. Und es kommen Compañeras, zu denen wir »Tercias Compas« sagen. Sie kennen sich mit Kamera, Aufnahmen, [Video-]Bearbeitung sowie der Übertragung der Treffen aus. Das Wichtigste jedoch ist, dass wir unseren Kopf, unser Herz, unser Innerstes mitbringen, mit der Lust zu lernen.

Im Video könnt Ihr sehen: Einige Compañeras mit ihren Babies stellen sich auf, so als wären sie für Wahrheit und Gerechtigkeit demonstrierende Familien Sucherinnen; und sogleich geht unsere Delegation oder ein Teil unserer Delegation an ihre Seite und umgibt sie wie ein Schutzschild.

Selbst das Comando Popcorn [der Kinder] übt, ein Schutzschild zu bilden, welches umsorgt, schützt, bewahrt.

Denn so haben es uns unsere Vorgänger*innen gelehrt, die uns sagten: Wir sind Bewahrerinnen und Bewahrer der Erde, der allerersten Mutter.

Wie Ihr in den Aufnahmen seht: Bei so viel während den Übungen produzierten Schlamm ist es fast eher so als ob wir ausrutschen anstatt zu gehen. Nun, wir schlittern. Dabei passiert es, dass die Sandale oder der Tennisschuh steckenbleibt, und mensch kann nicht anhalten, denn hinter einem*einer kommt ja schon die Menge an Compas. Zweifellos muss bis zum Ende der Übung gewartet werden, um im Schlamm nach Sandale oder Tennisschuh zu suchen. In der Zwischenzeit bewegen wir uns wie ein hinkendes Hündchen.

Compañeras Familien Sucherinnen.

Wir kommen nicht, um spazieren zu gehen. Wir werden Euch umarmen, wenn Ihr wollt; und falls nicht, nun, wir kommen ebenso um Euer Wort zu hören.

Wir wissen, es gibt Leute, die von der Gira [der Reise für das Leben – Kapitel Mexiko] falsch reden. Sie spalten, sie möchten bestimmen, wer oder wer nicht sich mit uns treffen kann. Das heißt, sie wollen andere Gruppen draußen lassen, weil sie sich nicht vertragen; und solcherart Dinge …

author: Kay Pacha / Equipo Pueblos Originarios del SERPAJ
title: Aucan Huilcaman; derribando la doctrina del descubimiento
content:
Así como difundimos informaciones de conflictos o de diversa índole, siempre relacionadas con el mundo indígena, en esta oportunidad queremos darle a conocer el testimonio de un hermano mapuche del Gulumapu, Chile, Aukan Huilcaman. Es una persona con mucha trayectoria y experiencia en defensa de los derechos indígenas y un importante protagonismo a nivel internacional.


https://argentina.indymedia.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Aucan-.mp3


https://argentina.indymedia.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Aucan-.mp3


Descargar audio


Ha participado en numerosos foros y encuentros internacionales, y últimamente lo hizo para analizar, junto con otros hermanos y hermanas, lo que se conoce como “Doctrina del Descubrimiento”, que es un principio legal y religioso que las potencias coloniales europeas utilizaron desde el siglo XV en adelante para justificar la exploración, la invasión, el despojo de tierras y la subyugación de los pueblos indígenas en América, África y Asia.


Esta doctrina está basada en una serie de bulas papales del siglo XV (como Dum Diversas en 1452, Romanus Pontifex en 1455 e Inter Caetera en 1493) emitidas en el contexto de la Era de los Descubrimientos. Y claro, en ese entonces, en esas bulas se  sostenía que las naciones cristianas europeas tenían derechos de soberanía y propiedad sobre cualquier territorio habitado por “no cristianos” en el momento en que un explorador europeo “descubría” esas tierras.


Asumía que los pueblos originarios no tenían derechos de propiedad legítimos ni soberanía sobre sus propios territorios debido a su condición de no cristianos o por considerarlos “no civilizados”, algo que con el tiempo, pasó del ámbito religioso al derecho internacional y civil.


Como dijimos, han habido varios encuentros analizando este tema y buscando estrategias para rebatir y eliminar esos conceptos que si bien se esgrimieron hace muchos años, sus consecuencias aún perduran.


En esta oportunidad Aukan participó en la conferencia internacional sobre el desmantelamiento de la doctrina del descubrimiento-terrorismo Maorí- en la ciudad de Roturua en el territorio de Aotearoa (Nueva Zelandia), del 1 al 18 de octubre de 2026.


Así que entonces escuchamos sus interesantes conceptos.


El Micro Kay Pacha se realiza con el apoyo de la organización Otto per Mille-Chiessa Valdense.


La entrada

 se publicó primero en

author: La Zarzamora
title: DESPEDIR A JUAN…
content:
Esta mañana nuestro compañero Juan Aliste Vega ha partido de su cuerpo, cuerpo que el poder mantuvo en encierro los últimos 16 años, cuerpo que practicó el conflicto y lo materializó en acciones armadas, que acompañó su vida en el álgido recorrido de ser él. Fue en el hospital penitenciario de Santiago, donde en compañia y calma, se fugó definitivamente.

Aún no podemos confirmar donde ni como será su despedida, ló que sí sabemos es que serán muchas, en muchos territorios, en las calles, en los puentes, en las jaulas, en avenidas y carreteras.

Juan Aliste es y será reivindicado, pese a los esfuerzos incansables de la prensa del enemigo y de sus múltiples intentos de desprestigiarlo, nosotrxs sus compañerxs sabemos que en este momento estamos despidiendo a un guerrero de gran envergadura. Pese a sus miserables conjunciones de palabras, el mundo sabe quien es Juan y en todos los territorios se levantará fuego en su memoria.

Que desesperanza deben sentir los poderosos, al saber que amamos pese a estar en guerra, que nuestra historia es escrita por nosotrxs, pese a sus asquerosos relatos oficiales, tan indignos como ellos mismos.

Hoy es un día de nuestra propia historia, hoy parte el guerrero combatiente que se alzó en armas contra la dictadura y la pestilente democracia de burgueses y traidores, el que no se dejó abatir, el que atacó y acertó, el que siguió compartiendo conocimientos y enseñanzas pese al encierro, el que enviaba notas y saludos, el que hacía llegar sus palabras a actividades y espacios.

Cada vez es más difícil despedir, esto no es una noticia, ni tampoco un comunicado, es nuestro adiós a un hermano…

A nosotrxs ahora nos quedará volver a mirarnos, tensionar el encierro de nuestrxs compañerxs, cuestionarnos y autocriticarnos, dejar de hacernos tolerantes al encarcelamiento, dejar de normalizar la sociedad carcelaria y hacer. Arduo camino nos dejas.

Juan que tu fuga sea eterna querido compañero.

Ternura y ataque frontal por ti y por todxs nuestrxs muertxs.

author: anred
title: La geopolítica pone a la defensiva a Milei, mientras la economía amenaza sus sueños de reelección
content:
No son días sencillos para el presidente Javier Milei y para el proyecto ultraderechista que gobierna la Argentina. Aquellas tendencias que parecían jugarle a favor tiempo atrás parecen agotadas o incluso contrarias a sus intereses. Nada definitivo aún, pero los ruidos empiezan a aturdir a una dirigencia oficialista que, por ahora, no duda en morir con las botas puestas.

Por Nicolás Salas, para Punto de Vista Internacional (PVI).


Los vientos internacionales que supieron envalentonar a la ultraderecha continental sufrieron un impasse en Brasil. El triunfo de Lula en la principal economía latinoamericana cortaron la seguidilla de victorias electorales derechistas en la región (Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Perú, entre otros), al tiempo que pusieron al presidente argentino en una situación incómoda, ya que no solo había apoyado a “su amigo” Flavio Bolsonaro sino que además participó de manera presencial y directa en la campaña electoral, viajando a tierras cariocas y propinando todo tipo de ataques públicos contra el candidato del Partido de los Trabajadores (PT).


Casi en simultáneo, la geopolítica volvía a jugarle una mala pasada. Esta vez, Estados Unidos, principal aliado del gobierno, solicitó en la ONU disolver el Comité Especial de Descolonización, principal ámbito multilateral donde Argentina mantiene el reclamo por la soberanía de las islas Malvinas. Para peor, la petición se llevó a cabo en el mismo momento en el que legisladores libertarios discutían en el Congreso su proyecto de “malvinización” (Ley de Defensa de la Soberanía Nacional), propuesta desde la cual el oficialismo buscaba recuperar la iniciativa política perdida tras su intento frustrado de extranjerizar la totalidad de las tierras del país

1

. En ese contexto, el subsecretario de Estado yanqui, Christopher Landau, le advirtió en persona a Milei que su idea de sancionar a las compañías que exploten recursos en las Malvinas afectaría los intereses de empresas cobijadas y tuteladas por el Tío Sam, situación que puse en un vericueto el intento oficialista de congraciarse, desde una óptica nacionalista, con vastos sectores de la población.


Dos reveses de peso en poco menos de diez días. Como si no fuese suficiente, todo ese río revuelto empalma con la llegada del Papá León XIV al país, acontecimiento que arrastrará la atención mundial sobre un gobierno que mantiene (y reivindica) una agenda económica y social antagónica a las máximas pregonadas por el Sumo Pontífice y su encíclica “Magnífica humanitas”. Tal es la incomodidad oficial que días atrás la Cámara de Diputados debió ceder y aprobar una nueva ley de discapacidad concediendo a reclamos opositores ya que entre el recorrido planificado por el Papa se encuentra la visita al cotolengo Don Orione, mítico centro de atención integral para personas con discapacidad, uno de los sectores más perjudicados por el ajuste mileista.


Si los vientos externos son poco auspiciosos, los locales no parecieran ser muy diferentes.  Ese mercado financiero tan provechoso para los primeros tiempos de la era Milei, entró en desconfianza y con algo escépticismo empezó a dudar de las posibilidades reeleccionarias del gobierno. No es para menos. La caída en la imagen del Jefe de Estado puso en duda su suerte para las presidenciales del próximo año y con ello la continuidad de las excepcionales ganancias que han logrado bancos, especuladores y evasores. A fines de septiembre, el JP Morgan, empleador de varios funcionarios nacionales, entre ellos el ministro de Economía, Luis “toto” Caputo

2

, revisó sus proyecciones para el país asumiendo una contracción en el tercer trimestre, por lo cual estimó un crecimiento para el 2027 de apenas el 0,4% frente al 3,4% planteado por el oficialismo en el proyecto de presupuesto presentado en el Congreso. Las previsiones se conocieron luego de que la principal institución financiera del mundo por capitalización de mercado le remitiera dicha información a los clientes de su cartera

3

. Esta situación junto a la valoración de sectores de bonistas que ven un “riesgo de repago de la deuda”

4

 generaron las condiciones de posibilidad para que se dispare el Riesgo País que, tras la elección de Brasil, rondó los 700 puntos tras acumular una suba de cerca de 100 puntos en diez días

5

.

author: Kodao Productions
title: Makabayan urges recall of House approved 2027 budget to correct ‘unconstitutional insertions’
content:
Makabayan urges recall of House approved 2027 budget to correct ‘unconstitutional insertions’


The Makabayan Coalition of progressive legislators suggests the recall of the House-approved 2027 proposed budget in order for flagged entries to be corrected before bicameral discussions.


ACT Teachers Party Rep. Antonio Tinio said such a move would give the House of Representatives (HOR) the chance to align the entire budget with the recent Philippine Supreme Court ruling that some budgetary practices in the last three years were “unconstitutional.”


“It is important for the House to accept the correctness of the decision, rather than adopting Malacañang’s stance that the Court committed ‘judicial overreach,’” Tinio said.


Tinio added provisions that need correction pertain to unprogrammed appropriations, insertions for thousands of questionable infrastructure projects in the guise of institutional amendments, as wells as lump sum allocations such as the so-called local government support fund.


He said the practice of project insertions and lump sump allocations are what fuels corruption in the Philippine government.


Road projects in the ocean?


Tinio’s statements came as the group People’s Budget Coalition (PBC) flagged farm-to-market road (FMR) and infrastructure insertions in the proposed P7.2-trillion 2027 Philippine national budget that have geographic coordinates plotted in the open sea and international/foreign locations.


A P23 million (Dh1.3 million) FMR project designated for the landlocked province of Nueva Ecija, but its coordinates plot out in the Pacific Ocean near the Philippine Rise.


A P30 million (Dh1.7 million) FMR project intended for Cebu Province, but its listed coordinates map far south into the Celebes Sea near Indonesia.


A P55 million (Dh3.15 million) proposed FMR project for Quezon Province, but its coordinates place it in the ocean near Brunei.


The Coalition also discovered at least two proposed projects whose coordinates turn out to be in faraway Africa.


A building project worth P7 Million (Dh 401,334) in Misamis Oriental but its listed coordinates originally pointed to the Sahara in Algeria or South Sudan in the proposed budget submitted by the office of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. This has been corrected in the HOR version.


Road Project in Negros Occidental but with coordinates pointing to Nigeria, which remained uncorrected in the House-approved version.


Honest mistake or deliberate acts?


HOR leaders meanwhile dismissed the revelations as mere “typographical errors” during the compilation of extensive budget amendments.


While acknowledging that coordinates provided in the budget are “misplaced,” HOR Deputy Speaker Ronaldo Puno and Committee on Appropriations Senior Vice Chairperson Albert Garcia stated that the items were results of honest mistakes.


Garcia asked the Coalition to provide a specific itemized list of the questioned projects so the chamber can review and correct them before the final enactment of the P7.2 trillion proposed budget.


But Puno went on attack mode, calling the PBC “ignorant” of the budget process. “I hope they get serious with their attacks, because it just betrays ignorance like that,” he quipped. He stated that the House does not create the budget but merely reviews proposals submitted by executive agencies.


PBC however dismissed HOR’s denials, revealing that nearly 7,000 House-inserted infrastructure and farm-to-market road projects worth around P190 billion — including 355 farm-to-market roads worth nearly P6 billion — also lacked proper project attachments or featured wrong coordinates.


Vigilance, not ignorance


PBC likewise clapped back at Puno, saying it is deeply disappointed by the HOR leader’s remarks dismissing corruption watchdogs as ignorant.


“We are more than 5,000 volunteers, alongside members of various civil society organizations, carefully scrutinizing the national budget as it passes through Congress. We analyze the figures, examine the details, question questionable allocations, and demand accountability for every peso of taxpayers’ money,” PBC convenor Kenneth Abante said.


Abante said they are not ignorant but citizens exercising their right and responsibility to hold those in power accountable.

author: groundxero
title: Villagers Barred from Public Hearing on Rs 10,000-Crore Steel Project in Raghunathpur, Purulia; Allege Police Repression
content:
Accusing the administration of staging a secretive, stage-managed public hearing for Shakambhari Ispat and Power Ltd in Purulia, villagers blocked a state highway, raising concerns over air pollution, water scarcity, and loss of farmland and the health of communities already living amid polluting industries.


 


Raghunathpur, October 28, 2026:

Residents of several villages in Raghunathpur sub-division of West Bengal’s Purulia district blocked the Raghunathpur–Santaldihi State Highway on Wednesday in protest against the public hearing for a proposed Rs 10,000-crore steel and power complex of Shakambhari Ispat and Power Ltd. The villagers accuse the administration of keeping them out of the hearing, held at the office of the Sub-Divisional Officer (SDO) of Raghunathpur, by deploying a large police force, barricading the approach and locking the main gate, while a handful of people allegedly handpicked by the company were allowed inside, so that what they describe as a farcical hearing could be staged to manufacture public consent for the project.


A large police force, barricaded the approach and locked the main gate of the SDO office


The hearing, scheduled for noon, has revived long-standing fears in a region that is already heavily industrialised, where communities have for years been living with the consequences of industrial pollution and now worry about further threats to their water, their agricultural land and their health.


 


In an emergency press release issued the same day, the

Forum for Opposition to Pollution and Protection of Life and Nature

 said that villagers from Durmut, Hurra, Nildi, Manipur, Kewabathan, Joradi, Jharukhamar and Layekdi had reached the SDO’s office before 11 am to exercise what they described as their constitutional right to take part in a hearing that would decide the future of their lives and livelihoods, only to find police barricades and a locked gate standing between them and the proceedings.


Villagers sit on road in protest against the sham public hearing


A hearing without notice or translation


 


The forum further alleged that the hearing had been organised without adequate public notice. According to its statement, there were no announcements by loudspeaker, no traditional forms of public announcement and no posters in the affected villages during the mandatory 30-day notice period. It also alleged that residents of the predominantly Adivasi villages were not given the relevant project documents in Bengali, or in Santali in the Ol Chiki script, leaving those most affected without any meaningful means of understanding what was being proposed.


 


These allegations go to the heart of the process. Under the Environment Impact Assessment Notification, 2006, the public hearing is the principal stage at which people likely to be affected by a project can place their concerns on record before environmental clearance is considered; the notification requires at least 30 days’ notice and the availability of a summary of the draft EIA report in the local language. A hearing from which the affected public is physically excluded, the forum argues, cannot be regarded as a hearing at all, and it has demanded that the proceedings be cancelled and the project’s environmental impact assessment (EIA) report be rejected.


 


Industrial expansion beside homes, schools and forests


 


The proposed complex is to comprise a steel plant with a stated capacity of 2.73 million tonnes, a ferro-alloy unit of 0.54 million tonnes per annum, a cement plant of 2 million tonnes per annum and a 484-megawatt power plant.


 


According to the press release, the facility would sit immediately adjacent to Hurra village, with Kewabathan reportedly 140 metres from the project boundary, Nildi 380 metres, Durmut 400 metres and Manipur 420 metres. Hurra Primary School is said to lie roughly 150–160 metres from the site and Nildi High School about 410–430 metres away, while seven protected forest areas are located between 200 metres and 1.7 kilometres from the proposed project.


 


The forum warned that the plant would add to the cumulative pollution burden of an area already ringed by major polluting industries. It identified five large red-category industrial units within a 10-kilometre radius of Durmut mouza:


 


Shakambhari Ispat and Power, Nakshit Iron and Steel, Odisha Alloy Steel/Odisha Metallics, the Damodar Valley Corporation’s Raghunathpur Thermal Power Station and Shyam Steel …

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Cyberlibel complaints vs journalists strengthen calls to decriminalize libel
content:
The criminal sanction for Philippine libel laws is “excessive” and is in violation of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) to which the Philippines is a signatory.

Libel complaints were recently filed against journalists and media company executives. For a journalists’ group, these validate the previous calls to decriminalize libel.

The GMA chapter of the National Union of Journalists of the Philippines (NUJP) stressed that libel laws silence journalism. “[C]riminalizing speech only undermines the public’s fundamental right to know,” the chapter said in a statement.

Davao City 1st District Rep. Paolo Duterte filed libel and cyberlibel complaints against GMA executives and broadcast journalists which stemmed from the network’s report about alleged cash deliveries to the Dutertes claimed by dismissed police officer Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.

Duterte filed the complaint before the Davao City Prosecutor’s Office on October 23, more than two weeks after his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte, made a joke about filing a multimillion-peso libel case against GMA Network. Her remarks happened during a press conference on October 6 while reading her affidavit which answers Gracioso’s claims.

Among the respondents were GMA executives Felipe Gozon and Gilberto Duavit, as well as journalists Mel Tiangco, Vicki Morales, Emil Sumangil, Darlene Cay, Marvin Parado, Joel San Luis, and other unidentified individuals.

In a statement released on October 23, the TV network said that they have not yet received the complaints.

Gracioso and National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) director Melvin Matibag were also named as respondents.

Meanwhile, veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. was arrested on October 24 over a cyberlibel complaint reportedly filed by Mans Carpio, Sara’s husband. He was unaware of the complaint, according to his legal counsel. He was released on bail on the same day.

NUJP has been campaigning for the decriminalization of libel, echoing the views of the United Nations (UN) Human Rights Committee that the criminal sanction for Philippine libel laws is “excessive” and is in violation of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) to which the Philippines is a signatory.

Right(s) Up: Why journalists and advocates push for decriminalization of libel

On September 18, NUJP released its policy review on libel laws, stating that the high court has already identified the problem of these laws but reform requires legislation. The review, to name a few, cited Justice Marvic Leonen’s opinion in Disini, Jr. v. Secretary of Justice which stated that libel was unconstitutional as penal sanctions impose “an invidious chilling effect.”

It added that removing jail time alone, as proposed by some legislators, is not decriminalization because of limitations of a fine-only regime, saying that if the accused cannot pay, subsidiary imprisonment may follow.

The review cited the data obtained from the Office of Cybercrime of the Department of Justice (DOJ), indicating that 3,770 cyberlibel cases had been filed, as of May 2022, since the enactment of the Cybercrime Prevention Act. More than 2,500 cases remained pending in courts and before the prosecution level. There were already 12 convictions.

In the 2023 study by NUJP, 61.5% of the libel cases against 50 journalists from 2021 to 2023 were filed by politicians.

ML Party-list Rep. Leila de Lima said that filing a libel suit against journalists and media workers for doing their job sends a “chilling message” to other members of the press. Parties being accused can just respond to the allegations, she wrote in a Facebook post.

Under the Journalist’s Code of Ethics approved by media groups, journalists shall recognize the duty to air the other side and the duty to correct substantive errors promptly.

“Contrary to allegations of malice or unverified reporting, the report went through standard, multi-layered editorial and legal verification procedures,” the NUJP GMA Chapter said. “The team conducted due diligence—verifying information through official sources, law enforcement documents, and background checks—and obtained proper clearance from network leadership and legal counsel before airing the story.”

author: Daniel Aloc
title: Ganggang ni JL Burgos bilang salamin ng lipunan
content:
Natatangi ang karanasan ng mga batang lumalaki sa kanayunan, malayo sa kalunsuran na may madaling access sa teknolohiya. Sa pagitan ng pagpasok sa paaralan at paglalaro sa mga burol at parang—kabilang na ang paghahanap ng mga gagambang panlaban sa kapwa gagamba—unti-unti nilang natututuhan ang mga realidad ng mundong kanyang ginagalawan. May nananalo, may natatalo; may nambubully, at may napipilitan lumaban upang hindi na lamang manatiling api.

Ngunit paano kung ang mga larong kinalakihan nila ay naging daan upang maaga silang mamulat sa karahasang umiiral sa lipunan? Paano kung ang mga batang dapat sana ay malayang naglalaro ay maagang nahaharap sa dahas, takot, at pang-aabuso.

Ilan lamang ito sa mga tanong na sinisikap sagutin ng Ganggang, ang kauna-unahang full-length narrative film ni JL Burgos, na unang ipinalabas sa Cinemalaya noong Agosto. Nitong Oktubre 21 ko lamang ito napanood sa Cinematheque Centre Manila, na ngayo’y matatagpuan sa bagong tahanan nito sa Philippine Film Heritage Building sa Intramuros, bilang bahagi ng Pelikula ng Bayan: Cinemalaya 22.

Hindi na katakataka ang tema at paksang tinatalakay ng pelikula, lalo na’t ang gumawa nito ay isang filmmaker na matagal nang nakatuon sa usapin ng karapatang pantao. Bago ang Ganggang, nakilala na si Burgos sa mga dokumentaryong Portraits of Mosquito Press at Alipato at Muog (2024). Ang huli ay nagwagi ng Best Picture, Best Documentary, at Best Editing sa ika-48 Gawad Urian noong 2025.

Hindi isang bagong proyektong biglaang nabuo ang Ganggang kasunod ng tagumpay ng Alipato at Muog. Ayon kay Burgos, isinulat niya ang kwento noon pang 2019. Sa halip na talikuran ang mga isyung matagal na niyang tinalakay sa kanyang mga dokumentaryo, pinili niyang ilahad ang mga ito sa pamamagitan ng naratibo ng isang pelikula—sa lente ng mga batang hindi pa lubusang nauunawaan ang bigat ng mga puwersang humuhubog sa kanilang buhay.

Sa pelikula, sina Ilay (Kenneth “Butchoy” Vincent Mendoza), Ten-ten (Don Rishmond Cerbito), at Mel (Raine Dela Cruz) ay tatlong batang naging magkaibigan sa paghahanap ng gagambang panlaban sa gagamba ni Anton (Prince Nathaniel España), ang bully sa kanilang paaralan. May kanya-kanyang pinagmulan ang tatlong bata. Anak ng isang desaparecido si Ilay, anak ng magsasaka si Ten-ten, at anak na naman ng isang sundalo si Mel.

Sa unang tingin, ang Ganggang ay isang pamilyar na bahagi ng pagkabata sa maraming pamayanan sa bansa. May tuwa sa paghahanap ng gagamba at sa pananabik na makita kung alin ang mananaig. Ngunit isa itong alegorya ng isang lipunang tila nakondisyon nang maniwala na kailangang maglaban-laban ang mamamayan upang mabuhay.

Sa talkback at Q&A session matapos ang screening, ipinaliwanag ni Burgos ang kahulugan ng tunggalian ng mga gagamba. Hindi naman likas sa mga ito ang mag-away sa paraang nakikita sa laro; inilalagay sila ng tao sa sitwasyong kailangan nilang magpatayan. Katulad ng mga mamamayang napipilitang mag-unahan at maglaban sa isang sistemang pinaghaharian ng iilan.

Sentrong usapin ng pelikula ang militarisasyon sa kanayunan. Binabago ng presensya ng mga sundalo ang pang-araw-araw na buhay ng mga residente, kabilang ang mga guro at magsasakang itinuturing na mga miyembro o tagasuporta ng New People’s Army (NPA) dahil lamang sa kanilang mga paninindigan.

Bukod sa karahasan at paglabag sa karapatang pantao na iniuugnay sa estado, ipinakikita rin nito ang epekto ng karahasan sa mga bata at kanilang pamilya.

Mahalagang banggitin na ang ilan sa mga karakter at eksena sa pelikula ay hango sa mga tunay na tao at pangyayari.

Isa rito si Rebelyn, ang gurong karakter sa pelikula na hango kay Rebelyn Pitao, anak ni Leoncio Pitao, na mas kilala bilang Commander Parago ng NPA sa Davao. Noong 2009, dinukot si Rebelyn at natagpuan ang kanyang bangkay kinabukasan. Ayon sa ulat ng Commission on Human Rights, ang biktima ay may mga saksak sa dibdib at iba pang palatandaan ng matinding tortyur. Ang sinapit ni Rebelyn ay isang paalala na ang mga taong hindi naman aktwal na nakikidigma ay maaari pa ring maging target ng estado.

Ang plaka naman ng sasakyang ipinakikita sa unang bahagi ng pelikula ay kapareho ng plaka ng sasakyang ginamit sa pagdukot sa kapatid ng direktor na si Jonas Burgos sa isang mall sa Quezon City noong 2007. Hanggang ngayon, hindi pa natatagpuan si Jonas.

Hango rin sa mga tunay na pangyayari ang eksenang nire-red-tag ng isang opisyal ng militar ang gurong si Rebelyn at ang kaniyang mga kasama bilang mga rebelde …

author: rti_admin
title: The Ahmedabad Reading Controversy and the Freedom to Read
content:
Who gets to decide what we should read? The question arose sharply in Ahmedabad this August, when two books were removed from a school reading list, and a silent reading session was later disrupted.

In August, an Ahmedabad school removed Malala Yousafzai’s I Am Malala and Anne Frank’s The Diary of a Young Girl from its reading list after objections from some parents and protests involving right-wing organisations. Later that month, a silent reading session organised in Vastrapur was reportedly disrupted by a group claiming affiliation with the Vishwa Hindu Parishad and Bajrang Dal. The gathering included students, lawyers, media professionals and others. The reading itself became the object of confrontation.

I Am Malala is the memoir of a girl who survived an assassination attempt after publicly advocating girls’ right to education. The Diary of a Young Girl records the experiences of a Jewish teenager hiding from Nazi persecution before Anne Frank died during the Holocaust. Whatever one thinks of Malala’s political views, or of the ways her story is interpreted, reading her memoir does not require accepting every view she holds. Anne Frank’s diary similarly allows readers to encounter the testimony of a young person caught inside one of history’s greatest crimes.

A book is not a political membership card.

Reading allows a person to encounter an argument without accepting it. A reader can examine its evidence, question its assumptions and reject its conclusions. The point is that judgement becomes possible through encounter.

Education is often described as the transmission of knowledge. But knowledge without the capacity to question it can become another form of conformity.

This question of who may read and what they may encounter carries a specific weight in the Indian context. For much of India’s history, access to formal education was deeply shaped by caste hierarchy. Ambedkar wrote that under the Chaturvarna system, the right to education was assigned to the Brahmins, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas, while Shudras were denied it. He also discussed the denial of education to women. The control of education was therefore connected to the wider system of graded inequality that Ambedkar analysed.

This was one of the structures challenged by Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule. Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule opened a school for girls in Pune in 1848, and Phule later set up schools for the Mahars and Mangs. In his 1882 testimony before the Education Commission, Phule criticised the concentration of education among the higher classes and called for a wider spread of primary and female education. His educational work treated access to knowledge as a social question rather than a privilege confined to a small section of society.

Dr B.R. Ambedkar’s conception of democracy makes this problem especially important. In Annihilation of Caste, he imagined an ideal society with “varied and free points of contact with other modes of association” and described democracy as “a mode of associated living.” For Ambedkar, fraternity was not sameness. It required people to participate in a common social world despite their differences. His writings on the Depressed Classes emerged from a context in which these communities faced restrictions on access to public wells and schools, and were subjected to social segregation and prescribed occupations. The “associated living” he imagined presupposes that those who were once excluded from classrooms are now full participants in the world of ideas.

A democratic society cannot expect citizens to form independent judgements while continually narrowing the range of ideas they are permitted to encounter. The democratic reader needs the freedom to examine an argument before deciding whether it deserves acceptance, rejection or further examination.

John Dewey understood education as inseparable from democratic life. For Dewey, democracy depended on communication, inquiry and shared experience. He saw education as a way of preparing people to participate intelligently in common life.

Not every book belongs in every classroom. Parents can question reading lists, teachers can challenge texts, and schools can make decisions about age, pedagogy and context. Citizens can protest. A democratic society must leave room for disagreement over education. The important distinction is between arguing that a book should not be taught and intimidating people who choose to read it. author: chuang
title: “Every War Is a World War”: Interview with a Member of Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine
content:
The following is an interview with friends from Taiwan who have formed the umbrella coalition Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP). The interview includes an overview of the rifts in the Taiwanese left, and the frustration of TWAFP organizers carving out their place amid divisions between pro-unification and independence, or pro- and anti-American positions, in the contentious and highly polarized politics on the island.


The organizer recounts their efforts to confront Taiwan’s growing ties with Israel and direct support for the genocide in Palestine. They speak with sadness that, even as Taiwan is now the fourth-largest supplier of arms to Israel, surpassing mainland China, most Taiwanese care little for the distant genocide and the struggle in Palestine seems far away. And yet, TWAFP has led successful demonstrations, pulled together a broad coalition of disparate groups in support of Palestine, and conducted research to expose Taiwan’s complicity in the ongoing genocide.


Be sure to read their

report


from 2025, outlining specific pathways of material component support for Israel, including radar, armor, and an array of military hardware.


See also a recent

piece

 submitted to us, outlining Taiwan’s deepening ties with Israel under the DPP government.


–

Chuang


Q: To begin, let’s just set the stage. Over the last few years, the Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP) has helped to organize the largest mobilizations against the genocide in Palestine seen in Taiwan. Can you tell us a little about how TWAFP formed and maybe review some of the protests it has organized?


A:

Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP)

 was founded in April of 2024. Prior to this, Taiwan had already seen several groups doing Palestine advocacy work arise spontaneously, including Palestine Action Front, Taiwan Palestine Solidarity Network, and Parallel Government. As its name suggests, TWAFP is an “Alliance” that brings together groups that were already involved in initiatives related to Palestine. In addition to the three groups already mentioned, the alliance also includes a migrant worker organization, the

Taiwan International Workers’ Association (TIWA)

; the human rights organization, Taiwan Association for Human Rights; the cultural collective, Taiwan Rave & Punk Solidarity Front for Palestine; the gender issues group, Queer Margins; and the Christian group, Taiwan Olive Branch Peace Collective. From 2024 to today, we have organized one petitioning campaign, issued two open letters, held one candlelight vigil, hosted one book club meeting, staged five protest actions, held three press conferences, and organized three marches. In the future, we plan to engage in a number of other activities, many of which may be smaller in scale.


Q: TWAFP also did some very interesting research on material links between Taiwan and Israel. We can link to the report here, but can you briefly go over the main findings, and maybe go over any new information that you’ve found since that report was released? For example, have there been more details since then?

      


A: In September of 2025, we released our report,

Taiwanese Companies’ Complicity in Israel’s Ongoing Genocide

, which identified specific manufacturers assisting Israel in the production of military weapons, including via the production of components. For example: Gloria Material Technology Corp (GMTC) supplies superalloys and high-grade steel produced through electroslag remelting, while ADLINK Technology supplies embedded computing systems and industrial-grade computers. In another case, Transcom marketed its vertically integrated capabilities—spanning chip design to module production—to enter the Israeli defense supply chain and is now a key, long-term supplier of components for the EL/M-2084 multi-mission radar, which is a core element of the Israeli “Iron Dome” air defense system designed by Israeli defense company Elta.

author: Ella Marchionda
title: Big opposition to WA government’s mega-university merger proposal
content:
The Western Australian Labor government is pushing ahead with its proposal to merge three of WA’s four public universities despite huge opposition among students, staff and the broader community. If the proposal to merge the University of Western Australia (UWA), Curtin University and Murdoch University goes ahead, the result will be a “mega-university” of 120,000 students, making it the biggest in the country. Both staff and students know that the merger will result in job losses, course reductions, larger class sizes and a decline in education quality. 

The proposed merger represents a corporate reorganisation of our universities to more effectively align with the priorities of capitalism in the state, particularly in defence and resources. Mark Barnaba, deputy chair of mining giant Fortescue Metals, will head the steering committee. 

The state government’s reasoning is straightforward: Western Australian universities are falling short in meeting industry needs, and their research income trails behind that of east coast universities. Nonetheless, the universities are already largely controlled by the needs of industry. Curtin University is already involved in the government’s “Critical Minerals Trailblazer programme,” which aims to “accelerate the commercialisation of university research” by increasing business investment in research and development related to defence and critical minerals. UWA hosts the Defence & Security Institute, which promotes the $368 billion AUKUS nuclear submarine program. 

The main problem with education is not that it isn't sufficiently competitive, but that it’s run as a business. Universities operate as degree factories, treating education as a commodity and students as consumers. University governance boards are more and more led by industry executives and those with corporate and business expertise, placing financial goals at the forefront. 

The corporate nature of universities has been highlighted by huge cost-cutting measures at multiple universities around the country, where staff, students and courses are attacked while executives’ million-dollar pay packages are protected.  Sydney’s UTS recently paid $7 million to KPMG to design course cuts and organisational restructures. Universities use faux crisis narratives to rationalize these cuts, with a New South Wales parliamentary inquiry reporting that six universities exaggerated financial issues to push through course and staff reductions.  In 2021, UWA implemented significant reductions in staff positions and the anthropology and sociology majors.  Murdoch University recently announced that budget cuts were necessary because of a decline in international student enrolments. A university system that relies on international students as cash cows is toxic.  

The proposed merger will only intensify corporate control of the university system. The new university will continue to have overpaid executives and rising student fees. The government-commissioned Deloitte report titled “Rapid Cost-Benefit Analysis” suggests that raising international student fees could increase revenue for the new university. But the recently merged Adelaide University has already revealed serious risks to university staff and the overall standard of education. Last month, the university introduced a voluntary early retirement scheme and indicated that voluntary redundancies might be considered. 

The proposed merger is extremely unpopular: two-thirds of National Tertiary Education Union (NTEU) members polled on the plan are against it. On 21 October, 300 students and staff rallied outside state parliament to oppose the merger. The turnout was impressive at the semester's end when students are swamped with assignments.  Students expressed concerns about the potential loss of Indigenous Studies courses, while staff worry the change will result in larger classes and heavier workloads. 

Rojin Didari, a member of Socialist Alternative and one of the speakers, stated what must be made clear: 

“There is nothing good about this merger. It is not about the betterment of our education. It is not about staff and students.  It is about corporate interests.”

Liberal Party Shadow Education Minister Liam Staltari addressed the protest after being invited by Curtin Guild President Dylan Storer. The Liberals are opposing the merger, but they are no friends of students or staff.  Under Scott Morrison, the Liberals brought in the Jobs Ready Graduate Scheme, which has …

author: Lance Selfa
title: What to expect in the US midterm elections
content:
The Republican Party, also known as the GOP or Grand Old Party, controls both chambers of the US Congress, allowing President Donald Trump to pursue his far-right agenda with little legislative resistance. But that may soon change.

In the United States, federal elections occur every two years. The congressional midterms, so named because they occur in the middle of a president’s term, will be held on Tuesday. Polling suggests Republicans will be trounced. Voters will elect all 435 members of the House of Representatives, who serve fixed two-year terms, and about one-third of the 100 Senators, who serve six-year terms. A range of state-level races, including for governors in California, Michigan and Florida, will also take place.

The Democratic Party is expected to win back control of the House and possibly even the Senate. But just how much difference will that make?

Lance Selfa

, author of

The Democrats: A Critical History

 and editor of

US Politics in an Age of Uncertainty

, previews the elections and what might come after them.

Multiple indicators point to a Democratic victory in the midterm elections. Trump is an historically unpopular president. Gasoline and diesel prices are at their highest in years because of Trump’s war in Iran.

Consumer confidence is at a 73-year low

, and

74 percent of Americans

 tell pollsters that the country is moving in the wrong direction.

So it’s no surprise that Democrats are favoured to win the House. In fact, Republicans have given up trying to forestall that.

Data-driven forecasters like G. Elliott Morris

 and Nate Silver place the probability of a Democratic House higher than 90 percent, and the probability of the Democrats winning the Senate at 70 percent or higher.

The well-regarded

New York Times

 poll

, published 21 October, estimated that, were the election held then, Democrats would receive 52 percent of the vote, compared to 41 percent for the Republicans. If that holds, it will be the biggest Democrat popular-vote margin in a midterm election since the Watergate scandal brought down the Republicans in 1974.

That result wouldn’t represent an endorsement for the Democratic Party, which remains as unpopular as the Republicans. But US midterm elections are classically “throw the bums out” elections. And the Republicans, who control all parts of the national government, are the bums this year.

Trump and his toadies declare the polls “fake” and promise a Republican victory. But their behaviour—Trump, Vice President Vance and other administration figures are campaigning almost exclusively in “red” conservative areas—suggests they know they are in deep trouble. Polls currently show that the Senate race in Kansas, where Democrats haven’t won since 1932, is a toss-up. And Democrat James Talarico is slightly favoured to win a Senate seat in Texas, where a Democrat hasn’t won statewide since the 1990s.

The last-minute campaign blitz and the truly obscene amount of money billionaires are spending to shore up Republican candidates may limit GOP losses. It seems clear, however, that the Democrats are headed for victory next week. The real question will be how high the Democratic wave will crest.

What will Trump do?

All the above assumes that 3 November will unfold as a “normal” midterm election. But Trump and his minions are talking openly about challenging or overturning the results. Given Trump’s attempts to overturn the 2020 presidential election, nothing is “off the table”.

Trump, his captive Supreme Court, and Republicans at all levels of government have conducted a years-long campaign to disenfranchise sections of the population and undermine democracy. This includes the Supreme Court’s evisceration of the Voting Rights Act, gerrymandering to lock in GOP majorities, and Trump’s so-far failed attempt to use the US Postal Service to make mail-in voting more difficult.

Trump and his Justice Department have continued to act on the lie that non-US citizens are voting illegally. The DOJ has tried to force state governments, constitutionally responsible for running US elections, to hand over their voter rolls. With voting data in hand, the Trump government says it can purge non-citizens from the rolls. So far, no state has complied, and the courts have ruled against Trump and the DOJ.

However, the DOJ has persisted. In late October, it indicted 28 individuals in California whom it claims voted illegally. Moreover, it sent lists of supposed non-citizen voters …

author: Robert Narai
title: Days of hope and rage in France
content:
At the centre of Paris, the Monument à la République looms over a square that has hosted every great mobilisation of the French left in modern history. The bronze statue of Marianne, symbol of the Republic, holds an olive branch above the words: 

Liberté. Égalité. Fraternité.

 During mass demonstrations on 17 October, dozens of young people scaled the monument while tens of thousands looked on. Some flew Palestinian and red flags. On the statue of 

Egalité

, someone had scrawled “jeunesse dorée” (“gilded youth”, an old term for the idle rich). Marianne herself was draped in a giant yellow vest bearing the words: “The police mutilate high school students”.

For almost a month now, a mass student revolt has been rocking France, in one of the deepest political crises seen in the country in decades. The state that claims to embody liberty, equality and fraternity has answered 

lycéens

 (high schoolers aged 15 to 18) demanding better conditions in schools with tear gas, rubber bullets and mass arrests. That the Republic’s police are maiming young people in the streets is an indictment of the capitalist system the Republic protects.

Days of rage

In response to a national day of action on 17 October, in which an estimated 800,000 people protested across France, the government of Emmanuel Macron unleashed a flurry of violence.

Police fired tear gas into the crowd gathering at Place de la République before the march had formed. Riot police armed with batons, shields and armoured vehicles charged into crowds in Paris, Lyons, Bordeaux and a string of provincial cities, attacking protesters and bystanders alike. According to the Interior Ministry, almost 1,800 people were arrested and more than 500 police were injured, with 855 arrests in Paris alone. A teenager lost a hand in Saint-Étienne and another lost an eye in Mulhouse. Street medics were dragged along the ground by police.

The new element on 17 October was the return of the Yellow Vests, the leaderless movement of rural and provincial workers against fuel taxes and the high cost of living that erupted in 2018, until it was crushed with brute force by the state. After weeks of watching 

lycéens

 face down riot police, the Yellow Vests called their own day of action protesting the cost of living. The Yellow Vests blocked roundabouts and fuel depots from the morning and declared their support for the student revolt. Among them was Pierre, a retiree from Bandol: “I’ve been gassed five times since this morning”, he told 

La Provence

. “[Macron’s government] is declaring war on the people.” The return of the Yellow Vests raises the possibility of the student revolt becoming a rallying point for broader working-class grievances.

Nurses, teachers and firefighters joined the Yellow Vests demonstration. In Lille, 20 rail workers marched together in their SNCF vests. Most of the working class support the movement (55 percent of the French population support the student-led protest movement, according to an Elabe poll) but are not yet part of it.

Whose Republic?

The Macron government’s strategy has been to paint the victims of violence as its perpetrators. Prime Minister Lecornu blamed “far-left groups”, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez targeted “ultra-left individuals”, while Macron declared that “nothing can explain, nothing can excuse” the violence. They pointed to a handful of burnt buildings, such as the town hall in Limoges, to paint a movement of hundreds of thousands as a mindless mob. “The perpetrators directly targeted the institutions of the Republic and the authority of the State”, wrote Bordeaux mayor Thomas Cazenave.

It is worth asking what sort of Republic the mayor of Bordeaux is defending: one in which a burnt town hall causes enormous outrage, but a sixteen-year-old losing an eye to a police grenade prompts hysteria about the need for more law and order.

The ruling class never calls the conditions that produced this revolt violence. Students in France’s poorest schools sit in classrooms infested with cockroaches and rats, in classes of up to 35. Outside school, the police stop, search and arrest young Black and Arab men from the 

banlieues

 (working-class suburbs) for the colour of their skin and the estate they live on, and their operations now cause more than one death per week. Fuel and food prices keep rising, while, according to Oxfam, 53 billionaires own as much as the poorest 48 percent of the population. This is the systematic violence …

author: Cas Smith
title: Brazil: Lula’s election victory was won in the streets
content:
Australia’s Brazilian community joined their compatriots worldwide in a wave of street mobilisations in support of incumbent President Luiz Inácio “Lula” da Silva, ahead of his election victory on October 25.

Lula, who was first elected president in 2002, pulled ahead of right-wing opponent Flávio Bolsonaro — the son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro — winning the second round run-off election by 4.4 million votes.

Significantly, this came after Bolsonaro won the first round on October 4, which prompted Brazilians to hit the streets in a significant movement to bolster Lula’s profile, and to prevent a “second Bolsonaro” presidency.

Students and the country’s working class largely led these mobilisations, which included a gathering of more than one million Lula supporters on Rio de Janeiro’s Copacabana Beach the day before the election.

Around Australia, similar protests were held prior to the election, including at Scarborough Beach in Boorloo/Perth, on October 22. Organiser Pedro told Green Left that many Brazilians were afraid their country could become mired in corruption and instability under a Bolsonaro government.

“Unfortunately, we experienced Bolsonaro snr’s government for four years between 2018 and 2022,” he said.

“They were the ones in power during the [COVID-19] pandemic, which was devastating for the country in many ways, because we were denied access to vaccines and the government failed to invest in our healthcare system; the doctors were completely ignored.

“This was only a tiny part of what this government did — we have seen enough.”

Pedro said Flávio Bolsonaro’s close ties to United States President Donald Trump was a concern, highlighting Trump’s coup against Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro earlier this year and his influence on far-right Argentine President Javier Milei.

The October 25 election delivered a comprehensive win to Lula, who received 64.3 million votes, compared to Bolsonaro’s 59.8 million. This was the first time that a candidate won the presidential election after a first-round defeat.

Despite Lula’s victory, when the new Congress convenes in February next year, Bolsonaro’s party will control 28 seats in the Senate (35% of the total) and 121 seats in the lower house (24%) as well as five governorships (19%), which — once alliances are factored in — will mean the right will have bigger majorities in both houses for Lula’s next administration.

“We are trying to unite the maximum number of people in this movement,” Pedro said.

“We want to show that we are here for our freedom, our democracy, and we have something to defend against the people who are trying to take over the government again in Brazil.”

Despite Bolsonaro’s initial pledge to annul the outcome, the leader of his Liberal Party, Valdemar Costa Neto, issued a statement on October 26 accepting the election result.

Bolsonaro’s protest revolved around a last-minute extension to voting hours, which prompted him to say, in a post-election speech to supporters, that “We will take legal action.”

This was despite the fact that both sides had called for the extension: Bolsonaro’s camp said that heavy rains in the country’s south (where he enjoys popular support) would prevent people from reaching polling stations.

Lula’s side meanwhile, said that extended voting hours were necessary, citing the alleged restriction of public transport by some city administrations, which they said was an attempt to curtail the working-class vote. Bolstering this interpretation were media reports that Pablo Souza, a transportation official in the city of Salvador, had been arrested on election day.

The decision to extend voting hours was made by Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin, who had been appointed to the court by Lula in 2023, and had previously been the president’s personal lawyer. These factors prompted Bolsonaro to cry foul, claiming the decision negatively impacted his voting base.

However, close analysis of the election results suggests the extension allowed for only 35,000 additional votes across Brazil, comprising 0.03% of the total. Given Lula’s victory by 4.4 million votes, this appears negligible.

Some of Bolsonaro’s supporters questioned the result, with Trump describing it as “another rigged election”. However, he did not go so far as to promise intervention on behalf of Bolsonaro.

Given Jair Bolsonaro’s failed coup against Lula after the latter’s election victory in 2022, many analysts are watching to …

author: April Holcombe
title: China’s forgotten miracle makers
content:
History has no parallel for modern China’s economic transformation. To what do we owe the China “miracle”, in which annual GDP growth averaged 9 percent over 40 years, wages up roughly tenfold in 30 years, and more high-speed rail built in ten years than the rest of the world in all time?

In the heyday of globalisation, people said China proved the magic of free markets and free trade. These days, people are more likely to attribute the country’s success to some special Chinese characteristic, such as its state-directed investment or its “Communist” dictatorship. 

These perspectives share in common a wilful or ignorant blindness to capitalism’s real wealth creators. Economic value comes neither from the market’s “invisible hand” nor the state’s “guiding hand”, but plain old everyday hands. The secret to China’s “miracle” is the not-so-miraculous condition of its working class.

Beginning in the 1990s, the greatest ever number of wage labourers was assembled through the collusion of profit-hungry foreign capital with millions of venal bureaucrats and their repressive state machine. Three hundred million people decamped from rural poverty to seek better lives in China’s cities, while urban compatriots in state-owned mines and mills lost their livelihoods through merciless privatisation.

China’s working class is legally stratified into “migrant” and “resident”, subject to the severest dictatorship of their bosses, and deprived of political rights to speak out or unionise. Apply hundreds of billions in Western and Taiwanese investments, lather, rinse, repeat for decades, and voilà! You have the most “miraculous” economic growth in capitalist history. 

China’s migrant workforce

We are used to hearing about how important migrants are to Western economies, but migration—the internal kind from village to city, not country-to-country—has been even more critical to China’s boom. In the 1990s, the government enticed young villagers with the prospect of independence, new experiences and better pay in newly established, deregulated Special Economic Zones with low wages and low taxes.

Lu Qingmin first left her family’s half-acre farm and came to Dongguan, a burgeoning megacity in the southern manufacturing heartland of the Pearl River Delta, in the early 2000s. Bosses preferred migrant women like her, considering them doubly docile. Writer Leslie Chang, in her 2008 book

Factory Girls

, described Lu’s experiences at her first job in a Hong Kong-owned alarm clock factory:

“A day on the assembly line stretched from eight in the morning until midnight—thirteen hours on the job plus two breaks for meals—and workers labored every day for weeks on end. From the moment she entered the factory she wanted to leave.”

The Pearl River Delta opened wide to investment in such sweatshops, and American-style hyper-individualism flowed in with it. Self-help books, life-coaching gurus, pyramid schemes, talent markets, unregulated colleges: each refracted through the false prism of empowerment what migrant workers already felt in their bones:

you are on your own

.

Hukou

: China’s internal visa system

Every migrant who left for the cities took the same thing with them: their rural

hukou

(户口), a residential registration that acts like an internal passport. Originally designed under Mao Zedong in 1958 to prohibit rural-to-urban movement altogether, the

hukou

household registration system was repurposed to create a pliant, defenceless workforce with second-class citizenship wherever it went.

Out-of-town

hukou

holders, also called the “floating population”, now represent just under half of the country’s workforce. Registered to villages far away, they are denied health insurance and pensions by the local government where they actually live. Many cities bar them from buying property, and local schools charge significant sums to teach their children. 

Think of them like the United States’ undocumented immigrants, who can get driver’s licences but not Social Security, who work in practically every key industry, but technically are not supposed to be there at all. Except there are now as many in China as the entire US population.

China does not offer the equivalent of America’s birthright citizenship: children inherit their parents’

hukou

 wherever they are born. Locked out by the prohibitive cost of urban schooling, tens of millions of “left behind” children grow up in the countryside with their grandparents, only seeing their …

author: Jeff Rickertt
title: Phil Monsour’s ‘Time of Monsters’ is a call to action against Israel’s genocide
content:
Time of Monsters Phil Monsour October 2026 Pre-order the album and lyric book at: pozible.com/profile/phil-monsour. Listen now on Bandcamp.

In the mythical Anglo-Saxon poem Beowulf, an entire population is subjugated by a bloodthirsty and seemingly invincible monster, Grendel. He “ruled in defiance of right, one against all”. “Malignant by nature, he never showed remorse.” (Seamus Heaney, Beowulf: A New Verse Translation, New York, WW Norton & Co, 2000, p11.)

With the genocide in Gaza now into its fourth year, and with Israel extending its military savagery to Lebanon, Syria and Iran, and tightening its bloody grip on the West Bank and East Jerusalem, it is clear the peoples of the Middle East are also living under the sway of a monster, malignant by nature, never showing remorse.

Unable to resolve the crisis of legitimacy generated by its founding act of land theft and dispossession, unable to quell the desire of the land’s indigenous people for liberation, the Israeli state, like Grendel, lashes out in rage, resorting to ever-increasing violence to sustain its power.

Halfway across the planet, in Magan-djin/Brisbane, Australia, a new album by Phil Monsour foregrounds the trauma, resilience, courage, fears and hopes of those resisting this evil; first and foremost the Palestinians themselves, but also the millions who have mobilised globally in solidarity with them over the past three years.

This album, Time of Monsters, adds to Monsour’s already impressive body of music about colonisation and war in the Middle East. It comprises 12 songs written over the past three years, each a response to Israel’s latest genocidal escalation of its never-ending war of subjugation.

One track is a rousing cover of Macklemore’s “Hind’s Hall 2”, the only song on the album not by Monsour. Another track, “Song for Fatima Hassouna”, honours the Palestinian photojournalist murdered by the Israel Defense Forces, alongside six members of her family, in April last year. The other songs respond to the genocide and Western complicity thematically. They invoke the visceral monstrousness of it, framing their narratives around recurring motifs: barbarism, loss, grief, survival, love and hope. The style is acoustic rock, although closer to Bruce Springsteen than Billy Bragg.

Monsour’s music is inscribed with activism. He is a founder and coordinator of Justice for Palestine Magan-djin, the Palestinian solidarity organisation that, since October 2023, has spearheaded the movement in Magan-djin, organising hundreds of rallies, pickets, vigils and public meetings. The size and intensity of this mobilisation has surpassed anything before it in the city’s history, including the struggle against the United States war in Vietnam.

Monsour composes and sings as a partisan of this uprising, a musician-activist, rather than a musician-ally. Without ever assuming to speak for Palestinians, some of his songs on Time of Monsters adopt a Palestinian first-person perspective. “Free Me from the Dust”, for example, addresses the horror in Gaza from the viewpoint of a Palestinian survivor: “In this shroud I bury soon something inside of me, flesh that binds me.” In “One Day in the Sun”, Monsour describes a Gazan’s daily struggle for survival: “All I can do is breathe, all I can do is wait, wait for tomorrow, and one day in the sun.” In another track, “I Am Not a Number”, the narrator tells us, “I live beyond your pictures; this land and I, we are the same.”

The Palestinian persona of these songs, however, is not ubiquitous across the album. The lens of the title song cuts away to an ally watching the genocide in livestream: “I am staring at something, can’t look away, the past the future is haunting me this day, crimes that echo on a million screens.”

The effect of this shifting perspective from song to song is a reframing of the Palestinian “I” as a “we” of the global liberation movement, positioning the Palestinians as a universal subject and Monsour himself (and us) as part of that multitude. “Our world is in pieces,” he declares in “Long List of Lost Things”, speaking for all of us. Monsour’s own place in the struggle — his own authorial “I” — is never far from the surface: “I can’t say if I’m broken, I can’t say if I’m whole, I just keep walking, nowhere else to go.”

This positioning gives the lyrical content of Time of Monsters urgency and emotional immediacy that sets Monsour’s songwriting apart in the genre of protest music. Woody Guthrie, Pete …

author: Unknown
title: İspanya’da can kaybı 69’a yükseldi, makinistler grevde: Demir yolu işçilerinin sesi duyulmadı, özelleştirme çarptı
content:
İspanya’nın Toledo bölgesinde iki hızlı trenin çarpışması sonucu hayatını kaybedenlerin sayısı 69 yükseldi. Kaza, özelleştirme tartışmalarını yeniden gündeme taşıdı. Geçtiğimiz 18 Ocak’ta bir başka tren kazasında 46 kişi ölmüş, demir yolu işçileri özelleştirmeyi ve yarattığı güvenlik risklerini protesto etmek için grev yapmıştı. Hükümetin taahhütleri üzerine grev tamamlanmamış ancak vaatler yerine getirilmediği için makinist sendikası Semaf, “demir yollarında güvenlik” koşullarının sağlanması talebiyle 29 Ekim için yeni grev kararı açıklamıştı. Kaza, grevden bir gün önce gerçekleşti. Sanchez Hükümeti kazanın hemen ardından “insan hatası” diyerek demir yolu işçilerini hedef gösterirken, Samef grevi iptal etmedi ve makinistler dün 24 saat iş bıraktı.

Toledo’nın Urda bölgesindeki kazada devlete ait Renfe şirketine ait bir AVE treni (hızlı tren), Madrid-Endülüs yüksek hızlı demir yolu hattının 118. kilometresinde durmakta olan Iryo şirketine ait trene arkadan çarptı. Çarpışmanın etkisiyle Iryo treninin en arkadaki iki vagonu raydan çıkarak yuvarlandı.

Kazadan birkaç saat sonra İspanya Ulaştırma Bakanlığı “insan hatası” açıklaması yaparak suçu işçileri yıkmanın yolunu açtı. Sendikalar ise özelleştirme sonrası arızalı sistemler, azaltılmış personel ve taşeronlara devredilmiş, finansmanı kesilmiş bakım hizmetleriyle ayakta durmaya çalışan demir yolu sistemine dikkat çekiyor.

18 Ocak 2026’da da Adamuz bölgesinde de yine bir Iryo treni raydan çıkarak yan hattın üzerine girmiş ve bu hattaki bir trenle çarpışmıştı. Iryo, kasım 2022’de hizmet vermeye başlayan İspanya’nın ilk özel hızlı tren operatörü. Bu kazada 46 kişi hayatını kaybetti, 126 kişi yaralandı. İspanyol Lokomotif Makinistleri ve Demiryolu Yardımcıları Sendikasının (Semaf), ağustos 2025’te demir yolu altyapısından sorumlu devlet kurumu Adif’e, daha sonra raydan çıkma olayının meydana geldiği bölgedeki rayların aşırı aşınması konusunda uyarıda bulunduğu, ancak herhangi bir önlem alınmadığı ortaya çıktı. Adamuz kazasından iki gün sonra, Barselona’da bir setin çökmesi sonucu stajyer bir makinist hayatını kaybetti.

Demir yolu işçileri o dönemde de taşeron şirketlere devredilen ve kaynak ayrılmayan bakım hizmetleri sorununa dikkat çekmiş ve 9, 10 ve 11 Şubat tarihlerinde grev ilan etmişti. İlk gününde greve, ülke genelinde 34 binden fazla demir yolu işçisi katıldı ve 350 trenin seferleri durduruldu. Grev çağrısını yapan CCOO, UGT, CGT ve Semaf sendikaları, hükümetin “sektörün yapısal sorunlarını” ele almasını talep etti. Bu dört sendikadan üçü olan CCOO, UGT ve Semaf, Ulaştırma Bakanlığı ile bakım harcamalarının artırılması konusunda anlaşmaya vardıktan sonra grevin diğer günlerini iptal etti.

Ancak bu taahhütler yerine getirilmediği gerekçesiyle İspanya’daki tren makinistlerinin yüzde 85’inin örgütlü olduğu Semaf sendikası 16 Ekim’de yaptığı açıklama ile 29 Ekim için 24 saatlik grev ilan etmişti. Grevin talepleri arasında “Raylar üzerindeki risklere karşı önlemlerin alınması” ve “Demir yolu araçlarında süregelen güvenlik ve güvenilirlik sorunlarına yönelik gerçek ve kalıcı teknik çözümler” yer alıyordu.

Semaf, Toledo’da meydana gelen kazadan sonra yaptığı açıklamada da, güvenlik konusunda yapısal iyileştirmeler ve verilen taahhütlerin yerine getirilmesi talebiyle çağrısını yaptıkları 24 saatlik grevden geri adım atmadıklarını duyurdu. Grev gece yarısı başladı ve dün gerçekleştirildi.

Ayrıca, önümüzdeki cuma gününden itibaren Ouigo’da altı günlük grev çağrısını da sürdürme kararı alındı. Ouigo, Fransa Devlet Demiryolları (SNCF) bünyesinde faaliyet gösteren, 2021’den itibaren İspanya’da da düşük maliyetli hızlı tren hizmeti sunan bir ulaşım şirketi.

Bu arada Genel Emek Sendikası (CGT) da Toledo kazasında bağımsız bir inceleme yapılmadan makinistlerin suçlanmasına tepki gösterdi. CGT Konfederasyon Komitesi Daimi Sekreterliği, “Demir yolu güvenliği için yatırım, bakım ve yeterli personel gereklidir. Bu on yıllardır talep ettiğimiz bir konudur” açıklaması yaptı.

Demir yollarının özelleştirilmesi sadece bir hükümet politikası değil, Avrupa Birliği’nin de üyelerine bir dayatması.

İspanya basınında demir yollarındaki güvenlik sorununun başlangıcı olarak 1991 yılı gösteriliyor. O yıl 91/440/CEE sayılı Avrupa Direktifi, demir yolu altyapısı ve tren işletmeciliğinin birbirinden ayrılmasını zorunlu kıldı. İspanyol demir yolu sistemi Adif ve Renfe olarak iki şirkete ayrıldı.
