author: Yasmine Benabderrahmane
title: Is "khawa khawa" a North African myth?
content:
In the haze of

el ghorba

 — the strangeness and alienation of living abroad — I gravitate toward the Maghrebi diaspora. For a moment, we relax our tongues from the unnatural twists of Arabic dialects foreign to us and speak in the Maghrebi

darija

s. Desperate to latch onto whatever whispers of home exist elsewhere, we claim that we are

khawa khawa

.

Among the Algerians, Moroccans, and Tunisians,

khawa khawa

 is an official nod to an unofficial alliance, loosely translating to

brotherhood

. It is an ode to our shared cultures and history in the face of North African identity discourses.

But what began as a salve for colonialism was lost in the monotonous chants for brotherhood.

Before the 19th century, North African states were “undefined” to European cartographers and authorities alike. Hence, like the concept of the Middle East and the Sahel, the Maghreb was prone to imperial invention. Unsurprisingly, this coincided with the Scramble for Africa — when the insatiable greed of European colonial powers took interest in dividing the African continent among themselves.

Encompassing other colonial legacies, the borders born out of the Scramble engineered the ethnic rivalries that persist in Africa today. Through the newly devised borders and the infamous “divide and conquer” regimes, the Maghreb was branded as distinct.

Despite the existing racial diversity of the region, the French colonial regimes rebranded the Maghreb as a biracial society: Amazigh or Arab. While the Amazigh identity was mislabeled in proximity to the whiteness of Europe, the Arab identity became an accusation of settler colonialism. North Africa became a geographic body for the Francophonie world, distanced from its neighboring regions’ cultures, politics, and society.

In 1962, Algeria — the last of France’s Maghrebi colonies — declared independence. In the years that followed, the Maghrebi people looked inwards and toward rebuilding the identity of North Africa. Thus,

khawa khawa

 was born and reinforced by the diaspora that fled their homes in the wake of political instability. It became a card dealt in moments of desperation to bond to something, or someone, that vaguely resembled home.

Khawa khawa

, and the brotherhood that blossomed with it, became the means to redress an identity obscured by European colonialism.

True

khawa khawa

 culture demands communal harmony void of ego. But when politics becomes inevitably entangled in the national identity of communities, the culture of Maghrebi brotherhood falls flat.

Shortly after 1962, newly independent Algeria and Morocco fell into border disputes. The following decades spiraled into attempted land grabs, fits of cultural monopolies, and accusations of expansionist ambitions. In response, the people cried out

khawa khawa; our governments do not define our brotherhood

!

But too often, the politics override the social bonds of Algerians and Moroccans (and occasionally, Tunisians). With the rise of the internet, discourse shifted, and social media became a useful mirror for the abstractions of the Maghrebi identity.

Most recently, the

khawa khawa

 culture was dramatically pronounced dead on social media platforms, following the 2025 African Cup of Nations (AFCON). Almost overnight, the football tournament became a litmus test for Algerian-Moroccan relations and spiraled into a warped perception of North African relations. A futile online back-and-forth that began as shared banter turned into personal attacks and political scrutiny.

The post-AFCON

guerre

 between Algerians and Moroccans — which coincided with the recent

UN support

 for Moroccan plans over the Western Sahara, disapproved by the Algerian government — is a recurring phenomenon of how Maghrebi culture wages war parallel to the political tensions of its respective countries. Despite the adamant denial, online Maghrebi communities fall into the habit of using our governments to verify the authenticity of

khawa khawa

.

The problem rests in the fact that both communities — Algerian and Moroccan — fall into the habit of claiming the minority of hateful comments as the consensus among the entirety of both nations. We see assertions made that we cannot prove, except that they are too insulting and their wounds far too inflicting to recover from. It has become a pattern of malice between both nations that resurfaces regardless of how loudly

khawa khawa

 is chanted.

Perhaps the fault is also in the fragility …

author: Tahrir Hamdi
title: Palestine Resists: From Fanon and Kanafani to Armed Struggle and Return
content:
How does one resist dispossession and displacement, ongoing genocide, culturicide, scholasticide and epistemicide, and all forms of erasure of a people’s past, present and future? The answer: Resist by all available means—armed resistance, cultural resistance, and economic resistance; this is a legal right recognized under international law, but before that, it is morally legitimate, justified, and necessary. Israel is a brutal settler colony that was made possible by two main strategies: the expulsion of the Palestinian people from their indigenous land (historic Palestine) and ongoing genocide that is now 78 years old.

Armed resistance, as theorized by anti-colonial theorists such as Frantz Fanon, Aimé Césaire, Amílcar Cabral, Ghassan Kanafani, and Edward Said, is an essential part of the anti-colonial struggle for the liberation of colonized minds and lands. In his book The Wretched of the Earth (1963), Frantz Fanon, a psychiatrist by training, forcefully argued for anti-colonial armed resistance, stating precisely because colonization is such a violent and dehumanizing process, “decolonization is always a violent phenomenon” (35). For Fanon, colonization always dehumanizes the colonized; therefore, the colonized must use violence against the colonizer to allow for the rehumanization of the colonized because revolutionary violence is meant to end the oppression, colonization and dehumanization of the colonized population (94).

The revolutionary thinker Amilcar Cabral argued in his speech titled “The Weapon of Theory, (1966)”: “the only effective way of definitively fulfilling the aspirations of the peoples, that is to say of attaining national liberation, is by armed struggle.” In his essay titled “National Liberation and Culture,” Cabral argues that the colonizer seeks to physically destroy a significant proportion of the dominated or colonized population; accordingly, the colonizer, in addition to resorting to mass killing and genocide, will always target the culture of the colonized. It is precisely for this reason that the preservation and continuation of people’s culture and their knowledge systems are essential to national liberation. Thus, cultural resistance and armed resistance go hand in hand.

The revolutionary Palestinian theorist and activist (who also wrote intellectual and theoretical pieces for the Arab Nationalist Movement and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine), Ghassan Kanafani, like Fanon and Cabral, emphasized the absolute importance of cultural and armed resistance. Kanafani argued for a vibrant culture of resistance that would enable the armed struggle for liberation. This is why Kanafani wrote stories of Palestinian resistance. In a novella titled Returning to Haifa, Kanafani makes it clear, through his character Said, that any genuine return to Palestine required a successful armed struggle, a war. Kanafani also emphasized the absolute importance of the unity of armed resistance organizations. In his essay titled “Towards a Constructive Dialogue on Palestinian National Unity,” Kanafani writes: “Any setback to any active fida’i organization, whether militarily or fundamentally, cannot be limited to that organization, but rather is immediately reflected on all other organizations” (262). Kanafani was well aware that divisions do not just weaken one Palestinian organization, but the Palestinian struggle for liberation as a whole.

Echoing Kanafani’s and other anti-colonial theorists’ position on armed struggle, the Palestinian American intellectual Edward Said told Tim Sebastian on the BBC’s “Hardtalk” program in 2002 that he is “for any kind of violence that would resist occupation and apartheid […] occupation and apartheid have to be resisted by whatever means bring about their end.” Thus, Zionist settler colonialism must be resisted “by whatever means bring[s] about [its] end” or in the words of Fanon, by the “use of all means, and that of force first and foremost” (61). As Said was nearing the end of his life, he wrote about the absolute refusal to surrender, which he theorized in his book published posthumously, titled On Late Style (2006). The inevitable link between armed resistance and the culture of resistance is of great importance—it is this link that guarantees the continuation of resistance to oppression and brutal Zionist settler colonialism.

There has always been Palestinian resistance to colonization, which in the early 20th century began with popular …

author: Joseph Lee
title: Long after the Maui fires, toxic metals linger in residents’ bodies
content:
In August of 2023, a series of wildfires broke out across Maui, killing more than 100 people, destroying thousands of homes, and causing billions in damage. Noelani Ahia, who is Kanaka Maoli and co-founder of Maui Medic Healers Hui, helped mobilize nearly 600 volunteers in Lāhainā, including doctors, nurses, and therapists. 


Three years later, the housing and health crises remain acute. Maui Medic Healers Hui runs a free clinic, but Ahia wishes it had 10 more to address the community’s needs. “The fire may be out, but the catastrophe is not over by any stretch of the imagination,” she said. 


The devastation extended well beyond the lives lost and buildings destroyed. Research published last year by researchers with the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa’s Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, or MauiWES, found that

more than 1 in 5 residents

 had reduced lung function.


Now, new research from the same project has

found elevated levels of toxic metals

 in the island’s residents months after the fires, with higher exposure associated with impaired lung function. The findings offer further evidence that

the health consequences of catastrophic wildfires

 can persist long after the flames are extinguished and the smoke clears.


“What we consider and sometimes look at as a one-time event isn’t really one-time anymore,” Alika Maunakea, who is Kanaka Maoli and co-director of MauiWES, told Grist. 


Researchers don’t yet know how much of the contamination came from the fires and how much was already present in the environment. That distinction matters as wildfires increasingly race through towns like Lāhainā and cities like Los Angeles, where burning

homes, cars and infrastructure can leave contaminants

 that

people encounter for months

 or years afterward.


Community members hold hands in a prayer circle at a “Lāhainā Strong” gathering in October 2023.


Mario Tama / Getty Images


“We have traditionally thought about wildfire exposure primarily through the lens of smoke,” Maunakea said in a press release. “But when an entire community burns, we are dealing with a much more complicated exposure environment.” Researchers must also understand what contaminants were already present, what the fire may have released, and what entered residents’ bodies, he said.


The research, which studied 1,400 adults across Maui six to 18 months after the fires, measured 24 metals in urine samples. It found that participants had higher concentrations of several metals than people in a nationwide health survey conducted before the fires. That included 2.2 times as much arsenic, 2.3 times as much barium, and 3.8 times as much manganese. Antimony, which is used in flame retardant materials and has been previously

linked to lung irritation, stomach pain, and other symptoms

, was found at levels nearly 40 times higher.


Because the researchers lack comparable data from before the fires, they could not determine how much of the metal exposure resulted from the disaster. Maunakea told Grist answering that question is the next step for the project, which has received a $3.6 million grant from the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences. That work will include investigating whether and to what degree past agricultural and industrial activity contributed to the contamination.


“It’s important to realize that these are all part of settler colonialism,” Ahia said. “So what we’re looking at is confounding factors that are to the detriment of the health of our local people.”


Read Next


Two years after a wildfire took everything, Maui homeowners are facing a new threat: Foreclosure


Anita Hofschneider


Decades of plantation agriculture altered water systems, introduced herbicides, and displaced native plants, leaving a legacy on the islands that is still felt today. Disasters like fires and storms can compound those ongoing environmental problems. 


“If we begin the story when the fire starts, we miss the decisions that shaped the landscape and the community’s ability to respond,” said Katie Kamelamela, who is Kanaka Maoli and an assistant professor at Arizona State University based in Hawaiʻi. “Micro climate change acts on places already shaped by histories of land ownership, water diversion, development, and unequal access to resources.”


Kamelamela said true recovery must look beyond the fire. “I want recovery to be measured by whether people can remain in their communities, care for ʻāina, and pass on their knowledge and …

author: Soreti Kadir
title: Finfinnee is the Third Space
content:
At the end of 2010, I took a trip to Ethiopia to visit my family. At the time, my parents worked in Bole, the commercial centre of Addis Ababa. Being only 16, my movements were more or less regulated by my parents, which meant that I would travel with them into the city each day, after which it was the extent of my curiosity and creativity (and pocket money) that determined what I did until evening, when I would head back to our house on the outskirts of the city. Slowly, interactions with the staff at a nearby cafe, just a few hundred meters from the building where my family worked, became routine. 


Over the two months that I was in Ethiopia, with much of this time spent in Addis Ababa, we spent most of our lunch breaks together, hanging out on the steps of the cafe, sharing stories to pass the time. One day, the conversation of our relationship to ‘Ethiopia’, as a national identity, came up. It’s important to note that I was raised in the Oromo diaspora, a community that, in the years my mother and I migrated to Australia, was made up mostly of political refugees who fled the country after the adoption of the “Transitional Period Charter of Ethiopia” and the official establishment of a transitional government. 


This eventually led to the Tigrayan People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) monopolizing power within the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), a process that resulted in the isolation of those seeking political power within the EPRDF through the ballot. Given the size and economic importance of the Oromia region, it was the Oromo Liberation Front (OLF), amongst others, that became a key target of political violence, creating political communities in exile exactly like the one that I grew up in.


I inherited a different definition of Ethiopia, coloured by memories and experiences of violence and displacement that informed my relationship to the state as a place of unbelonging for those who shared my identity. The day that the conversation with these two new friends wandered into political territory, we all engaged passionately, striving to reflect the extent of both our personal experiences and hopes for our country. They found my reflections to be overly nostalgic and antagonistic towards the country’s future.  Unconcerned for the good of the future. I found their insistence that we shared a national identity to be inaccurate and offensive. We agreed on little, and I found it exhilarating. 


That evening, I was restlessly anticipating the opportunity to tell my mother about what I thought was the most exciting experience of my trip to date. In recounting the story, I almost gave my mother a heart attack. Angry, afraid, and in shock, my mother warned me sternly against ever engaging in such conversation in public again. She asked me many questions about who these men were, how I knew them, and if we’d ever had such conversations before. What I was blind to, and what was the daily lived experience of my parents, was that Addis Ababa, primarily but not exclusively, was a heavily surveilled city, the State looking for the people doing exactly what I found myself doing that day – discussing the political reality of our country. Thereafter, I was careful, out of curiosity more than fear (being 16 with a high risk tolerance will do that), and refrained from fully-fledged conversations, opting for quiet enquiry when the opportunity presented itself. Although our conversation never veered down the road of politics again, I continued to visit my friends every day and remember rushing to say a heartfelt goodbye on the day I was due to fly back to Australia. 


For this piece, I will centre the discussion on Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, as opposed to extending the conversation to other parts of the country which exist with their own nuances and political realities, requiring more space for analysis than I have here. I share the introductory anecdote to forward the idea that, in Ethiopia, to nurture spaces of connection, community-building, and care, we must first invest in collective repair of the damage wrought by decades of state surveillance that has defined the range and breadth of relational life the city space can hold, and from the legacy of what can only be defined as settler colonialism. ‘Where’, figuratively and literally, can this process of repair take place? I argue that it must take place in Finfinnee, geographically the same location as Addis Ababa, but sociologically and …

author: Ramzy Baroud
title: What Does the Green Party’s Historic Anti-Zionist Motion Mean for Palestine?
content:
The Green Party has put the conversation back on track: the problem is not the lack of creative solutions to the Israeli occupation of Palestine. The problem is Zionism itself.

To appreciate the significance of Motion A105, adopted by the Green Party of England and Wales on October 4, consider its basic tenets.

The party is now formally anti-Zionist. It endorses the Palestinian right of return, supports one democratic state throughout historic Palestine, reaffirms its commitment to the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement, distinguishes anti-Zionism from antisemitism, and calls for a full arms embargo against Israel.

Though the decision may seem revolutionary within British politics, it is hardly revolutionary when examined against the history of Palestinian dispossession, beginning long before the Nakba of 1948.

Indeed, the Greens were not the first to equate Zionism with racism. That history owes much to Africa’s anti-colonial movements and their struggle against apartheid.

In 1975, the Organization of African Unity, meeting in Kampala, Uganda, drew explicit parallels between the racial systems governing South Africa, Rhodesia and occupied Palestine, identifying their common imperialist origins.

This position helped lay the groundwork for UN General Assembly Resolution 3379, adopted on November 10, 1975, which determined that Zionism was a form of racism and racial discrimination.

Under intense American and Israeli diplomatic pressure, the UN eventually reversed that determination on December 16, 1991.

Israel, however, was not required to dismantle the discriminatory structures that had prompted the original condemnation. The revocation changed the UN’s position, not the realities confronting Palestinians.

Those who yielded to American pressure in 1991 must therefore confront a troubling question of moral responsibility: did their decision help legitimize the very political structures that have sustained Palestinian dispossession, occupation and settler colonialism?

The Greens have now reopened that historical debate. But they have also done something more consequential.

By adopting the motion with 1,022 votes against 813, party members demonstrated that ideas once dismissed as radical are increasingly challenging the boundaries of mainstream British politics.

Yet within this achievement lie important fault lines, revealing the nature of the struggle ahead.

Four of the party’s five MPs opposed the resolution. More tellingly, Sandy Ruthven, chair of Amnesty International UK’s charitable trust, resigned his Green Party membership altogether.

In explaining his decision, Ruthven accused the party of seeking to court the hard-left vote while failing to confront prejudice within its own ranks.

His resignation exposes a contradiction worth examining, particularly given his association with an organization that has already documented Israeli apartheid against Palestinians.

In February 2022, Amnesty International published a landmark report concluding that Israel maintained an institutionalized system of oppression and domination over Palestinians amounting to apartheid.

That recognition was belated, but critically important. Apartheid, however, does not emerge in an ideological vacuum. It is sustained by political assumptions about belonging, sovereignty, demographic control and the unequal distribution of rights.

The question, therefore, is not merely whether Israeli apartheid exists, but what political principles have made its establishment and perpetuation possible.

The Zionist movement emerged in late nineteenth-century Europe as a nationalist project seeking a Jewish homeland, eventually pursuing Jewish statehood in Palestine. Its implementation ultimately led to the mass displacement of Palestinians in 1948.

The connection between that foundational project and the discriminatory structures documented by Amnesty itself is impossible to ignore. How, then, can the likes of Ruthven condemn apartheid without confronting the ideology that underpins it? And if that ideology is not Zionism, what is it?

The larger issue, however, is not a lack of historical knowledge among Britain’s political and intellectual elites.

Rather, these elites have long positioned themselves as guardians of the permissible discourse on Israel and Palestine – a narrative that accommodates occasional criticism, sometimes even harsh condemnation, but rarely permits a fundamental challenge to the political structures …

author: Monthly Review Press
title: In NYC or DC in coming days? See Aymeric Monville, Jennifer Ponce de León and Gabriel Rockhill, speaking live on “Requiem for French Theory”
content:
NYC, on October 29th, at CUNY (25 Broadway) * DC, on October 30th at Busboys and Poets (235 Carol St NW) * (And a couple of days ago in Philly’s Free Library)


APPEARANCES


Coming from Left Field

 (Episode 152)


In this episode of Coming From Left Field, philosopher and cultural critic Gabriel Rockhill joins

Greg Godels & Pat Cummings

 to explore the Ford Foundation, the 1966 Johns Hopkins conference often cited as a launching point for French Theory in the United States, Cold War cultural politics, and the wider political economy of academic knowledge production. Rockhill argues for rebuilding a class-centered, internationalist Marxism and joins a thoughtful exchange on China, Vietnam, socialism, imperialism, inequality, and the challenges of assessing existing socialist projects without demonization or uncritical celebration….


Marx Memorial Library

in London hosted a dual book launch for

Requiem for French Theory

 and

Who Paid the Pipers of Western Marxism?

with Gabriel Rockhill, Aymeric Monville, and Jennifer Ponce de León, who engaged in a discussion regarding the effects of imperialism on the production and dissemination of knowledge.

Watch here

or below


Far from simply engaging in a critique of the faux radicalism of the prominent discourses within the imperial theory industry, the discussion was grounded in a reasoned defense of the vibrant international tradition of anti-imperialist Marxism. Topics included the imperial promotion of Western Marxism and postmodern French Theory, the international war of ideas, the failed efforts to discredit anti-imperialist Marxism, culturalism and identity politics vs. a materialist analysis of the colonial question, fascism past and present, the dialectics of actually existing socialism, and the current state of global class struggle in theory and practice.


REVIEWS


Marxism-Leninism Today,

 by

Greg Godels

:


“During the 1960s and 1970s, it was an oft-repeated quip that the European left was long on theory and short on practice, while the North American left was strong on action, but allergic to theory. In West Germany, Italy, and France, young leftists would often passionately debate theoretical questions deep into the night, while seldom coming to a common commitment to action the next day. Their youthful U.S. counterparts—revived after the retreat from High McCarthyism–counted on spontaneous action and a firm commitment to common, inherited political values rather than the ideas buried in deep theoretical tracts. But those observations were far from completely true. The often student-driven U.S. New Left developed a thirst for a broader, deeper explanation of the injustices that they were rejecting. Many of those committed to action turned to left classics–quite often a reconsidered Marx–and others favored a wave of West European radical-oriented thinkers….”

Read more…


ZZ’s Blog

, as reviewed by Zigedy:


“During the 1960s and 1970s, it was an oft-repeated quip that the European left was long on theory and short on practice, while the North American left was strong on action, but allergic to theory. In West Germany, Italy, and France, young leftists would often passionately debate theoretical questions deep into the night, while seldom coming to a common commitment to action the next day. Their youthful US counterparts–revived after the retreat from High McCarthyism– counted on spontaneous action and a firm commitment to common, inherited political values rather than the ideas buried in deep theoretical tracts. But those observations were far from completely true. The often student-driven US New Left developed a thirst for a broader, deeper explanation of the injustices that they were rejecting. Many of those committed to action turned to left classics– quite often a reconsidered Marx– and others favored a wave of West European radical-oriented thinkers. It is the rise and importation to the US of one particularly influential “brand” of European theory to which Aymeric Monville and Gabriel Rockhill’s new book is devoted.


In

 Requiem for French Theory: Transatlantic Funeral Dirge in a Marxist Key

 (New York,

Monthly Review Press

, 2026, $22.00, 168 pp.), Monville and Rockhill show that what became known as “French Theory” in the US was both a calculated interruption of the rediscovery and study of Marxism and an intellectual trend hostile to anti-capitalist and socialist currents….”

author: LCM-Redaktion
title: Eine Welt zu Gewinnen! – Interview zur Konferenz und dem Anspruch des Internationalismus im 21. Jahrhundert
content:
„

In Zeiten der Zuspitzung der globalen Systemkrise und im Angesicht ihrer direkten Auswirkungen auf uns hierzulande wollen wir eine neue Debatte über internationalistische Praxis und Ausrichtung hier in Deutschland anstoßen. Wir stellen uns die Frage, wie sich unser Anspruch in einer an den konkreten Verhältnissen orientierten Praxis verwirklichen kann.“ – S

o wirbt die Tagung „Eine Welt zu Gewinnen“, die anlässlich des 109. Jahrestages der Oktoberrevolution am kommenden Wochenende in Berlin stattfinden wird.


Wir sprechen mit Ayşe vom Bund der Kommunist:innen

1

 in Berlin und Lena von YUNA – Demokratische Jugend

2

, welche die Konferenz zusammen mit der Akademie der demokratischen Moderne ausrichten.


In Berlin findet ja kommendes Wochenende die Konferenz „Eine Welt zu Gewinnen“ statt. Könnt ihr uns einen Einblick geben, was denn da so geplant ist?


Lena:

 Die Konferenz wird einen ganzen Tag lang gehen und ist in drei Blöcke aufgeteilt: Zu Beginn haben wir Brigitte Studer eingeladen, die ihre Recherchen zur KomIntern vorstellen wird. Dabei werden wir natürlich Publikumsfragen stellen können, um zusammen herauszufinden, welche Lehren wir aus der Vergangenheit ziehen können. Im zweiten Panel teilt dann Torkil Lauesen seine Analyse des globalen Kapitalismus und seine Perspektiven mit uns. Was vor allem im Hinblick auf eine spezifische Praxis in den Zentren des Imperialismus sehr spannend wird.


Ay

ş

e

:

 Das Podium im Anschluss ist ein Ausdruck von dem, was wir mit der gesamten Konferenz versuchen: Wir schauen uns nicht nur die Geschichte der imperialistischen Epoche des Kapitalismus an, sondern auch, was die Bedeutung des Internationalismus in den imperialistischen Krisen war. Wie war unsere internationalistische Praxis in Deutschland in den letzten Jahrzehnten und wie muss eine zukünftige internationalistische Arbeit aussehen? Wir sehen die imperialistische Weltlage einerseits und haben viele internationalistische Erfahrungen. Wenn wir uns zum Beispiel Kurdistan anschauen, vollzieht sich ja ein Umbruch. Deshalb muss die konkrete Analyse, zu der wir gemeinsam an dem Tag kommen, auch dazu führen, dass die Art und Weise, wie unsere Praxis aussieht, sich sozusagen daran anpasst. Und das werden wir eben auf dem Podium gemeinsam, auch aus unseren verschiedenen Erfahrungen und Perspektiven, zusammenbringen.


Worin seht ihr die Herausforderung eines proletarischen bzw. sozialistischen Internationalismus in der heutigen Zeit?


Lena:

 Was wir vielleicht erstmal grundsätzlich zum Verständnis von Internationalismus sagen müssen: Aufgrund des global organisierten Kapitalismus brauchen wir auch eine internationale Strategie. Probleme dabei gibt es viele. Die subjektive Situation, also die Situation von uns organisierten Kräften, müssen wir dabei hervorheben: Auch wenn wir sehen, dass es einen Aufschwung bei den sozialistischen Kräften gibt, sind wir nicht so breit aufgestellt und stabil verankert. Es braucht eine gut organisierte gesellschaftliche Bewegung, um mit einer Relevanz tatsächlich in internationale Beziehungen zu gehen. Ein weiteres Problem ist die Trennung, die wir sowohl als Jugendliche, Frauen, als auch ArbeiterInnen anhand von nationalen Grenzen als auch anderen Machtgrenzen erfahren.


Ay

ş

e:

 Ja, viele Sachen, die Lena genannt hat, würde ich genauso teilen. Ich würde noch hinzufügen, dass, wenn man sich spezifisch die Arbeiterklasse anschaut, das Problem eben die extreme Heterogenität dieser ist. Nicht nur innerhalb der globalen Waren- und Produktionskette, sondern selbst hier in den Betrieben in Deutschland sehen wir: Okay, es gibt eigentlich verschiedene Stellungen in jedem Betrieb, es gibt Festangestellte, Subunternehmer, ganz prekär arbeitende Leute, die ja nicht mal in einem Betrieb ein gemeinsames Interesse formulieren können. Wenn man sich das über nationale Grenzen hinweg anschaut, ist es noch schlimmer.


In Deutschland haben wir das Problem, dass wir es tatsächlich großflächig mit einer Arbeiteraristokratie zu tun hatten. Gerade da, wo eigentlich ganz viel Macht bei der Arbeit liegt: Die Leute, die bei BMW und Mercedes und Volkswagen an den teuren Anlagen sitzen, wo ganz viel Mehrwert in wenigen Sekunden produziert wird, das sind natürlich auch die Leute, die am meisten befriedet sind, weil es einen super Kündigungsschutz gibt, die ein ganz gutes Gehalt bekommen und so weiter und so fort.


Das hat historisch in Deutschland dazu geführt, dass es die Notwendigkeit nach einem Kampf …

author: anred
title: La derrota de Bolsonaro es un golpe a los Trump y los Milei
content:
El candidato presidencial brasileño Flávio Bolsonaro, del Partido Liberal (PL), reacciona mientras habla tras perder la segunda vuelta de las elecciones presidenciales, en Brasilia, Brasil. 25 de octubre de 2026. Foto: REUTERS/Adriano Machado


La derrota de Bolsonaro es un golpe político a los Trump, Milei y toda la fracción del imperialismo que había apostado por el mentor de los “milicianos” (parapoliciales) brasileños. Flávio Bolsonaro ha anunciado que impugnará la segunda ronda. Le sirve para la tribuna: la mayor parte de la burguesía mundial ha cerrado filas con la victoria de Lula. El ecológico Lula ya ha anunciado la intención de instalar a Petrobrás en la Amazonía, con la vista puesta en la exportación de carburantes a China. Las empresas chinas de vehículos eléctricos se han asociado a europeas y norteamericanas, para distribuirse el mercado brasileño y las cadenas de exportación. Con el telón de fondo de esta crisis por arriba, la campaña del balotaje fue el escenario de movilizaciones imponentes, que por una simplificación de una situación compleja han sido consideradas de apoyo a la candidatura de Lula. No hay trabajador de a pie en Brasil, sin embargo, que no tenga críticas severas a Lula y a la burocracia política, sindical y educacional del lulismo. La segunda vuelta ha consagrado presidente a Lula, pero la primera vuelta le dio a la derecha el control de parlamentos, gobernaciones y municipios. Es una herencia del PT y de su sucursal política, el Psol, que reúne a la izquierda antisocialista. La victoria de Lula no abre una perspectiva para los trabajadores.

Por Marcelo Ramal y Jorge Altamira (Política Obrera).


Lula ha dado vuelta la elección del primer turno electoral y consiguió una victoria inapelable -más de tres puntos de diferencia- sobre Flávio Bolsonaro. El candidato del Frente Brasil Popular, una coalición con partidos de la gran patronal brasileña, obtuvo nada menos que 10 millones de votos más que hace tres semanas, ocasión en la que había perdido unos 3 millones de votos en relación al balotaje de octubre de 2022. La magnitud de la transferencia de votos de ayer es atribuida a la participación del electorado que no lo había hecho el 4 de octubre pasado y a la mayoría de los que habían votado por los candidatos que no llegaron al segundo turno, pertenecientes a la derecha. La manifestación de apoyo a Lula, en la avenida Paulista de la capital del Estado, habría reunido 1.300.000 asistentes, la mayor, según los entendidos, de la historia de Brasil.


La derrota de Bolsonaro es un golpe político a los Trump, Milei y toda la fracción del imperialismo que había apostado por el mentor de los “milicianos” (parapoliciales) brasileños. En alusión al cuarto mandato de Lula, Trump señaló que “los comunistas se perpetúan en el poder”, a sabiendas de que tiene un gran margen de entendimiento con el ganador. La frase no lo predispone bien frente a Xi Jinping, a quien quiere asociar a su ‘plan de paz’ para Ucrania. Dentro de diez días, Trump perderá distritos que los republicanos han conservado como propios durante los últimos cien años.


La media vuelta de los resultados electorales está asociada a un distanciamiento de la derecha brasileña con respecto a la candidatura de Bolsonaro, que tuvo su expresión en el acogimiento que Diputados y Senado, controlados por ella, dieron a diversos proyectos de ley de Lula para ser votados de inmediato, en el transcurso de la campaña del balotaje. Bolsonaro, en cambio, fue denunciado en la prensa por lo que en Brasil se conoce como “ja ganhou”, en referencia al inmovilismo de quien asegura que no habría una modificación de los resultados previos. Flávio Bolsonaro, cuyo partido pasará a controlar el Senado a partir del 1 de enero próximo, anunció que iniciaría un juicio político y destitución del establishment judicial de Brasil, algo divisorio en la derecha y considerado peligroso para la llamada institucionalidad. Esta amenaza convirtió a Lula en el único defensor del “orden” en Brasil. Flávio Bolsonaro se vio obligado a votar el proyecto de Lula que reduce la semana laboral de 6 a 5 jornadas y a apoyar, en el debate presidencial, las medidas asistenciales de Lula -Bolsa Familia, Sistema de Salud-, las cuales, bajo el propio gobierno del Frente Brasil Popular, se encontraban en la ruina.


El impasse de la campaña bolsonarista fue precipitado por una fractura interna del bloque derechista. Según la prensa, Tarcisio de Freitas, reelecto gobernador por San …

title: 25 organizations in Europe seek to strengthen joint struggle and solidarity
content:
25 political and civil society organizations from Turkey and Kurdistan have agreed to establish a joint alliance for struggle and solidarity in Europe. The initiative aims to bring together different political currents and strengthen resistance against the rise of right-wing and fascist forces, imperialist war policies, and state repression. At the same time, the participating organizations intend to support the peace and democratic society process in Turkey and advocate for a democratic solution to the Kurdish question.


The agreement stems from a meeting held on October 17 at the Cologne headquarters of the Federation of Alevi Communities in Europe (AABK). Representatives from various political traditions and social movements gathered at the invitation of eight organizations. In a joint final declaration issued today, the participants reaffirm their determination to preserve their organizational independence while establishing a lasting foundation for joint political action.


Against militarism, fascism and imperialist war policies


In their declaration, the organizations describe a world marked by growing international tensions. They warn that wars and conflicts driven by imperialist centers of power are increasing the risk of a broader military confrontation, potentially escalating into a new global war over the redistribution of power and resources. While ever-greater resources are being devoted to armament and warfare, they say, poverty and social inequality are deepening. The consequences, they argue, are borne primarily by working and oppressed sections of society, women, and the natural environment.


The signatories view the growing strength of right-wing and fascist movements as part of this development. They argue that militarism, racism, sexism, hostility toward refugees and migrants, and the destruction of the natural foundations of life are interconnected. At the same time, social forces opposing these developments are increasingly being criminalized.


The organizations therefore call for stronger international coordination among movements of struggle. They remark that resistance movements from India to France and the United States, as well as Yemen and Rojava, must not remain isolated from one another. “Their experiences must be brought together and transformed into a shared framework of internationalist solidarity. Peace, democracy, and social justice cannot be expected from the very power structures responsible for war, exploitation, and oppression. Instead, the key lies in strengthening ties between working and oppressed populations across national borders.”


Joint resistance against AKP-MHP policies


Another key focus of the declaration is the political situation in Turkey. According to the organizations, the AKP-MHP government is exploiting the international shift to the right to consolidate its authoritarian system of rule on a permanent basis. They point out that repression against the political opposition, arrests, bans, and restrictions on democratic rights are aimed at suppressing social resistance and weakening organized opposition forces.


According to the organizations, those particularly affected include workers, trade unions, democratic organizations, intellectuals, artists, and opposition political groups. At the same time, the collective rights of the Kurdish and Alevi populations continue to be disregarded. Women face patriarchal violence and discrimination, while the protection of children and the right to life of animals, as well as the preservation of nature, are systematically neglected.


The organizations do not regard these policies as an isolated development in Turkey. Rather, they see them as part of a broader authoritarian offensive through which capitalist centers of power and reactionary governments are responding to social crises. This, they argue, makes it necessary to connect democratic and social struggles in Turkey with those in Europe and other regions of the world.


Democratic solution to the Kurdish question as a shared responsibility


The participating organizations explicitly address the peace and democratic society process, stating: “Although Abdullah Öcalan and the PKK have paved the way for political and democratic dialogue through their decisions to end the armed struggle, the AKP-MHP government and the Turkish state continue to refuse to take the necessary steps toward genuine progress.”

title: Posición del colectivx anarquista NOS en las elecciones generales en Brasil en 2026
content:
POSICIÓN DEL COLECTIVX ANARQUISTA NOS EN LAS ELECCIONES GENERALES EN BRASIL EN 2026


A todxs


Este domingo, 25 de octubre de 2026, habrá segunda vuelta de las elecciones de la “democracia” burguesa en el espacio ocupado por la república Federativa de Brasil. Habrá elecciones para gobernador en algunos estados de la federación y para el cargo de presidente de la república. Los candidatos son: el actual presidente Lula da Silva en un intento de reelección; y Flavio Bolsonaro, senador e hijo del psicópata Jair Bolsonaro que gobernó Brasil entre 2019 y 2022.


Por un lado, Lula da Silva, representante de la izquierda institucional y del campo “progresista”. Notorio conciliador de clases y celoso gestor del capital en Brasil, Lula da Silva, su partido PT y su central sindical CUT representan la “democracia” de los ricos, con una política socialdemócrata disfrazada de socialismo donde las élites (financiera, industrial, terratenientes) siguen siendo élites y el pueblo permanece en una posición subalterna, con algunas migajas siendo distribuidas a los más pobres (subsidios en dinero, pequeños aumentos por encima de la inflación para jubilaciones y asalariados de bajos ingresos, ascenso social limitado para hijos de pobres a través del ingreso en universidades, etc.), y convivencia conciliadora más o menos pacífica con los dos bloques que se están formando en el mundo y que caminan hacia la Tercera Guerra Mundial: los Atlantistas (EE. UU., Unión Europea, “israel”) y el Mundo Multipolar (China, Rusia, Irán).


Por otro lado, Flavio Bolsonaro, representante de la extrema derecha y títere del imperialismo yanqui-sionista. Tan celoso como Lula da Silva en la gestión del capital, Flavio se diferencia de él por ser la figura clave en el proyecto del dictador yanqui Donald Trump de imponer gobiernos de extrema derecha en toda Sudamérica. Flavio mantiene una alianza con el dictador argentino Javier Milei y con el carnicero Benjamín Netanyahu, y ya ha advertido que aplicará la misma política económica que Milei en Brasil, que formará una alianza político-económica-militar con el Estado terrorista de “israel”, e incluso invitará a Marco Rubio, Secretario de Estado de Trump, A formar parte de su equipo de gobierno. Una de las principales bases de apoyo de Flavio son las iglesias evangélicas neopentecostales sionistas vinculadas a Estados Unidos y “Israel”.


Flavio es amigo íntimo del banquero Daniel Vorcaro, autor del mayor fraude financiero de la historia de Brasil, quien robó aproximadamente R$ 57.000.000.000,00 (US$ 11.000.000.000,00/EUR 10.000.000.000,00) de fondos de pensiones pertenecientes a empleados de empresas estatales, seguridad social y inversionistas privados. Flavio Bolsonaro recibió R$ 134.000.000,00 (US$ 26.000.000,00/EUR 23.000.000,00) de Vorcaro, supuestamente para la producción de la película Dark Horse, una biografía ficticia del psicópata Jair Bolsonaro. La mayor parte del dinero robado del pueblo fue desviado para el disfrute personal de la familia Bolsonaro.


Flavio tiene vínculos en el submundo del crimen con la cúpula de la organización mafiosa Comando Vermelho y con narcomilicias de extrema derecha.


Flavio actuó, sin cobrar honorarios, como abogado de Bruno Dias Delaroli, cabo de la despreciable PMERJ — Policía Militar del Estado de Río de Janeiro, quien en 2021 mató a la niña Ana Clara Gomes Machado, de 5 años, disparándole dos veces en la cabeza con un fusil de calibre 7,62x51mm NATO, sin motivo aparente alguno. El asesino permanece impune hasta el día de hoy gracias a las maniobras jurídicas de Flavio.


Flavio y su asesora económica, Daniella Marques, han declarado que las políticas criminales de Milei constituyen un “excelente ejemplo”; planean reemplazar a los funcionarios públicos por inteligencia artificial, modificar la Constitución de Brasil sin contar con una asamblea constituyente elegida para tal fin y cancelar las elecciones burguesas de 2030, con el objetivo de que Flavio ejerza un mandato ilegal y dictatorial de ocho años para, supuestamente, “poner a Brasil en su lugar”.


En definitiva, Flavio Bolsonaro es una figura similar a un Ramfis Trujillo o un “Tachito” Somoza: un *playboy* y vividor, hijo de un dictador, elevado a la categoría de político; alguien incluso peor, más perverso y maligno que su propio padre, que pretende transformar Brasil en una dictadura narco-fascista, evangélica, sionista y personalista al servicio de la familia Bolsonaro.


Ante este panorama alarmante …

author: Danica Rachel
title: Operation Paperclip: The Nazis behind the US space program
content:
The Apollo moon landings are some of the most impressive technical feats ever achieved, and, for capitalism’s boosters, definitive evidence of the superiority of Western capitalism over all other social systems. The United States beating the Soviet Union to the finish line in the space race is held up as the ultimate triumph of capitalism over communism. But the path that took humans to the heavens began in the depths of hell: the Mittelbau-Dora concentration camp in Nazi Germany.

Built near the town of Nordhausen in central Germany, Mittelbau-Dora provided its prisoners as slaves to the Mittelwerk. This was a factory built under a mountain for the mass production of the V2 rocket, the world’s first long-range guided ballistic missile. The several thousand civilians killed in London and Antwerp by V2s were not the only victims of these Nazi weapons: at least 20,000 prisoners died as a result of the conditions in Mittelbau-Dora and the Mittelwerk.

Edwin Katzenellenbogen, who was convicted for crimes committed as a doctor at the Buchenwald camp, described Dora as “the Hell of all the concentration camps”. Tens of thousands of prisoners worked in interchanging 12-hour shifts, first to dig the kilometres-long tunnels of the Mittelwerk, then on the dark production lines within.

Sanitation was absent, disease and starvation were rampant, and collective punishment was common. Prisoners were hanged in groups of up to a dozen at a time, and on at least one occasion, bodies were left to dangle over the areas where others were forced to continue working.

Wernher von Braun was an SS officer, scientific director of the V-weapons project, and head of the Mittelbau-Dora planning office. He came from an aristocratic family in the German empire, and was among the first pioneers of advanced rocket science. Through the interwar years, Germany was banned from investing in many kinds of weaponry under the Treaty of Versailles, but rockets were obscure enough to avoid being on the list. During this time, von Braun became a leading designer and inventor of the engines needed to propel explosive missiles over incredible distances.

He joined the Nazi Party in 1937. If you believe his version of events, he joined only to be allowed to continue his scientific work. Regardless of his political loyalty, he was at least comfortable enough with the genocidal policies of the Third Reich to enjoy the slave labour it provided to him from Mittelbau-Dora. He was certainly aware of the reality of the Mittelwerk, having visited the tunnels himself at least ten times.

As the walls closed in on the Third Reich, with US and British forces moving in from the west and Russians from the east, von Braun hid the most important of the design documents for constructing V2s. Alongside Major General Walter Dornberger, head of the German army’s weapons department, von Braun used the hidden documents as leverage to get an amnesty with the Americans, betting that the US wanted the weapons more than they cared about prosecuting war criminals.

He was right. Von Braun, Dornberger and many other German experts in weapons of many terrifying forms—ballistic, chemical, and biological—were brought across the Atlantic under a secret program known as Operation Paperclip. They began work in the US, making weapons for a new, but no less bloodthirsty, empire. Their pasts were whitewashed, with the story being that they were innocent scientists forced by circumstance into working for the Nazi regime.

For his part, Joseph Stalin got the Mittelwerk factory itself, which continued operation for a few years before its machinery was brought back to Russia, along with thousands of German technicians needed to operate it. The USSR also got the equipment and methods to manufacture sarin gas, a chemical weapon so potent that contact with a single droplet causes a painful death.

Sarin was invented by Nazi chemists, among them Otto Ambros, who tested it on Auschwitz prisoners. Ambros was convicted for crimes against humanity in the Nuremberg trials, but that wasn’t a barrier to later working for US chemical companies and the US army. Within a few years of the end of the war, both imperial superpowers were producing large quantities of sarin and other chemical weapons.

The Cold War and the arms race 

The new phase of world imperialism had the globe divided into the West, with the US on top, against the East orbiting the USSR. The prospect of direct hot war between the empires gave …

title: Int’l solidarity vs Pax Silica
content:
At the Shut the Pax Down: Resistance and Solidarity Against Imperialist Plunder workshop in Bangkok, Thailand on October 14, 2026. (Photo from ILPS Philippines Facebook page)

Despite the advancements of AI technology, there is also the growing resistance.

BANGKOK – Organizations from different parts of the world are now united against the Pax Silica Initiative to be signed by the United States and the Philippines in November. US President Donald Trump reportedly will visit the Philippines to sign the agreement.

“We are in a period of extreme conflict between two very powerful and imperialist countries and the US is trembling and shaking. We have to maintain that fervor of revolution, that ability to throw stones at them, to bring them down and to make sure that the US imperialist power is no more,” said Azra Sayeed, secretary-general of the International League of Peoples Struggles (ILPS) during an activity in Bangkok, Thailand dubbed “Shut the Pax Down: Resistance and Solidarity Against Imperialist Plunder” on October 14.

The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank (IMF-WB) held its annual meeting in Bangkok from October 12 to 18. Participants included central bank governors, economic policy makers and business leaders.

In a statement, the Campaigners of the Peoples Global Campaign (PGC) Against IMF and World expressed concern over IMF-WB’s push for new technologies, including the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in Global South economies.

The group said that the “frantic race” for AI dominance intensified mining and extraction in resource-rich countries in the Global South. Transnational corporations are extracting rare earth elements (REEs) and other critical minerals to meet the growing demand for AI infrastructure. To secure control over the AI supply chain, countries like the US initiated the formation of Pax Silica and other similar formations.

“We know that imperialism is about world domination and control over resources. In the previous century, the rivalry among imperialist powers centered on oil because whoever controlled oil could wield significant influence over the military and the economy,” Arnold Padilla, secretary-general of ILPS-Philippines said during the event.

Now, he stressed, the battle is over critical minerals as whoever controls AI and the critical minerals needed to build its infrastructure could gain a significant advantage in dominating the world. “Essentially, that’s the battle now between the US and China. So, who will control this critical sector?”

This is why, Padilla said, the Philippines is up for a major battle to halt the signing of the US-led Pax Silica Initiative this year in time for the Asean Summit from November 16 to 18.

He said that AI is not just about the software that people use but also about weapons like drones “that can make decisions in actual battles without any human intervention.” He added that these sophisticated weapons will be made of minerals to be extracted from the Philippines.

Read: Critical minerals policy framework linked to Pax Silica? Read: War and plunder: US imperialism in the Philippines

“Pax Silica is made up of 24 countries, of course, led by the US. And it’s a special coalition. Specifically chosen by the US because countries that belong to Pax Silica perform a specific specialized role because it’s about controlling the supply chain,” Padilla said. “We don’t have high technology, we don’t have the logistic network, we don’t have capital or energy. But what do we have? We have the critical minerals. So for us in the Philippines, this is all about plunder.”

Donna Denina, secretary-general of International Women’s Alliance (IWA), said that US Undersecretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg, former tech executive and adviser tied to the controversial software firm Palantir, designed Pax Silica to give the US control over the global technology supply chain.

Palantir is a technology firm with clients from the Pentagon and foreign militaries including the Israeli government. But Denina said that Palantir is now expanding its influence beyond military tech into the health care sector.

In the US, she said that Palantir’s AI software is being used to manage hospital staffing and scheduling. This raised concerns among healthcare workers and prompted protests.

She said that more than 1,000 nurses from the National Nurses United union protested against healthcare institutions’ contracts with Palantir …

author: ROAPE
title: Eusi Kwayana (1925-2026)
content:
Eusi Kwayana was born Sydney King, as he was known initially for his first, more than two decades in public life. In 1968 he took on his African name which in Swahili means ‘Black man of Guyana.’


Eusi Kwayana was a founding father of post-colonial independence Guyana and Caribbean politics and was associated with the triumvirate of personalities that shaped them: Cheddi Jagan, Forbes Burnham, and Walter Rodney. He came to write the anthems of the three parties they led. Yet his own contributions to the Black and global radical traditions are still being recognized and recorded. This will be challenging in an environment where he receives national and regional honors for being a mere educator, writer, and cultural activist. It’s undeniable; he was a revolutionary.


What does it mean that Eusi Kwayana was a revolutionary? He was a campaigner against white supremacy, empire, capitalism, patriarchy, and ecological destruction. More than that, where he led breakthroughs against colonialism that denied Guyana, the Caribbean, and the Global South self-government, at the post-colonial independence moment he continued to confront the African and Caribbean political class, whether aristocratic or progressive. As historian and political activist, he always wished for everyday people to directly hold the reins of society. Of course, it was a matter of positioning ourselves to bring this about. His strategies of what to do and how to do it, must be revisited.


Detained When Guyana was Occupied by Anglo-American Imperialism


Eusi was detained when the Cheddi Jagan-led People’s Progressive Party (PPP) was overthrown by Anglo-American empire after winning election to Guyana’s colonial legislature in 1953. The country was occupied for 133 days. Before the Cuban Revolution of 1959, the PPP of Guyana was seen as a major threat to US and British hegemony during the Cold War in the Western hemisphere.


Eusi, with Rory Westmaas and Martin Carter, were perceived as the ‘ultra-left’ of the PPP.  In 1956, the split with Cheddi Jagan came, not over disagreements about commitments to a multi-racial party or movement. Rather, when Eusi and others advanced and defended the inclusion of Guyana in the movement for West Indian Federation. It was a permanent concern.


Multi-Racial Unity, Black Autonomy, and Caribbean Federation


This was part of an unfolding process of awareness. Cheddi Jagan was a socialist cosmopolitan when he faced the wider public. But he was also an ethnic leader of the Indo-Guyanese. Eusi concluded that it was no creative conflict to be an advocate for Afro-Guyanese as well. And it was important to address his Afro-Guyanese constituency

within the hearing

 of the Indo-Guyanese.


In 1959, Eusi became friendly with CLR James and Selma James in Trinidad at the height of the movement for colonial freedom led by Eric Williams’s People’s National Movement (PNM). He learned some important things about political journalism and activism in dialogue with CLR as he was editing

The Nation,

and Eusi was responsible for the People’s National Congress’s (PNC)

The New Nation

in Guyana.


Making Guyana a Global Refuge


In 1961, Eusi founded African Society for Racial Equality (ASRE) with the scientist H.H. Nicholson, known as ‘Vigilance’, and in 1964, co-founded African Society for Cultural Relations with Independent Africa (ASCRIA). With his wife

Tchaiko Kwayana

, an African American from Georgia in the US, who made her own mark as a teacher in New York and California, and her own sojourns to Nigeria, Ghana, and Latin America, Eusi pioneered the African cultural revolution in the Western Hemisphere, and was a transmission belt for African Americans and continental Africans finding a refuge from white supremacy and empire in Guyana as they pursued self-reliance and cooperative living. He was instrumental in making powerful ties between Ghana and Guyana.


It was Eusi that in 1966 gave Forbes Burnham the idea for Guyana being known as the ‘cooperative republic’ at official independence. In the early 1970s, Eusi was a supporter of the most dedicated cooperatives in the hinterland, such as the one at Marudi led by Joe Maxwell. The most dynamic cooperatives would be repressed by the state before the famous Jonestown fiasco.


An Original Educator of the African World

author: Yohannes Woldemariam
title: From Haile Selassie to Abiy Ahmed: the Human Cost of Imperial Nostalgia
content:
The irony is difficult to escape. Haile Selassie became a symbol of resistance to foreign aggression while denying Eritreans the right to self-determination. Abiy Ahmed was rewarded for accepting Eritrea’s internationally recognized border, yet within a few years his government began advancing claims to sovereign access to the Red Sea. The very territorial settlement that helped earn him the Nobel Peace Prize now stands in tension with his maritime ambitions.

Both men benefited enormously from international recognition. Their reputations gave them prestige and influence, but those reputations have too often overshadowed the suffering of the people under their rule. Haile Selassie’s imperial government suppressed resistance in Tigray and annexed Eritrea. Under Abiy Ahmed, Ethiopia has endured devastating wars, while his government’s Red Sea rhetoric has renewed Eritrean fears of territorial aggression.

I have written about the dangers of romanticizing Ethiopia’s imperial past, most recently in Imperial Nostalgia: History, Sovereignty, and the Unfinished Work of Decolonization in the Horn of Africa. What concerns me today is that this nostalgia is no longer confined to history books or monuments. It has returned to contemporary politics, and the consequences could be catastrophic for another generation of Ethiopians and Eritreans.

Haile Selassie’s reputation rests heavily on his resistance to Italian fascism. His appearance before the League of Nations in 1936 became one of the defining moments of his international career. But the familiar account gives the emperor far more prominence than the people who actually fought the occupation.

Haile Selassie left Ethiopia in 1936 and spent the following years in Britain. Meanwhile, Ethiopian patriots remained behind, fighting a brutal occupation. They lived in the mountains, organized resistance, endured enormous hardship and risked their lives. The emperor became the international face of their struggle, but he was not the one carrying its daily burden.

Consider Belay Zeleke, one of the patriots who fought the Italians. After the emperor returned to power, Belay came into conflict with the imperial government. In January 1945, he was executed alongside his brother and other associates. Think about the irony. A man who had fought foreign occupation was hanged under the authority of an emperor celebrated around the world for resisting that same occupation.

The emperor’s record in Tigray reveals another contradiction. In 1943, when people in Tigray rose against imperial authority during the first Woyane uprising, Haile Selassie turned to Britain for military assistance. British Royal Air Force aircraft bombed Mekelle and other locations. As Human Rights Watch documented, British air power helped suppress resistance to the imperial government.

Here was an emperor celebrated for standing against European aggression using European aircraft against people resisting his own rule. How does that fit the image of a champion of freedom?

Haile Selassie’s reputation as a Pan-Africanist also deserves scrutiny. His role in establishing the Organization of African Unity in Addis Ababa in 1963 was important. But diplomatic achievement should not be confused with a consistent commitment to African freedom.

Haile Selassie and his foreign minister, Ketema Yifru, worked to establish Ethiopia as a center of African diplomacy. Hosting the OAU gave the emperor enormous prestige. Yet the same government was denying Eritreans the right to determine their future.

Eritrea’s federal autonomy had been systematically dismantled before Haile Selassie annexed the territory in 1962. While the emperor was celebrated as a defender of African independence, Eritreans were beginning a liberation struggle that would last thirty years.

The OAU largely treated Eritrea as an internal Ethiopian matter. Its silence is especially striking when compared with Western Sahara. The organization admitted the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic despite Morocco’s fierce opposition. It was prepared to confront one African government over self-determination but failed to extend comparable recognition to Eritreans struggling against Ethiopian rule.

The romanticization of Haile Selassie reached extraordinary heights through the Rastafari movement. Emerging from racial oppression in Jamaica, the movement invested in the Ethiopian emperor with immense spiritual and political significance. For some Rastafarians, he became a …

author: Sarah Raymundo
title: On liberal opportunism and the “purity” smear
content:
Photo from Naga City Tourism Facebook page

Accusing leftists and activists of demanding a “useless politics of purity” is a classic liberal defense mechanism designed to shift the burden of moral failure onto the critic.

Why did former Vice President and now Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo roll out the pink carpet for the Zionist war machine? When Robredo hosted Israeli Ambassador Dana Kursh for an official courtesy visit, she was not merely performing the routine gestures of local hospitality. She was actively welcoming and legitimizing representatives of the US-Israeli genocidal apparatus. This intervention centers an anti-imperialist analysis to dismantle the liberal apologetics surrounding this act. Rather than an isolated error in judgment, this diplomatic encounter exposes the persistent, foundational tension within the Philippine political landscape: the contradiction between liberal reformism and anti-imperialist national liberation.

Dismissing progressives’ critique of Robredo’s hosting of the Israeli envoy as mere “political purism” is politically and morally impoverished. The underlying mechanism demands a total, systematic critique. To understand why her defenders deploy the “politics of purity” accusation, and why that defense completely falls apart when examining real power dynamics and economic interests, we must lay bare both the liberal class position and the ideological sleight of hand at work.

To make sense of Robredo’s pivot toward imperial hospitality, we must look directly at the liberal class position. Her stance is neither an accidental misstep nor a personal failure of political intelligence but the direct expression of her class character and political alignment. Liberal reformism in the global periphery operates strictly within the legal, institutional, and geopolitical framework dictated by US imperialism.

While Robredo served as a focal point against the overt state terrorism of the Marcos-Duterte dynasties, her opposition was strictly intra-class—a feud over how to manage the neocolonial state, pitting rule-of-law decorum against autocratic violence.

Because her political legitimacy rests upon acceptance by the global capitalist order, her opposition stops at the border of imperial interest. When forced to choose between international solidarity with an anti-imperialist national liberation movement and alignment with the Washington-Tel Aviv axis, liberal reformists invariably side with the imperial core. They cannot critique the drain of value, the extraction of labor, or the military hegemony of US imperialism because their entire political project depends on remaining within that very apparatus.

This structural subservience explains why defenders deploy the “purity politics” weapon whenever that alignment is exposed. Accusing leftists and activists of demanding a “useless politics of purity” is a classic liberal defense mechanism designed to shift the burden of moral failure onto the critic. From a materialist standpoint, this argument relies on three ideological fallacies:

First, it replaces a materialist baseline with ideological absolution. Opposition to active genocide, ethnic cleansing, and imperialist aggression is not a performative or elevated ideological standard; it is the absolute baseline of human solidarity and anti-imperialist struggle. Labeling principled opposition to mass slaughter as “purity” redefines baseline morality as an unreasonable demand, attempting to pass off complicity as pragmatic maturity.

Second, it operates on the logic of liberal idealism, which treats political stances as abstract moral choices made in a vacuum. Political actions reflect concrete class interests. Shielding a public figure from accountability for legitimizing a settler-colonial state serves a specific political function: it conditions the middle forces to accept imperial violence as a routine, acceptable feature of global diplomacy.

Third, it trades scientific alignment for unprincipled unity. Transformative praxis distinguishes between principled unity—built on anti-imperialist struggle and mass interest—and unprincipled unity, which colludes with reaction to preserve electoral coalitions. Demanding that the progressive movement remain silent on international solidarity to protect a liberal politician’s image trades human rights and anti-imperialist consciousness for temporary electoral expediency.

This dynamic reveals the distinct role of the middle forces—segments of the …

author: Monthly Review Press
title: The latest on Gabriel Rockhill’s “Who Paid the Pipers of Western Marxism?”
content:
Controversy, controversy…it’s no surprise that this book is selling very well. See more on this from

Bisharat Abbasi

, in his post: “

In Defence Of Gabriel Rockhill’s

Who Paid the Pipers of Western Marxism: Anti-Imperialist Marxism Versus The Imperial Theory Industry

.

“


DIGEST: Reviews, interviews, appearances


Marx Memorial Library

in London hosted a dual book launch for

Requiem for French Theory

 and

Who Paid the Pipers of Western Marxism?

with Gabriel Rockhill, Aymeric Monville, and Jennifer Ponce de León, who engaged in a discussion regarding the effects of imperialism on the production and dissemination of knowledge. Far from simply engaging in a critique of the faux radicalism of the prominent discourses within the imperial theory industry, the discussion was grounded in a reasoned defense of the vibrant international tradition of anti-imperialist Marxism. Topics included the imperial promotion of Western Marxism and postmodern French Theory, the international war of ideas, the failed efforts to discredit anti-imperialist Marxism, culturalism and identity politics vs. a materialist analysis of the colonial question, fascism past and present, the dialectics of actually existing socialism, and the current state of global class struggle in theory and practice.

Watch here

or below


The Left Chapter

, reviewed by Leo Schwarz:


“Shortly before his death, Herbert Marcuse wrote an essay on Rudolf Bahro’s book

The Alternative in Eastern Europe

. In the essay, Marcuse hailed Bahro’s ‘critique of actually existing socialism’ as ‘the most important contribution to Marxist theory and practice in decades.’ This statement was part of a coordinated campaign for the book and for Bahro that swept through the major media outlets of the Western world between 1977 and 1979–80. As we now know (or can know), a striking number of the key figures in this campaign maintained connections in the postwar decades to the Central Intelligence Agency or to various institutions and organizations that were either controlled, funded, or considered ‘friendly’ by the CIA or the U.S. State Department. In the first volume of his three-volume reconstruction of the ‘intellectual world war’ against actually existing socialism, Gabriel Rockhill examines the history and specific function of these networks of the ‘imperial theory industry’ that emerged after 1945, with his interest focused primarily on the Frankfurt School and the academic “Marxisms” of the Western world, which are usually categorized as ‘Western Marxism’…..”

 Read more….


Kaanan

,

 reviewed by Adel Samara


“…I was among those who criticized the Soviet system in its post-Stalin decades, and the lesson learned was that the greatest losers were the peripheral countries, especially the Arab nation, since the Soviets had long acted as a force restraining the imperialist beast. More importantly, this collapse was, in historical-materialist terms, a setback—an exception—because history fundamentally advances upward. Though our wounds were deep, the class enemy emerged victorious but also wounded, most notably by becoming the sole superpower, exposing its flaws and unleashing its brutality. In this brief context, I attempt to summarize Gabriel Rockhill’s book—a painstaking and rigorously documented scholarly work. Yet its timing is no less important than the work itself, for it constitutes a bold revolutionary confrontation that demonstrates the author’s profound communist commitment in an era when loyalty to communism has become rare and the fungi of internalized defeat have spread everywhere, filling the burrows with fleeing rats….”
