author: Unknown
title: Elisée Reclus - The Vivisection of China
content:
Author

: Elisée Reclus

Title

: The Vivisection of China

Date

: 1898

Notes

: From the September 1898 issue of The Atlantic

Source

: Retrieved on October 22, 2026 from an archived copy of https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/1898/09/the-vivisection-of-china/636369/


 THE great events which are creating such an excitement in the West Indies over the last shreds of the ancient colonial empire of Spain will undoubtedly have consequences of extreme importance, and become, in the fullest sense of the term, a part of history. But, however intense their interest, and however marked the change which they are certain to occasion in the equilibrium of the world, they remain altogether inferior in real significance to the revolutions which are taking place in the Far East.


 War of some sort between America and Spain on the subject of Cuba had long been unavoidable. No less than a century ago, — at the time when France lost her plantations in San Domingo, and the republic of Hayti was born, — it was easy to foresee the rupture of the ties which had bound to the Spain of Cortez and Pizarro the insular fragments of the great hemisphere appropriated by Pope Alexander VI. The various colonies were sure to break away, one by one, from their metropolitan stepmother, set up for themselves, and live their own life. Cuba and Porto Rico, sucked into the whirlpool of war, are but accomplishing their “manifest destiny,” and fulfilling the prophecies repeatedly uttered by the historians of the last generation but one.


 The progress of events in the eastern portion of the Asian continent had by no means been so fully anticipated. One might certainly have ventured to predict that there, also, populations long crushed by civil and military oppression would one day lay claim to the rights of free men; but it could never have been foreseen under what amazingly dramatic conditions the claim would be asserted. Our ancestors, at the beginning of the nineteenth century, would never have harbored, in their wildest dreams, the fantastic notion that Japan, the empire of the Rising Sun, would spontaneously transform itself into a “European power;” European, at least, if not in language, history, and traditions, in the complete recasting of its administration, institutions, customs, and theories, in its devotion to science, and in its entire and unreserved acceptance of a policy based on observation and experience.


 This is the great event of the century, — one which casts into the shade all the other occurrences of an epoch which has nevertheless been rich in memorable events. And it will be no solitary

avatar;

 there are unmistakable signs that other transformations of the same character are about to take place in the vast empire of China, and in all those countries where inhabitants of different race, yellow, red, or black, are brought into close contact with the men of our own Aryano - Greco - Latin civilization. So vanishes that oft-repeated assertion of the ethnologists, that

race

 is a final and irreducible fact, and that no possible progress in the perception of scientific or moral truths can ever prevail against it. It is from this point of view that the recent history of the Far East presents phenomena to which it behooves us to devote our most serious attention.


 There are those, of course, who tell us that all these events are illusory; that the prodigious changes which have taken place in the Japanese world are a lying phantasmagoria and a vain show; that the national mind and character have undergone no real modification; and that the Japanese are sure to escape, sooner or later, from the sphere of European attraction. We hear them compared to savages, who, having learned in the schools of London or Paris the customs of civilization, make haste, as soon as they get back to their forests and savannas, to cast aside their conventional garments, and array themselves in the toggery consecrated by ancestral instinct and hereditary custom.


 Such assertions appear to us to rest on a complete misconception of indisputable facts. The Japanese have most certainly entered into that realm of civilization on which Bacon and Darwin have set their seal; for if imperial caprice and the spread of bourgeois fashions have power to alter the external aspect of a nation, such influences can have but little effect on its underlying moral sense, its religious beliefs, its educational theories, and the essential principle of its …

author: Benji
title: Töten im Takt – Die grausamste Maschine bei Tönnies
content:
Töten im Takt – Die grausamste Maschine bei Tönnies

Tiere leiden vor dem Schlachten Höllenqualen bei CO₂-Betäubung

ARIWA veröffentlicht jetzt erstmals umfangreiche Aufnahmen aus einem Schlachthof von Tönnies. Schlachthöfe gehören zu den schwierigsten Herausforderungen für Undercover-Aufnahmen, da sie extrem gut gesichert sind. Die Betreiber setzen alles daran, dass das, was dort geschieht, nicht an die Öffentlichkeit gelangt.


19.10.2026, Deutschland


 NDR berichtet mit Videomaterial von ARIWA.


Er ist Deutschlands größter Schlachtkonzern und gilt als eines der mächtigsten Unternehmen der europäischen Fleischindustrie: Tönnies. Als Marktführer produziert er 30 Prozent des gesamten deutschen Schweinefleischs. Allein 2023 meldete der Konzern einen Jahresumsatz von über 7 Milliarden Euro. Dafür tötet Tönnies jedes Jahr 16 Millionen


Schweine. 


Das uns vorliegende Material zeigt, wie Mitarbeiter*innen die Tiere beim Zutrieb schlagen und sie unter automatischen Toren eingeklemmt werden. Es zeigt den grausamen Erstickungskampf in der CO₂-Anlage mit Tieren, die in Gondeln vor Angst schreien und versuchen zu fliehen. Und es zeigt zahlreiche Verstöße gegen die gesetzlichen Vorschriften vor und während der Schlachtung.


Von der Ankunft bis zum Tod:

Erste Undercover-Aufnahmen aus Tönnies Schlachthof


Das vorliegende Material dokumentiert erstmals unabhängig den gesamten Ablauf der Schlachtung von der Ankunft der Tiere im Schlachthof bis zur Tötung. Die Aufnahmen zeigen, wie leidvoll die letzten Stunden im Leben der Tiere sind. Das liegt auch an einer Maschine im Schlachthof, die grausamer nicht sein könnte: Die sogenannte CO₂-Betäubungsanlage.


Die Betäubung vor dem Schlachten ist gesetzlich vorgeschrieben. Die Tiere sollen so vor Schmerzen und Stress geschützt werden. Auch zur Betäubung selbst gibt es eindeutige Vorgaben: Paragraf 12 der Tierschutz-Schlachtverordnung legt fest, dass Tiere “schnell und unter Vermeidung von Schmerzen oder Leiden in einen (…) Zustand der Wahrnehmungs- und Empfindungslosigkeit” versetzt werden müssen. Der Betäubungsvorgang darf also keine Schmerzen oder Leid auslösen und muss bis zum Tod des Tieres anhalten. Doch die Aufnahmen zeigen eindeutig, dass die Betäubung mit CO₂ gegen diese Vorschrift verstößt!


Ankunft im Schlachthof


Am frühen Morgen kommen die ersten LKWs auf dem Schlachthof an. An den aufgenommenen Tagen werden mindestens fünftausend Schweine pro Tag hier angeliefert und getötet. Tönnies verfügt über ein riesiges Netz von Zulieferbetrieben in ganz Deutschland.


Nach ihrer Ankunft werden die Tiere in enge Wartebuchten gebracht. Hier läuft sanfte Musik, sie soll die Tiere entspannen. Es wirkt makaber. Neunzig Minuten lang sollen sich die vom Transport und Ausladen gestressten Schweine hier beruhigen, dabei ist zu erkennen, wie ängstlich sie sind.


Doch das wahre Grauen kommt erst noch. Nach anderthalb Stunden öffnet sich ein Tor. Ein Mitarbeiter beginnt, die Tiere in einen Treibgang zu scheuchen. Dabei kommt Gewalt zum Einsatz: Wenn die Schweine panisch versuchen zu fliehen, schlägt der Mitarbeiter mit der Treibstange zu, auch ins Gesicht. Die Schweine werden nach und nach in Sechsergruppen aufgeteilt. Als nächstes geht es für sie in die Betäubungsanlage.


Per Gondel in den Erstickungskampf


Die Schweine sind jetzt in einem engen Abteil, aus dem es kein Zurück gibt. Ein Mitarbeiter treibt die Gruppen nacheinander in die Gondelkäfige, mit denen es in wenigen Augenblicken gut 9 Meter nach unten in eine mit CO₂ gefüllte Grube geht. Manche Tiere werden von den schweren hydraulischen Trenngittern eingeklemmt und können sich nicht alleine befreien. Sie schreien vor Schmerz.


Sobald die erste Gruppe von Schweinen in ihre Gondel getrieben wurde, schließt sich der Käfig aus dicken Metallstangen. Kurze Zeit später setzt sich die Gondel in Bewegung. Die versteckte Kamera fährt mit. Innerhalb weniger Sekunden reagieren viele Schweine mit Panik. Viele schreien, schnappen nach Luft, werfen sich gegen die Gitterstäbe und steigen aufeinander. Die Fluchtversuche können so heftig sein, dass manche Tiere sich verletzen und Blutspuren an der Anlage zurücklassen.


Je tiefer die Tiere in den Schacht fahren, desto heftiger werden ihre Fluchtversuche. Die CO₂-Konzentration beträgt nach wenigen Metern schon 80 Prozent. Zeitgleich wird oben die nächste Gruppe in die Gondeln getrieben. Sie können die Angstschreie ihrer Artgenossen aus den Gondeln unter ihnen hören.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Animal Rights Advocates Call for Referendum on Snare Traps
content:
ANIMAL RIGHTS ADVOCATES are currently campaigning for a referendum to be held on the use of wild boar snares.

In particular, animal rights advocates have long criticized wild boar snares as overly cruel. Such traps use spring-loaded mechanisms to tighten around animals’ limbs when triggered.

Nevertheless, such traps have also been criticized for ensnaring other species, as they do not distinguish. Endangered species such as Formosan black bears and leopard cats had also been killed by such traps, as have cats and dogs, sometimes resulting in their losing limbs if they survive.

Though claims had been made that Indigenous hunters used such traps as part of traditional hunting rights, animal rights groups have generally cited that this was rarely the case, in that Indigenous hunters generally do not use such traps. By contrast, such animal rights advocates state that Indigenous hunters more commonly use traps made from wood, bamboo and vines, and other natural materials. In the past, the Central Election Commission turned down calls for a referendum on the use of wild boar snares on the basis that the referendum was unclear as to whether it pertained to traps used by Indigenous hunters.

Otherwise, such traps are sometimes used by farmers as a means of preventing damage to their crops. Animal rights advocates have called on the government to provide electric fencing, protective netting, or other means for farmers to protect their livestock and crops.

The proposals called for by animal rights advocates are relevant to the use, display, and sale of wild boar snares, as well as their import and export. It is thought that China is a major source of some of the wild boar snares used in Taiwan.

It is unclear as to whether the Central Election Commission will approve the referendum currently called for by animal rights advocates. At the same time, without a major political party endorsing it as an issue, such a referendum is unlikely to gain traction. It is to be seen if either the DPP or KMT, or perhaps even both parties, throw their weight behind the proposal.

One notes that there have been cases of political bipartisanship between both major parties on the issue of animal rights in past years, as seen with politicians of both parties supporting enshrining animal rights in the constitution. Even so, such politicians ultimately did not prove serious about such promises outside of election campaigning, as a result of which neither the KMT nor DPP acted on claims in past election cycles that animal rights would see constitutional protection.

author: Sophie Lemcke
title: So ist es, als weibliches Rind in der Milchindustrie zu leben
content:
Die Milchindustrie ist ein grausamer Kreislauf des Leids und endet mit einem gewaltvollen Tod.


Wie fühlt es sich an, in dieses System hineingeboren zu werden, ohne die Möglichkeit, dem zu entkommen?


Der einzige Grund, weshalb die Industrie dich „produziert“ hat: Auch du sollst Kinder gebären, immer wieder, damit du Milch produzierst. Milch, die dann von Menschen, statt von deinem Kalb konsumiert werden kann.


Du wirst fixiert, während jemand das Besamungsgerät in deine Vagina sowie seinen Arm in deinen Anus einführt. Wenn die Zwangsbefruchtung nicht beim ersten Mal zur Trächtigkeit führt – was oft der Fall ist –, wird dieser Vorgang mehrfach wiederholt.


Neun Monate – wie bei uns Menschen – wächst dein Kalb in dir heran. Du spürst eine Verbindung, merkst, wie es sich bewegt und immer größer wird. Je schwerer du selbst wirst, umso stärker werden deine Gelenkprobleme. Die rutschigen und harten Spaltenböden, auf denen du fast dein ganzes Leben verbringst, führen oft zu Verletzungen.


Dann bringst du dein Kalb zur Welt. Um dich herum riecht es extrem nach Kot und Ammoniak, von den Ausscheidungen der Tiere.


Endlich ist es da, noch ganz nass und schwach. Du leckst ihm über das Fell, um es zu wärmen. Es sucht deine Nähe und will an deinem Euter die für ihn so wichtige Erstmilch trinken. Sie stärkt sein noch schwaches Immunsystem und gibt ihm Kraft. Doch dann kommen die Arbeiter*innen.


Sie zerren dein noch ganz wackelig stehendes Kalb weg von dir. Es ruft nach dir. Du versuchst, bei ihm zu bleiben, aber du hast keine Chance. Die Menschen haben es weggebracht – du wirst es wahrscheinlich nie wiedersehen und nach nur zwei Monaten direkt wieder gewaltvoll befruchtet.


Du wirst nach der Geburt monatelang mehrmals täglich in den Melkstand getrieben – und die meiste Zeit davon bist du bereits wieder schwanger. Dein Körper muss gleichzeitig ein neues Kalb versorgen, das in dir heranwächst, und täglich über 22 Liter Milch produzieren. Dein Euter und deine Zitzen schmerzen. Aufgrund der extremen Überzüchtung produzierst du viermal so viel Milch, wie du es natürlicherweise für dein Kind tun würdest.


Die Prozeduren und Haltungsbedingungen zehren stark an deinem Körper. Dein Euter ist entzündet und schmerzt bei jeder Berührung. Andere Tiere humpeln, weil ihnen jeder Schritt wehtut. Viele sind schwach und ausgelaugt.


Wenn du nicht schon vorher stirbst oder getötet wirst, weil dein Körper nicht mehr kann, dann wirst du voraussichtlich nach nur fünf Jahren getötet – obwohl du unter natürlichen Bedingungen 25 Jahre alt werden könntest.


Dann kommt der Tag, an dem du als nicht mehr profitabel giltst. Du wirst aus dem Stall getrieben – das erste Mal nach Jahren verlässt du ihn, aber das ist kein Grund zur Freude.


Zusammen mit anderen erschöpften „ausgedienten Milchkühen“ wirst du auf einen Transporter verladen. Du hast Mühe, über die Rampe zu gehen. Deine Gelenke schmerzen vom jahrelangen Stehen auf Spaltenböden. Im engen Transporter stehst du dicht an dicht mit den anderen Tieren, der Lkw wackelt. Manche fallen hin und werden versehentlich getreten. Eure Fahrt in den Schlachthof dauert mehrere Stunden, ohne Wasser, ohne Nahrung, ohne Pause.


Angekommen erwartet dich ein brutaler Tod. Überall riecht es nach Blut, du bekommst Panik, aber es gibt keinen Ausweg. Dann ein Bolzenschuss in deinen Kopf. Wenn die Betäubung korrekt durchgeführt wurde und wirkt, brichst du zusammen. Wenn nicht, kann es sein, dass du bei Bewusstsein und unter extremen Schmerzen erlebst, wie dir deine Kehle aufgeschnitten wird und du verblutest.


Es ist unvorstellbar, was Mutterrinder in der Milchindustrie erleiden müssen.


Der wahre Preis von Milch


Ein Ermittler von Animal Equality hat mehrere Monate undercover in einem deutschen Milchgewinnungsbetrieb gearbeitet und den Alltag der Tiere dokumentiert. Was unsere Undercover-Recherche zeigt, ist der wahre Preis von Milch: Ausbeutung, Gewalt, Schmerz, Leid und Tod.


Auf unserer Webseite erfährst du mehr und kannst die Stellungnahme des Betriebs nachlesen:


Zur Undercover-Recherche


Unterstütze dieses grausame System nicht!


Entscheide dich konsequent für pflanzliche Lebensmittel. Im Supermarkt findest du zahlreiche Alternativen zu Milch, wie:


Hafermilch – mild, cremig, perfekt für Kaffee und Müsli (oft die günstigste Option!)


Sojamilch – proteinreich, ideal zum Kochen und Backen


Mandelmilch – leicht nussig, besonders lecker in Smoothies


Reismilch – süßlich und gut verträglich …

author: Sabrina Engel
title: Weniger Schutz für „Versuchstiere“: 80.000 Menschen unterschreiben gegen neues Gesetz
content:
Die Bundesregierung plant ein eigenes Gesetz für

Tierversuche

 und die Herausnahme der Tierversuchsregelungen aus dem Tierschutzgesetz. Dies könnte den Schutzstandard der Tiere enorm schwächen und es könnte erlaubt werden, was zurzeit noch strafbar ist, unter anderem massenhafte Tötungen, Eingriffe ohne Betäubung und Verstümmelungen. Weniger strenge Kontrollen könnten ebenfalls eine Folge sein.   


Ein solches Gesetz könnte Tieren den ohnehin unzureichenden Schutz nehmen und sie noch größerem

Leid im Versuchslabor

 aussetzen.  


Daher haben wir von PETA Deutschland gemeinsam mit zahlreichen weiteren Tierschutzorganisationen Anfang des Jahres eine Bundestagspetition gestartet – mit großem Zuspruch: Innerhalb von sechs Wochen haben weit über 80.000 Menschen die Petition unterzeichnet. Damit wurde die erforderliche Zahl von 30.000 Stimmen für die weitere Behandlung im Bundestag weit übertroffen. [1] Die Petition fordert die Bundesregierung auf, Regelungen zu Tierversuchen im Tierschutzgesetz zu belassen und aktuelle Standards zum Schutz der Tiere nicht noch weiter herabzusenken.   


Anhörung im Bundestag legt Mängel im Vorhaben der Bundesregierung offen

 


Am 12. Oktober 2026 fand die offizielle Anhörung vor dem Petitionsausschuss statt. [2] Der Jurist und Hauptpetent Dr. Christoph Maisack (Deutsche Juristische Gesellschaft für Tierschutzrecht) – unterstützt von Dr. Tamara Zietek (Ärzte gegen Tierversuche) – machte die Mängel des Vorhabens der Bundesregierung sowohl in seiner Rede als auch während der Diskussion deutlich.  


Die zahlreichen Fragen der anwesenden Bundestagsabgeordneten an die Regierungsvertreter:innen legten vor allem offen, was wir in der Petition schon darlegen: Ein eigenständiges Tierversuchsgesetz ist weder notwendig noch der richtige Weg, um die Forschenden zu entlasten – birgt aber die große Gefahr, dass Tiere in Laboren noch weniger gesetzlichen Schutz bekommen.  


Die Petition befindet sich nun in der Prüfung. Wir setzen uns weiterhin dafür ein, dass die Regelungen zu Tierversuchen im Tierschutzgesetz bleiben und der ohnehin unzureichende Schutz der Tiere nicht weiter geschwächt wird. Dazu arbeiten wir beispielsweise gemeinsam mit anderen Organisationen an der Modernisierung und Aktualisierung anderer Dokumente (z. B. der Allgemeinen Verwaltungsvorschrift für das Tierschutzgesetz), die die Umsetzung des geltenden Tierschutzrechts einheitlich für alle Tiere festlegen.  


 

Wir bedanken uns bei allen, die die Petition unterschrieben, verbreitet und gemeinsam mit uns zur erfolgreichsten Bundestagspetition im Bereich Tierschutz aller Zeiten gemacht haben!

  


Hintergrund zum geplanten neuen


TierVERSUCHSgesetz: Das könnte die Entkopplung vom TierSCHUTZgesetz bedeuten 

 


Die Bundesregierung kündigte an, ein eigenständiges Gesetz für Tierversuche erschaffen zu wollen: 

Tierversuche sollen damit vom Tierschutzgesetz abgekoppelt werden

. Für 

die unzähligen Tiere

, die in Versuchen missbraucht werden, könnte das noch 

weniger Schutz

 und noch 

mehr Leid

 bedeuten: 


Das 

Tierschutzgesetz

 enthält zentrale 

Schutz- und Wertungsnormen

. 


Diese Grundnormen gelten bislang 

für alle Tiere gleichermaßen

, auch für Tiere in Tierversuchen. 


Sie stellen eine wesentliche 

rechtliche Schranke

 gegen das 

Zufügen von Schmerzen, Leiden und Schäden

 und gegen das 

Töten von Tieren

 aus wirtschaftlichen Gründen dar. 


Genau diese 

Schutzwirkung

 könnte durch Herausnahme der sogenannten Versuchstiere aus dem TierSCHUTZgesetz und die Einführung eines TierVERSUCHSgesetzes 

beseitigt

 werden. Auch die Tierärzteschaft spricht sich deutlich gegen dieses Vorhaben aus. [1] 


Mögliche Folgen eines neuen Tierversuchsgesetzes

 


Eine zentrale Konsequenz dieser Entkopplung könnte z. B. für sogenannte

ausdrücklich erlaubt

Darüber hinaus könnte ein eigenständiges TierVERSUCHSgesetz zu einer weiteren

author: The Canadian Press
title: Youths tell trial of climate change toll, from anxiety to flood and heat impacts
content:
Sadie Vipond says she was just seven years old when she began noticing the impacts of climate change.


Now a 20-year-old plaintiff in Canada’s first youth-led climate trial, Vipond described experiencing catastrophic floods in Calgary in 2013 that the city says resulted in mass evacuations, one death and $6 billion in financial losses.


“I was beginning to see different actions in my community around the climate crisis, and so I was also feeling very anxious about my future,” she told the Federal Court in Vancouver.


Vipond is one of 15 plaintiffs who are arguing that federal legislation violates their constitutional rights by continuing the trajectory of greenhouse gas emissions.


The trial that began Monday heard in an opening statement from the youths’ lawyer, Catherine Boies Parker, that the case is not about the existence of climate change but rather whether the government is “constitutionally required to stop making it worse.”


She said the Charter must protect youth from their own government’s actions.


Vipond told the court on Tuesday that she had experienced several climate change events since the floods, including wildfire smoke and intense heat.


“I’ve been seeing these impacts all my life, and I’ve been seeing how these impacts are getting worse,” she said, adding that they had taken a toll on her mental health.


“I am very nervous for these one-in-a-century events to become more frequent and more and more impactful.”


Vipond testified that she joined the case when she was 13 years old, after appealing to Calgary City council to adopt a climate recovery plan. Now, she’s looking for a more national response.


“I want to see the creation of a plan for my country because I’m scared for what my future is going to look like and what the future for future generations will look like,” she said.


“I want the courts to know we are doing this for our future and we are all, at the end of the day, kids wanting to hold our governments accountable to be able to make our future safer and better for everyone to come after us.”


Sophia Sidarous of the Metepenagiag First Nation in New Brunswick told the court on Tuesday that

climate change

 has had an impact on Indigenous cultural practices, including the cancellation of sacred fires and sweat lodges for safety reasons due to intense heat or to comply with provincial fire bans.


She said it took away their ability “to be cleansed” and to “learn from the elders while they’re still here.”


She described removing herself from powwows to sit in air-conditioning with her young son, and the decline in availability of traditional foods, including salmon and moose.


Traditional plants such as chaga, a type of medicinal fungus that grows on birch trees, have started disappearing, she said.


“Due to the rising temperatures and unprecedented wildfires in the Atlantic, a lot of the birch bark trees are being impacted by that, and so the chaga that grows on those birchbark trees are burning or dying because the tree isn’t healthy,” she said.


She described moving to Halifax and reflected on experiencing the record-breaking hurricane Fiona in 2022, then preparing for possible evacuations caused by flooding and wildfires in 2023 and 2025.


“It’s just very depressing to have to deal with constant crises all the time and a constant survival mode to be in,” she told the court.


When asked why she decided to join the case seven years ago, she said she felt it was important to represent her First Nation.


“Indigenous peoples are experiencing a very specific type of impact that deals with their way of life and a very severe way of moving forward with a lot of these things disappearing in front of our eyes, and I also wanted to make sure that the future generations knew that we tried.”


Others among the 15 youth plaintiffs from seven provinces and two territories are expected to testify about how they have suffered what their lawyers call “specific harms connected directly to the government’s conduct.”


The court has heard these include respiratory illness worsened by wildfire smoke, displacement due to extreme weather, mental health impacts, such as climate anxiety, and loss of cultural connections to the land that has been lost due to climate disasters.

title: Soma’dan Ankara’ya yürüyen İmbat Madencilik işçilerine polis müdahale etti
content:
Manisa — Soma’dan Ankara’ya yürüyüş başlatan İmbat Madencilik işçileri, güzergahta ulaşım engeli ve biber gazlı müdahale ile karşılaştıklarını söyleyerek yaşananlara, "Bize biber gazıyla müdahale ediliyor. Geldiğimiz nokta bu” diye tepki gösterdi.

Manisa’nın Soma ilçesinde bir yılı aşkın süredir ücret ve alacaklarının parça parça ödendiğini belirterek Ankara’ya yürüyüş başlatan maden işçileri, eylemlerinin ilerleyen saatlerinde sorunlarla karşılaştıklarını anlattı.

Türkiye Maden İşçileri Sendikası Ege Bölgesi Şubesi öncülüğünde düzenlenen basın açıklamasının ardından yürüyüşe geçen madenciler, Maden Şehitliği’ni ziyaret ederek hayatını kaybeden arkadaşlarını andı. Yürüyüş sırasında güvenlik güçlerinin engellemesiyle karşılaşan işçiler, engellere rağmen yollarına devam etti.

İmbat Madencilik işçileri alacakları için Ankara'ya yürüyor

Kırkağaç çamlık mevkisinde mola veren madenciler, yürüyüşlerini sürdürmekte kararlı olduklarını ancak güzergahta biber gazıyla müdahaleye maruz kaldıklarını ifade ederek, yaşananlara tepki gösterdi.

Yürüyüşün 17’nci kilometresindeki bir tesiste akşam yemeği molası veren madenciler, Ankara’ya ulaşmak için otobüs bulmakta da sorun yaşadıklarını bildirdi. İşçiler, otobüs firmalarından araç temin edilemediğini, araç bulunması durumunda ise otobüsün Ankara yerine Kırkağaç Çamına yönlendirilmesinin istendiği söyledi.

Yaşadıkları duruma tepki gösteren madenciler, “Bize biber gazıyla müdahale ediliyor. Geldiğimiz nokta bu” ifadelerini kullandı.

Ücret ve alacaklarının ödenmesi talebiyle Ankara yoluna çıkan madencilerin, karşılaştıkları engellere ve ulaşım sorununa rağmen Kırkağaç Bakır mevkisinde bulunan tesiste bekledikleri öğrenildi.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Shannia Cabuello
title: Proposed foreign-funded wind projects threaten Bicol fishers
content:
Photo frrom Province of Camarines Sur

“If they say this project is for development, development for whom? This is not for us fisherfolk.”

Norberto Tobias of Tanggol San Miguel Bay (SMB) Network stressed this point as he and other fisherfolk from Bicol expressed opposition to the planned 1,000-megawatt San Miguel Bay Offshore Wind Farm.

They joined the Kampuhang Magbubukid (peasant camp) in front of the Department of Agrarian Reform from October 15 to 20.

The proposed wind farm covers 23,307 hectares of coastal waters across municipalities in Camarines Sur and Camarines Norte, including the fishing communities in Calabanga, Cabusao, Tinambac, Siruma, Sipocot, Basud, and Mercedes. This affects at least 6,000 small-scale fisherfolk.

Tobias said in a statement that the planned wind project is only for the profit of foreign companies and its local partner.

The project reportedly started its pre-development phase in 2023 but the fisherfolk communities countered that they only learned about it in 2025.

It is just one of the three Offshore Wind Projects of the Copenhagen Infrastructure New Market Fund Corp. (CINMF), the first 100% foreign-owned company to be granted a wind energy service contract (WESC) by the Department of Energy (DOE). It acquired exclusive rights to explore and develop SMB for wind energy in electricity generation.

The wind farm was developed under the partnership of CINMF-affiliated and Denmark-based Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) and local tycoon Ayala group’s ACEN Corp which has a 25% stake.

In 2024, the project was also granted Green Lane status by Philippine Board of Investments (BOI), a Certificate of Energy Project of National Significance (CEPNS), and pre-development Environmental Compliance Certificate (ECC) which expedited the project’s necessary licenses and permits processes.

The Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP) described the Marcos Jr. administrations’ promotion of large-scale renewable energy investments as aggressive, citing its insufficient protection for coastal resources-dependent communities.

The group condemned how the government opened the renewable energy sector in 2022 to 100% foreign ownership, streamlining approvals for strategic investments.

Since August 2024, a total of 91 offshore wind contracts nationwide has been approved by the Department of Energy.

Along the same coastline, six other planned offshore wind projects also raised concerns on combined impacts on marine resources and fisherfolk way of living.

Calabanga fisherfolk leader Norberto Harukhok said in an interview with Climate Change Network for Community-based Initiatives (CCNCI) that fisherfolk in coastal areas are united to stop the power plant from pushing through as they do not want the future generation to suffer.

“We don’t have a problem if they put it there as long as they follow our request to build it 15 kilometers away. Not by the shore,” Harukhok said.

“This is where we catch fish, earn a living, and get food for our families. If they prohibit us from fishing, where would we go?” Tobias asked, stressing that they may suffer from fishing access restrictions, marine habitat damage, and declining catches.

The CCNCI interview also highlighted that effects on ecosystems may result from the project’s regular operations. Coastal families may also face much lower incomes and worsen hunger.

“Once it is placed there, the fishes would not come closer because of the loud vibrations. Muds would go on the shore. Once they dug it up, the fishes would die from toxicity,” Harukhok said, adding that small-scale fishers with no motorized boats would struggle more as it would be difficult to go far to fish.

Harukhok said that only the government and capitalists would benefit from the project, leaving the fisherfolk without any benefits.

“So-called solutions to the climate crisis must not create another crisis for fishing communities already struggling with poverty, rising costs and impacts of climate change,” KMP Secretary-General Ronnie Manalo said in a statement. (DAA)

author: Tik Root
title: Long-Awaited Climate Change Case Finally Goes to Court in Canada
content:
The outcome could prove persuasive in other climate litigation or spur new cases.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Climate change gets a rare day in court as 15 Canadian youth accuse the federal government of violating their constitutional rights by failing to adequately address the country’s role in global warming. Although thousands of similar cases have been filed across the globe, legal experts said this long-awaited case is arguably the most consequential to reach trial.

The lawsuit is the latest in a yearslong campaign by young people who are using the courts to force elected officials to mitigate climate change. Like similar cases in the United States, including the landmark Held v. Montana, the plaintiffs in La Rose v. His Majesty the King argue that the government has violated their constitutional rights by allowing the crisis to continue.

Set in Vancouver, the proceedings are slated to last five weeks, with the 15 plaintiffs expected to testify alongside climate scientists and other experts. “It’s the chance for the young people to tell their story,” said Kelly Matheson, deputy director for global strategy at Our Children’s Trust, the nonprofit behind this case and many similar efforts around the world.

The outcome, while not precedent-setting outside of Canada, could prove persuasive in other climate litigation or spur new cases. “We found that some of the positive decisions from some countries have been inspirational in other countries,” said Michael Gerrard, faculty director of the Columbia University’s Sabin Center for Climate Change Law. “This trial will be closely watched.”

The case began in 2019, when the youth, six of whom identify as Indigenous, filed suit. They alleged, among other things, that by not doing enough to combat climate change, the government had violated Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which guarantees “the right to life, liberty, and security of the person.” They also argued that federal action breached their equality protections granted under Section 15 of the charter because, as young people, they will bear a disproportionate share of the impacts of the crisis.

The original lawsuit took aim at much of Canada’s approach to climate change. The plaintiffs argued that the government had allowed emissions to remain dangerously high, set targets that fell short of what scientists said was necessary to avoid the worst outcomes, repeatedly failed to meet those targets, and continued supporting the development and expansion of fossil fuels.

Although the government did not challenge the reality of climate change, its arguments included a claim that the accusations were overly broad and the lawsuit improperly asked the court to resolve a political matter. A federal judge agreed and dismissed the case without a trial in 2020. The plaintiffs appealed. In 2023, the Federal Court of Appeal upheld the dismissal of the Section 15 claim but allowed the Section 7 arguments to proceed if the plaintiffs more specifically detailed the government conduct that violated their protected rights.

The plaintiffs amended their complaint to focus on the Canadian Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act of 2021, which commits the country to achieving the law’s objectives by 2050, and the 2030 emissions reduction plan adopted under that law. They argue that the efforts don’t go far enough to avoid violating their charter rights in the context of climate change and that the government committed to the net-zero law.

“Increasingly, people across Canada and the world are seeing the direct impacts of climate change,” said Andrew Gage, a staff lawyer for West Coast Environment Law who has worked on this case alongside Our Children’s Trust. “The plaintiffs will have their day in court.”

The Canadian Department of Justice referred a request for comment to Environment and Climate Change Canada, which declined an interview request but provided a written statement to Grist. “Our commitment to net-zero by 2050 has not wavered, and we are implementing an ambitious climate agenda,” a spokesperson, Samantha Bayard, wrote in an email. “The Government of Canada respects the role of the courts, the right of Canadians to bring matters before the courts, and the important role that an independent judiciary plays in our democracy.”

title: Şener: Flood disasters are not caused by heavy rainfall alone
content:
The floods that followed heavy rainfall in Istanbul last week have once again brought the destruction of the city's ecosystem and unplanned urbanisation into focus. The increasing spread of concrete development, the destruction of natural areas and the disruption of ecological balance are also heightening the risk of disasters.


At least four people lost their lives in the floods. The devastation in Ayazağa, where construction has expanded alongside the destruction of the Northern Forests, has renewed criticism of Istanbul's urban development policies.


Umut Şener from Polen Ecology spoke to ANF about the floods in Istanbul and the consequences of the destruction of the city's ecosystem.


‘The underlying problem is the city's lack of drinking water’


Umut Şener pointed out that ecological destruction in Istanbul has a long history and discussed the environmental problems the city has faced over the centuries.


Şener said, “In the case of Istanbul, it is possible to trace the transformation of nature as far back as antiquity. The environmental problems inherited by the Ottomans when they conquered Istanbul, following centuries of Roman and Byzantine rule, and the measures introduced to address them, demonstrate just how far back this history extends. The decrees concerning ecological matters issued during the Ottoman period, beginning with Sultan Mehmed the Conqueror, along with decisions made by the state bureaucracy and the legal authorities of the time, provide concrete examples of this.


The underlying problem is that Istanbul, surrounded by seas and with enclosed inland water basins, has faced a shortage of fresh water, particularly drinking water, since it first began to develop as a settlement. Over the centuries, population growth and expanding construction have added further problems to this shortage. Istanbul had previously served as the capital of the Byzantine Empire. When it became the capital of the Ottoman Empire, the existing problems were inherited, while the state's land-based system, implemented through conquest and settlement policies, contributed to the city's expansion and steadily growing population.


The destruction and pollution of wooded areas established to protect water resources, the discharge of rubbish and sewage into the Sea of Marmara, and the transformation of areas containing waterways and streams into residential neighbourhoods to meet housing needs were among the problems inherited by the Republic of Turkey from the Ottoman Empire. Of course, ecological problems that emerged with the development and acceleration of capitalism gradually turned into deliberate and increasingly intensive plunder of nature. Because the prevailing political outlook has never incorporated an ecological approach, these problems have become structural, compounded by new environmental problems, and continue to have devastating consequences.”


‘The effects of the Menderes era continue to this day’


Şener said that the plunder of Istanbul had been paved by the approach introduced during the Adnan Menderes era, which promoted the idea that “roads are civilisation”. 


He continued: “As is well known, Adnan Menderes is associated with roads. Roads were built recklessly to facilitate the spread of mechanisation, symbolised by cars in cities and tractors in rural areas. Of course, this must also be considered in the context of the Marshall Plan. Roads were presented as civilisation and development, but they also laid the foundations for the ecological problems that have become increasingly severe today. This was capitalist development that disregarded social needs.


A road was built along the Florya-Sirkeci-Sarayburnu route without any consideration for ecological, economic or aesthetic concerns in urban planning and architecture. Its construction involved expropriations that seriously damaged the cultural and historical fabric of the coastline, the building of seawalls and the creation of land reclamation areas.


The consequences continue today, from the disappearance of species in the Marmara ecosystem and problems such as marine mucilage to the destruction of public spaces inland, as seen in the Yedikule Gardens. These projects destroyed micro-ecosystems, disrupted water current patterns and caused pollution in water resources, including those flowing into the Sea of Marmara, to reach critical levels. The coastline was subjected to outright plunder, and that plunder continues.”

author: Albashir Dahab
title: Delayed Rains and Broken Routes: War and Climate Crisis in North Darfur’s Jebel Issa
content:
All names of individuals interviewed for this article have been changed their safety and privacy. 


The Fatal Rain of Wadi Saleh


In mid-September 2026, when rain finally touched the parched soil of Jebel Issa in North Darfur’s Al-Malha locality, it did not bring life, but rather severe ecological and economic devastation.


Under normal conditions along this fragile Sahelian belt, the rainy season begins in mid-June or early July and extends through late September This predictable precipitation serves as the ultimate lifeline for rainfed millet and sorghum farming, as well as the primary water source for livestock grazing across the northern Darfur plains. This year, however, unprecedented climate variability left the skies dry until 12 September.


When a sudden isolated downpour finally struck the western sectors of Jebel Issa livestock already severely weakened by months of starvation, scorching heat, and gruelling treks between depleted pastures and distant wells suffered immediate thermal and physical shock. Over three consecutive days, from 12 to 14 September, more than 420 head of sheep perished in Wadi Saleh alone, with additional unrecorded livestock deaths reported across neighbouring valleys.


Local livestock that have died from thermal shock after delayed rain. Photo credit: Albashir Dahab / Local Reporting Network.


‘The animals had been walking exhausting multi-kilometer distances every day searching for withered pasture left over from the previous year just to reach the few functional water points,’

explains Hassan Ahmed (name changed), representative of the Jebel Issa Emergency Response Room. ‘They arrived at the wells severely malnourished and dehydrated When the sudden downpour hit, accompanied by an abrupt steep temperature drop their weakened bodies simply could not endure the extreme climatic shock.’


In rural Darfur, livestock ownership carries a deeply collective social weight. ‘These 420 sheep were managed collectively by 16 caretakers, but under our traditional social structure, each caretaker manages a combined herd belonging to extended families brothers and kin’ Ahmed adds: ‘Wiping out these herds means destroying the entire financial safety net and accumulated wealth for dozens of vulnerable households in a single weekend’.


Regional Climate Anomalies and Sahelian Pressure


The crisis in Jebel Issa is not an isolated weather anomaly. It reflects a broader accelerating climate shift across the northern Sahelian belt. According to regional climate assessments and data from international bodies like the

Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change

 (IPCC), this zone is experiencing extreme rainfall variability characterised by shorter highly erratic rainy windows interspersed with prolonged, intense dry spells.


In Jebel Issa where subsistence farming relies strictly on rainfall without irrigation machinery or artificial reservoirs these delayed rains have disrupted the delicate ecological balance. According to estimates from the

Food and Agriculture Organization

 (FAO), regional cereal production across vulnerable belts in Darfur has plummeted sharply due to the convergence of delayed rainfall and conflict. Furthermore, the localised nature of the recent rainfall left the northern and eastern sectors of Jebel Issa completely dry, creating stark disparities where some farming councils received a single downpour while adjacent areas received not a single drop.


Weaponised Geography: Blocked Routes and Economic Siege


Jebel Issa sits roughly 35 kilometers from the administrative centre of Al-Malha. Jebel Issa serves as the central economic agricultural and water hub for a vast cluster of surrounding village councils including Wadi Hora, Jabra, Wadi Bisha, Wadi Tandis, and Del Sari. Neighboring areas such as Wadi Akhdar, Al-Har, Um Saro, Aito, Ashar, and Abkran face identical climatic conditions and rely entirely on Jebel Issa’s central infrastructure.


Wells in Jebel Issa are a source of water for a much wider region. Some currently stand empty. Photo credit: Albashir Dahab / Local Reporting Network.


Historically, communities in North Darfur weathered severe dry spells through vibrant cross-border trade and commercial supply lines moving along three major trade arteries: the Al-Dabbah route connecting to Northern Sudan, the Mellit route leading deeper into Darfur, and the northern Triangle (Al-Muthalath) border highway linking Sudan to Libya and Egypt.

title: In Amsterdam in November? Join Chris dePloeg, Jason Hickel and more, live, for “The Exterminating Empire”
content:
Pakuis de Zwijger

, Monday, November 23rd: :ive with Jason Hickel,

Ghassan Abu-Sittah

,

Harriët Bergman

,

Chihiro Geuzebroek

,

Max de Ploeg

 and the author!


In collaboration with In collaboration with Pijke ter Laak, join

Pakuis de Zwijger

 for a conversation with author Chris de Ploeg about his new book, a radical and urgent indictment of the global capitalist system and the imperial violence it unleashes upon people and planet alike. At its core, the book argues that genocide and ecocide are not tragic byproducts of capitalism – they are its fundamental features.


Together with renowned climate author Jason Hickel (in person), frontline Palestinian surgeon Ghassan Abu-Sittah (joining online) and our moderator, climate justice activist and researcher Harriët Bergman, we will dive deeper into the interconnections of the great challenges of our time–and more importantly, how to fight back. There will also be cultural performances from Chihiro Geuzebroek and brothers Chris and Max de Ploeg, tying their ancestral struggles in Bolivia and Armenia to the global struggle for liberation.

REVIEWS:


Morning Star

:

 “How did such a horror come to pass?” by Alex Hall


“

The Exterminating Empire

 began life as a Master’s thesis, nurtured into book form by Jason Hickel — the degrowth economist and author of The Divide, who contributes the foreword. The mentorship was well placed and De Ploeg has produced an impressively searing panorama of our global predicament…”


Counterpunch

, “

Resisting Annihilation: Reviewing “The Exterminating Empire”

, by Seth Sandronsky


“…de Ploeg, who does far more than compile lists of atrocities, draws parallels between the American holocaust of the native inhabitants’ relations with buffaloes and Israel’s genocide against Palestinians and their farming of olive trees. Land theft and separating those living on the land from it are nothing new. The author has skin in the game, given his family survived the Armenian genocide and Nazi holocaust…”


Counterpunch

, “

Capitalism is Waging War on Palestine While Creating a Burning Planet

” by Daniel Falcone:


Daniel Falcone:

What is the central argument of

The Exterminating Empire

 and how is the book structured? It looks as though the book serves as an intervention as well as an addition to current scholarship.  


Chris Kaspar de Ploeg:

 I open the book with some jarring facts that seem paradoxical at first sight. We need about 30 percent of our productive capacity to

give everyone on the planet a good life

. Not just the basics like housing, clothing and healthcare, but also modern appliances like refrigerators, laptops, access to the internet and more. At the same time, that standard of living is denied to about

80 percent of the world population

. Green energy has been cheaper than fossil fuels for years, yet climate breakdown is only accelerating. We could

solve world hunger

 with about 0.03 percent of global GDP, but hunger is only increasing.


That looks like an extraordinarily wasteful system, and it is. The point, however, is that under capitalism, these are not paradoxes at all. In fact, they are signs of capital’s success. Under our current economic system, the primary goal, ruthlessly pursued, is

profit maximization

. That profit maximization is reached through pushing down costs–and we are those costs, our labour, our environments, our lives–and by conquering markets, often through a mix of military and economic warfare. That essentially puts

capitalism on a warpath against life

. The system is working exactly as it is supposed to.


We see, for example, that profit rates are higher in the fossil fuel industry because it essentially

functions through monopolies

, despite the higher costs. We see that the military-industrial complex is growing exponentially, targeting any vestiges of resistance against

US-led global hegemony

, which globalized harsh budget cuts in social welfare, healthcare and education. These very conditions of

structural impoverishment

 then create the conditions of desperation necessary for people and countries to accept their status as sources for cheap labour, resources and land for global corporations, mostly centered in the Global North.


In the book I write about a dialectic between slavery and genocide, and between structural genocide and active genocide. A good way to understand that relationship is by going back to the

author: Joseph Lee
title: For Indigenous peoples in Brazil, the election results offer a reprieve — not a resolution
content:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s reelection as president of Brazil gave Indigenous communities a measure of relief after a campaign in which his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, promised to halt recognition of new Indigenous territories and push for more mining and development.


“For Indigenous Peoples, the reelection of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is more than a victory, and it is bigger than Brazil,” said Edson Krenak, who is Indigenous Krenak. “It is not about victory; it is about the possibility to dream and to fight without fear of death.”


But Sunday’s runoff election strengthened Bolsonaro’s movement in Congress, where his Liberal Party won the largest number of seats in both houses and the broader right gained a Senate majority. Leaders warn that this could open their territories to mining, weaken environmental protections, and roll back land rights, making it much harder for Lula to advance his Indigenous and environmental agendas.


Climate Observatory, a nonprofit coalition of 172 organizations, says

70 percent of the incoming lawmakers

 oppose the climate and environmental agenda, according to The Associated Press.


The stakes were especially high for Indigenous peoples because Bolsonaro campaigned on policies aligned with those of his father Jair Bolsonaro, whose presidency from 2019 to 2023 saw an increase in mining, land grabs,

deforestation

, and

attacks on their rights

. Amazon deforestation reached a record in 2022, and Indigenous leaders say their communities endured unchecked violence from illegal mining operations during the elder Bolsonaro’s time in office.


His son finished more than 2 million votes ahead of Lula in the first election earlier this month, but neither candidate secured the 50 percent required to win outright. That result sparked fear in Indigenous communities and environmental advocates, who warned that

the future of the Amazon was at stake

. Lula came back to win Sunday’s runoff by roughly 4.4 million votes, securing a fourth, nonconsecutive term as president.


In an interview between the two rounds of voting, Toya Manchineri, the general coordinator of the Coordination of Indigenous Organizations of the Brazilian Amazon, or COIAB, said Indigenous peoples across the rainforest were deeply concerned about the possibility of a Bolsonaro win. Much of the last three years of Lula’s administration were spent undoing the damage the Bolsonaro administration caused, Manchineri said.


Manchineri said Lula’s term has largely been a period of rebuilding as Indigenous peoples gained greater roles in decision making. “We were only beginning to see the resources returning,” he said.


In 2023, the administration established the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples and appointed Sônia Guajajara to lead it. Lula also revitalized the federal Indigenous affairs agency FUNAI after Bolsonaro had used it to support agribusiness, despite Indigenous resistance. The government also announced just before the election that Amazon

deforestation had fallen to its lowest level

 since recordkeeping began in 1988, according to the AP.


Still, Indigenous leaders say the progress made under Lula has not resolved deeper conflicts over land, development, and decision-making.


“Lula’s victory prevents a president who promised to halt Indigenous land demarcation from taking office, but our territories are far from safe,” Alessandra Korap Munduruku, coordinator of the Munduruku Pariri Indigenous Association,

said in a statement

. “We have demanded that Lula’s government respect our decisions and listen to Indigenous Peoples before advancing projects that affect our rivers and forests. Congress has become more dangerous for us, and we must remain organized. Our struggle does not end with an election’s outcome.” 


For Indigenous organizations, Lula’s victory is cause for hope, but they must now work with a Congress dominated by lawmakers who have already voted in favor of easing environmental protections and against Indigenous land claims. Given that dynamic, Krenak expressed concern about the difficulty Lula may face advancing his agenda. “The costs of negotiating with the Congress and senate will be very high, if ever successful,” he said.


The election also came amid years of Indigenous voters struggling to access the polls. Earlier this month, a court denied a request for transportation assistance filed by Indigenous peoples in the Javari Valley in northern Brazil. Other efforts were more successful: Court …

author: Petala Ironcloud
title: Data Center Near Yellowstone River Would Cause “Irreparable Harm,” Activist Says
content:
The Northern Cheyenne Tribal Council voted to ban data centers, but the Apsáalooke have yet to take a position.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The Northern Cheyenne Tribal Council voted unanimously this October to ban data centers on tribal land in Montana. The ban follows a decision in August by the Fort Peck Tribes to bar officials from projects involving data center developers.

But Montana’s Tribes are now split. Next door to the Northern Cheyenne, the Apsáalooke, or Crow Tribe, has not taken an official position and remains open to hearing proposals from companies, according to Shane Doyle, an Apsáalooke tribal member and The Nature Conservancy’s Indigenous right relations director. Doyle grew up on the Crow Reservation and has consistently advocated for reciprocity with the land, rendering him a voice in the dissent, whether he intends to be or not.

The stakes are highest in Crow country. In the small city of Hardin, at the Crow Indian Reservation’s northern edge, a former cryptocurrency mine is being actively converted into an AI data center. About 14 miles northwest of the reservation, Texas-based Quantica Infrastructure plans to build its Big Sky campus on nearly eight square miles of ranchland near the town of Broadview, north of Billings, Montana’s most populous city. As it’s currently planned, the data center would rank among the largest data centers in the world. The Yellowstone River Valley is “the heart of the Crow Nation,” Doyle said.

Krystal Two Bulls, who is Oglala Lakota and Northern Cheyenne, has been tracking these data centers closely. As the executive director of Honor the Earth, a nonprofit tracking data centers on or near reservation lands, she takes an extensive view of history and geography when it comes to tribal land and AI developments.

“Broadview is still a traditional territory of the Northern Cheyenne and also the Crow,” she told Truthout. “It may not technically be on the reservation, but it definitely is still going to have an impact on the land and the people around it.”

The divide over data centers comes as developers eye Montana for its land, water, and power, and as Tribes test how far their sovereignty can actually reach. Bans like the Northern Cheyenne’s are enforceable on tribal land, said Matthew Fletcher, a University of Michigan Law professor and member of the Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians. But tribal bans on off-reservation data centers that affect reservation waters are “unlikely to be enforceable,” Fletcher said, unless a tribe can show a very significant threat to its waters, enterprises, or citizens’ health.

Quantica has asked Northwestern Energy for more than 7,000 megawatts. The utility currently serves about 750 average megawatts, said Anne Hedges, executive director of the Montana Environmental Information Center. “We’ve never imagined something this massive,” she told Truthout. The company’s plan includes about 1,700 megawatts of gas generation, which alone would be more than the gas generated by all Montana’s existing gas plants combined.

The gas would affect more than just the rural Broadview community. A retired Billings pulmonologist modeled the air-quality impact of 1,700 megawatts using EPA tools, Hedges said, and found fine-particulate pollution spreading to communities east of the site, including the Crow, Northern Cheyenne, and Fort Peck reservations. “It’d be a disaster,” she said.

The Northern Cheyenne resolution, which passed by a vote of 8-0, covers all land on the reservation, says Melissa Lonebear, a Northern Cheyenne citizen and tribal council member. It quashes any extant or future data center discussions on their territory. (None are currently active.) “We have fought historically to preserve our land,” says Lonebear. “We have fought against coal development, coal bed methane, all these things.”

The Northern Cheyenne own nearly all of the land within their reservation, which makes the Tribe a target for developers looking for large, contiguous sites, Lonebear said. She added that the governor had remarked in a closed meeting with tribal leaders that big corporations were looking for land. “I almost felt like we would be targeted,” she said.

Fort Peck’s ban bars the tribal government, individuals, and entities from discussing proposals to build data centers on the tribe’s reservation. The tribe passed the ban after three companies …

title: ‘We changed the system’: how Serbian students ended Alexander Vučić’s 12 years in power
content:
“I see the glimpse of hope that this is our future and that actually we can say to our kids, our grandkids, we changed the system, we were the change.”


Gavin Brent Sullivan

 and

Tereza Capelos


 


Serbia’s student-led political movement has secured a historic election victory. Preliminary results suggest the so-called Student List has won 141 of the 250 seats in parliament, with the ruling Serbian Progressive Party taking 104. The result brings the 12-year rule of Alexander Vučić to an end.


 


The Student List’s story is remarkable. It has no standalone leader and fielded candidates without political experience from across

Serbian

 society. Stemming from student-led protests against the entrenched corruption and

creeping authoritarianism

 of the ruling regime, it has now achieved an improbable dream.


 


In late 2025, one of us (Gavin Brent Sullivan) conducted focus groups with members of the student protest movement as part of the

Pledge EU Horizon project

. The project explores the emotional dynamics of political grievances and their democratic implications.


 


The protesters’ grievances were centred on the 2024 collapse of a roof at the newly renovated

Novi Sad train station

 in northern Serbia, which killed 16 people. Allegations of state involvement through corruption in the procurement process and lowered building standards have been denied by the government. But they nonetheless sparked large nationwide protests.


 


Focus group participants expressed anger and underlying fear about harassment during the protests by what they said were government-funded gangs. They also spoke of their concern at the threats and violence directed towards them, not only as they protested but also when walking in areas near government buildings in main cities. Several students reported feeling threatened even in their own homes.


 


At the same time, the students voiced dissatisfaction with teachers who were not supportive of their movement, and other students who opposed them. This dissatisfaction extended to older family members and relatives who repeated government-controlled media fabrications about the protests. These included claims that the students were being paid by foreign anti-Serbian groups.


 


Despite the fear of arrest or worse, and despondency that change could really occur, the students who took part in the focus groups were resilient. They were focused on their long-term goal of regime change, with many students talking with pride about creating a leaderless movement that was organising candidates to challenge Vučić in an election.


 


Several participants reported feeling spontaneous, intense experiences of national pride when taking part in the protests. Some spoke of taking back national symbols such as the Serbian flag to counter propaganda that they were not patriotic and wanted to destroy the country.


 


Feelings of solidarity

were also experienced

 when minority Bosniak Muslim students from Novi Pazar University in south-western Serbia joined the protests. As one participant said:


 


They’re a minority which was at odds with Serbia, with Serbian nationals actually. So now we had that part of reunification with them and they’re a Muslim minority. They are really active in these protests and student protests and it’s been wonderful.


 


Another member of the focus group noted that they expected elections to be “brutal”. But they were optimistic about the prospect of unseating the Vučić government. They said: “I see the glimpse of hope that this is our future and that actually we can say to our kids, our grandkids, we changed the system, we were the change.”


 


At the same time, most of the students did not dare to dream that they would succeed in ousting a government that had held a 12-year grip on power. It is stunning now after Vučić’s concession speech in which he admitted “it is clear that we have lost these elections” to know that they were successful just one year later.


 


What’s next?


 


The remarkable victory of the Student List should give hope to any group opposing a corrupt, authoritarian regime that a core commitment to democracy is precisely what attracts voters to choose progressive change.


 


However, while there will be euphoria, pride and tears of joy in Serbia as the election result sinks in, there may also be groups who are fearful of change and that the new government

may seek accountability

 for members of the ousted regime. Some …

author: Tam Saavedra
title: WEI and UN Women Co-Launches Guide for Disability-Inclusive
content:
Across Asia and the Pacific, 350 million women and girls with disabilities navigate conflict, crisis, and climate instability. While they are frontline peacebuilders, community leaders, and human rights defenders, they remain systematically excluded from formal peace and security decision-making.

To break down these barriers, Women Enabled International (WEI) and the UN Women Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific have officially launched a landmark publication today: the Guidance Note on Disability-Inclusive National Action Plans on Women, Peace and Security in Asia and the Pacific. Released ahead of the annual UN Security Council high-level debate in New York, this first-of-its-kind guide provides a practical, policy-oriented blueprint for governments, policymakers, and civil society.

Read the full Guidance Note on Disability-Inclusive NAPs on WPS in Asia and the Pacific

Historically, women with disabilities in peace policies have been viewed narrowly as victims or passive recipients of protection. Co-drafted through consultations with 26 women and gender-diverse people with disabilities, in collaboration with Women Enabled International and the UN Women Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific, this guide directly challenges that narrative. It grounds its framework in a human rights model of disability and the core movement principle: “Nothing about us without us”.

As WEI Executive Director Maryangel García-Ramos Guadiana stated during the launch:

“The true value of this Guidance Note is that it exists, not as a siloed document, but as a means to ensure we, as feminist disabled change-makers, are not left out of the agenda, but we are the ones who get to set the agenda.”

UN Women Regional Director for Asia and the Pacific, Christine Arab, added:

“National Action Plans on WPS that include everyone lead to peace that lasts.”

The publication was shaped by participatory research, drawing on focus groups and surveys with 26 grassroots leaders with diverse disabilities across the region. It addresses critical ground-level hurdles—including digital exclusion, inaccessible evacuation infrastructure, and ableism in mainstream spaces—ensuring that the voices of women, girls and gender-diverse people with disabilities form the foundation of the guidance.

The publication urges stakeholders to align National Action Plans (NAPs) with international standards—including the CRPD, CEDAW, and UN Security Council Resolution 2475—across all four WPS pillars:

Participation: Reserve seats for organizations of persons with disabilities (OPDs)—especially women-led OPDs—on NAP steering committees with full accessibility support.

Participation: Reserve seats for organizations of persons with disabilities (OPDs)—especially women-led OPDs—on NAP steering committees with full accessibility support.

Prevention: Recognize women and gender-diverse people with disabilities as active peacebuilders and integrate intersectional early-warning indicators.

Prevention: Recognize women and gender-diverse people with disabilities as active peacebuilders and integrate intersectional early-warning indicators.

Protection: Address unique forms of violence (such as caregiver abuse or institutionalization) and guarantee accessible shelters and evacuation procedures.

Protection: Address unique forms of violence (such as caregiver abuse or institutionalization) and guarantee accessible shelters and evacuation procedures.

Relief & Recovery: Ensure transitional justice mechanisms, reparations, and post-conflict upskilling actively include women with disabilities.

Relief & Recovery: Ensure transitional justice mechanisms, reparations, and post-conflict upskilling actively include women with disabilities.

The guide also features a practical Disability-Inclusive WPS NAP Checklist to help stakeholders evaluate progress at every stage of policy implementation.

This Guidance Note was made possible with the generous support of the Government of the Republic of Korea (through the Ministry of Gender Equality and Family) as part of the project “Promoting Leadership of Future Generation Peacebuilders and Change-makers in Asia and the Pacific”, and of the Australian Government under the Regional Framework Towards Peaceful, Inclusive Societies (2023–2027).

author: Sara Luterman
title: Nursing Home Residents Have a Right to Vote — Despite What Trump CMS Agency Says
content:
The Nursing Home Reform Act of 1987 requires facilities to support their residents in exercising their rights.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Cindy Napolitan and her daughter Melissa have multiple sclerosis, a degenerative condition in which the immune system attacks the brain, spinal cord and nerves. They have lived together at a nursing home in Mesquite, Texas, for nine years. In previous elections, Cindy and Melissa Napolitan voted by mail, but this year they took an unusual step: They voted in person. They worried their mail-in ballots — and even their in-person votes — may not be counted.

“I’ve never worried like this before. I’ve never worried that I don’t have the proper ID. I’ve never worried that somebody is going to intimidate me. Will I encounter somebody that’s going to threaten me or make me feel less than? So yeah, I’m very worried, and I shouldn’t be,” Cindy Napolitan said. “I shouldn’t have to be worried about stuff like that. This is the 19th Amendment. I’m allowed to vote.”

Nursing home residents are guaranteed the right to vote. Around two-thirds of all nursing home residents in the United States are women, making aging and long-term care gendered issues.

There is no data on how many nursing home residents exercise that right. Cindy, 70, and Melissa Napolitan, 48, at least, feel like they’ve had good experiences with voting at their facility. Cindy Napolitan, in particular, has worked with the activities coordinator to organize rides to the polls for her, her daughter and other interested residents.

“We are scheduled to go on the first day of early voting. So in case there are any issues that we come across, we still have time to rectify the situation and be allowed to vote,” Cindy Napolitan said.

Cindy and Melissa Napolitan are more concerned this year than in previous years about government interference and voter suppression. Their fears are not unfounded: Experts and advocates for the rights of nursing home residents, older adults and people with disabilities are worried too.

In July, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services rescinded previous guidance affirming that nursing home residents have the right to vote.

“The memo does not alter the underlying law. Nursing homes are governed by the Nursing Home Reform Act of 1987 and its implementing regulations,” said Nina Kohn, a professor at Syracuse University and expert on elder law. “That law still requires facilities to support their residents in exercising their rights as Americans.”

The memo also emphasized voter fraud in nursing homes, specifically around mail-in ballots. For years, President Trump has disparaged mail-in ballots, insisting without evidence that fraudulent votes by mail had a role in his loss during the 2020 presidential election. His comments have led to some states restricting who can use a mail-in ballot and in what contexts.

According to experts, including Kohn, there is no evidence that voter fraud is a serious or widespread problem in nursing homes. Instead, Kohn is concerned about the chilling effect that it may have on residents’ rights.

“The language in the memo itself is intimidating, and it may understandably make staff think that they could face criminal prosecution or be in some other form of legal trouble if they help residents vote,” Kohn said.

Cindy and Melissa Napolitan do everything together — and on Monday, they voted together. They are also roommates at the facility; most people living in nursing homes are assigned roommates who are strangers.

“Unlike other people that have roommates that don’t get along, I’m very lucky and fortunate that I have somebody that loves me and I love her,” Cindy Napolitan said.

This is the second time Cindy and Melissa Napolitan have voted in person since entering a nursing home. The first time was during the 2024 presidential election.

“I’ve been checking my status weekly to make sure that I haven’t been dropped off the voter rolls, making sure my daughter and I don’t have some sort of issue that says that we can’t vote,” Cindy Napolitan said.

People living in nursing homes and other long-term care facilities face specific barriers. Some residents may need assistance filling out their ballots because they lack the movement or dexterity to hold a pen or press buttons on a computer screen. People with dexterity or coordination issues may also be unable to produce the same signature twice …

author: Mostafa Hosny
title: ‘Citizens’ health’ session at Egypt Forum 2026 boasts spending success with no mention of declining hospital bed numbers
content:
On Tuesday, the second day of Egypt Forum 2026, Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar described the political leadership’s support for the healthcare sector as unprecedented.


Speaking at the “citizen’s health”

session

 of Egypt Forum 2026, he said the approach dated back to the beginning of President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s presidency in 2014, when, he

said,

 Egypt faced a massive “disease burden,” with a lack of data and years of inadequate budget allocations that had failed to meet developmental ambitions for the system, particularly as population growth accelerated.


The minister said the state’s development plan had delivered gains in the sector, citing 16 presidential initiatives that had benefited 95 million citizens at a cost of LE44 billion. 


Abdel Ghaffar stressed that success in healthcare should not be measured by spending levels, but by the results citizens ultimately experience.


Mada Masr looked into some of those results, drawing from government

data

 published by the Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics (CAPMAS).


One clear result over the time period is the notable decline in the number of beds in public hospitals between 2013 and 2024, with a drop from around 98,291 to 84,225. 


Over the same period, the number of beds in private hospitals rose from 26,009 to 36,014. 


Still, the combined total of beds in public and private hospitals fell from 124,300 in 2013 to 120,239 in 2024.


While Abdel Ghaffar portrayed inadequate budget allocations as a problem of the past, the state

has consistently fallen short

 of the constitutionally mandated minimum for healthcare spending.

 Article 18 of the Constitution requires the state to allocate at least three percent of gross national product to public healthcare starting in FY 2016/17 and gradually increase spending over time. The state has not met this threshold since the Constitution was adopted in 2014. Since then, healthcare spending has not exceeded 1.7 percent of GNP in most years.


The government allocated 1.51 percent of GNP to healthcare in the current fiscal year’s budget, half the constitutional minimum. 


Meanwhile, the government has

introduced

 a different method for calculating budget allocations that allows it to claim it is meeting the minimum spending threshold.

 


Rather than using its previous classification, which was based on the Health Ministry’s expenditure, the government now uses a “broader and more comprehensive” definition. Under this new definition, healthcare expenditure also encompasses spending by a number of off-budget economic authorities and companies as well as “any other entities providing healthcare services, such as police and military hospitals, Al-Azhar hospitals, the comprehensive health insurance system and its associated programs,” a Finance Ministry source previously told Mada Masr. Without publicly available data on these entities’ healthcare spending, it is impossible to verify whether they bring total annual healthcare spending to the constitutionally mandated minimum.


The same expansion of what constitutes annual “health spending” also allows the government to include the budgetary allocation for these entities’ debt repayments as investment in the sector, according to the same source.


The president

confessed

 three years ago that the state is not meeting the constitutional requirements, saying in a public address that “the required numbers aren’t available, folks.”

 His comment came days after the government’s assertion that it was meeting the required spending levels.


Aside from its commentary on expenditure, the government’s Egypt Forum 2026 also highlighted the Universal Health Insurance System, one of the leading presidential health initiatives.


Egypt’s Healthcare Authority head, Ahmed al-Sobky,

described

 the system as a comprehensive reform of Egypt’s healthcare sector, capping an “enormous leap forward” under Sisi, following earlier historic transformations under King Fouad I and former President Gamal Abdel Nasser.


Shortly before the forum, the government began promoting the second phase of the Universal Health Insurance System, launching a pilot phase in Minya Governorate. 


The first phase launch in the governorates of Port Said, Ismailia, Suez, South Sinai, Luxor and Aswan began in 2018 and was

completed

 in 2025.
